en: Table of Contents for Volume One, Part One of the *Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*:
Śākyamuni’s Initial Ground of Causality— His First Trace-Manifestation Purchasing Flowers to Make Offerings to the Buddha and Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven.
Gautama was born of the noble lineage of the holy King Śuddhodana; Queen Māyā conceived him in a dream and gave birth beneath a tree.
Upon his return from the garden to the city, seers divined his marks, a general amnesty was proclaimed, and merit was cultivated.
He was nurtured by his maternal aunt and visited celestial shrines. He frolicked in the gardens and practiced the arts of writing, arithmetic, and martial skills.
The Crown Prince undergoes the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), tours the agricultural laborers, competes in strength with the various kings,
accepts Yaśodharā as his consort, enjoys the pleasures of the five senses, is admonished by a voice from the sky, provides food for the King in accordance with a dream,
encounters an old man on the road, sees one lying sick on the road, beholds a corpse, meets a śramaṇa, and [Yaśodharā] experiences a dream in accordance with [the Prince's].
At the outset of his renunciation, he leaped over the city walls at midnight; with golden scissors he shaved his hair, and Chandaka took his leave to return home.
Upon Chandaka’s return to the palace, the King questioned him; the forest seers urged him to return to the palace, but he subdued the two sages.
For six years he practiced austerities, yet when his provisions were exhausted, the cowherd girl offered him milk-rice. He then bathed in the river of meditation.
Śakra offers robes at the Bodhimaṇḍa; devas and humans offer grass; the Nāga King praises him as he sits upon the Bodhi seat;
Māra has a dream; the Māra sons admonish their father; the Māra daughters display their charms; the Māra host engages in battle;
the Māra troops drag away the cauldrons; the Earth Goddess bears witness; and the Māra sons repent.
The Bodhisattva Subdues Māra and Attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, Volume One, Part Two:
The Devas Offer Praise and Congratulations; Contemplating the Great Dharma of the Avataṃsaka; Gazing upon the Bodhi Tree; Entering Samādhi in the Dragon Palace.
Sitting in meditation amidst the forest, the Four Heavenly Kings offered him alms bowls; two merchants presented him with food; Brahmā entreated him to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma;
he delivered Pūrṇa; a seer sought deliverance; the boatman repented his faults; those bound by greed were delivered;
he subdued the fire dragon; the swift current was severed; and he discarded the sacrificial vessels.
At the Bamboo Grove Monastery, he led his disciples to seek refuge with the Buddha; Kāśyapa requested a period of leave due to pregnancy;
the Buddha was slandered; the Buddha was invited back to the kingdom; he recognized his son and resolved doubts; he ordained his younger brother Nanda and Rāhula;
and Sudatta beheld the Buddha.
Volume One, Part Three: Spreading Gold to Purchase Land;
Yama’s Daughter Receiving Instruction; The Fisherman Seeking Deliverance; Moonlight Admonishing Her Father; Shenri and the Poisoned Meal;
The Buddha’s Transformation to Eliminate Distress; Subduing the Six Heretics; Attempting to Harm the Buddha with a Sword.
The Buddha rescued the Nirgranthas and first established the *sīmā* altar to proclaim the Dharma of the precepts;
his maternal aunt sought ordination, and he ordained the daughter of Bhadra; returning once more to his native land, he preached the Dharma for the king;
the Buddha left behind an image and ordained the Śākyas; he subdued the venomous dragon and transformed the courtesans; Ānanda requested milk.
Taming the Intoxicated Elephant; Drawing the Bow to Harm the Buddha; The Buddha’s Transformation of Lu Zhi;
The Poor Man Who Saw the Buddha; An Old Man Leaves the Home Life; A Ugly Woman Changes Her Appearance.
Part One of the Lower Scroll.
The Lady Pūrṇamanorathā; the Parrot who invited the Buddha; the Wicked Ox who attained liberation; the White Dog who barked at the Buddha;

taking a child from the midst of fire and seeing the Buddha, thereby giving rise to faith; attaining liberation through the wife; the Blind Boy who saw the Buddha; the Old Maid who attained liberation;
exhorting relatives to invite the Buddha; entrusting a child to serve the Buddha; and lending money to prepare food.
The Elder Beggar Meets the Buddha; The Buddha Speaks of Suffering; The Buddha Comes to Discourse on Joy; The Buddha Arrives at a Sacrifice to Heaven;
Meeting the Buddha; The Buddha Converts the Butcher; The Buddha Converts the Net-Fishing Man; The Buddha Converts the Hunter; The Buddha Transforms the Ugly Boy;
Saving and Delivering the Thief; Delivering the Dung-Remover; The Origin of the Gift of Food; Maudgalyāyana Saves His Mother.
The Buddha Saves the Infant; Vajra Invokes the Mother of Ghosts to Seek Her Child; Bestowing Earth, Willow Branches, and Pure Water;
Plucking Flowers to Offer to the Buddha; Lighting Lamps That Never Extinguish; Hoisting Banners Above to Make Offerings to the Buddha;
Receiving Prophecy upon Bestowing Robes; Saving the Dragon from Calamity; Reciting Mantras to Eliminate Disasters; Testifying to the Efficacy of Reciting Mantras.
Preaching the Dharma in the Dragon Palace where devas and nāgas gathered like clouds; the Buddha praising Kṣitigarbha; Śrīprabha inquiring about the Dharma;
Vimalakīrti manifesting illness; Mañjuśrī visiting him in his sickness; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* for repentance; the preaching of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;
the three contemplations of the *Awakening of Faith*; the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; the true emptiness of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; and the entrustment to the kings.
The Lotus Sutra, the Wondrous Scripture: King Bimbisāra Falls Ill, Part Two of the Lower Volume;
The Buddha Returns to Pay His Respects to His Father and Conducts the Funeral for the King; The Buddha Saves the Śākya Clan and Preaches the Dharma for His Mother.
The initial creation of images; the bathing of the Buddha’s image; the姨母 (Auntie Mahāprajāpatī) requesting the Buddha’s entry into *nirvāṇa*;
the Buddha pointing his finger to move the stone; the entrustment of the distribution of the *śarīra* relics; the entrustment to the devas and the entrustment to the *nāga* kings;
the request for the Buddha to remain in the world; the weeping of the devas and *nāgas*; the Māra King reciting incantations; and the final offering of Cunda.
The Buddha’s crossing over of Subhadra, the manifestation of Vajra-Tathāgata, the prophecy, the final instructions,
the bequeathed teachings for the time of death, the rules for cremation, the methods for constructing stupas, the return to the ultimate source,
and the entry into parinirvāṇa at the twin śāla trees.

Volume Lower, Part Three: Vajra’s Lamentation for the Buddha-Mother; Receiving the Dream of Ascending to Heaven as a Reward for the Buddha-Mother; The Buddha-Mother Scattering Flowers; The Buddha Rising from the Coffin;
The Golden Coffin Remaining Immovable; The Golden Coffin Raising Itself Up; The Buddha Manifesting His Two Feet.
When ordinary fire does not burn, the Sage-fire burns itself; the *śarīra* relics were distributed equally and the Dharma-treasury was compiled.
King Aśoka erected stūpas, and King Aśoka obtained the jewel; Kāśyapa transmitted the Dharma, and Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption while Śaṇakavāsin received the Dharma.
Kumāralāta performed the counting of tally-sticks, and Nāgārjuna held the banner; Aśvaghoṣa’s arguments were exhausted [in defeat].

The Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Nāgārjuna in Composing Treatises, Āryadeva in Piercing His Eyes, Vasubandhu in Composing Treatises, the Divine Monks and Arhats, the Ten Great Vidyārājas, the Transformation of the Various Deva Teachers, Siṃha in Transmitting the Dharma, and the Western Arrival of Bodhidharma;
the Catalogue of the Records of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. (End)
Record of the Manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
Volume One (Part 1) Compiled by the Śramaṇa Baocheng of Baoen Temple The Descent of Śākyamuni’s Trace of Activity
"Śākyamuni" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the language of China, it means "The Capable One" (Nénrén). He is the surname of the transformation Buddha within the Sahā world.
Regarding his "manifestation of traces": Bodhi is the ultimate state. His spirit is wondrously quiescent and pervasive; his perfect wisdom is profoundly illuminating.
His Way transcends the boundaries of form and consciousness, while his principle reveals the realm of birth and extinction. Thus, after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni first attained Buddhahood...
With great compassion benefiting all beings, [the Buddha] manifests a beginning and an end.

When a sage appears in the world for the benefit of others, there must necessarily exist the subtle mystery of descending from the fundamental to manifest traces, and opening up those traces to reveal the fundamental. Now, the "fundamental" refers to the Dharma-body;
the "traces" refer to the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]. From the Dharma-body, the eight phases descend; through the eight phases, the Dharma-body is revealed.

The fundamental and the manifested are mutually integrated; both are inconceivable. How could it be that he was truly born in a royal palace? How could it be that he truly passed away at the twin śāla trees?

It is only out of compassion for the masses who are lost in long-term slumber that he returns to the Great Enlightenment; when the conditions arise, he manifests this transformation. When the resonance reaches him, he must respond.
If he were to respond without being born, who could awaken to the mundane world? If he were to transform without a name, how could he guide the age? For this reason, he established [the teaching].
He is titled Śākyamuni; his lineage is the Kṣatriya. By nature he is the most honored within the realm, and by excellence he is the crown jewel of both humans and devas.

Thereafter, casting off his royal sandals as the Crown Prince, he truly contemplated beneath the Bodhi tree. He relinquished the golden wheel to govern the great trichiliocosm, and with the brilliance of his white tuft of hair, he brought the Dharma-realm under his command.

Now, based on the Tathāgata’s causal practices, I shall cite sūtras and śāstras to describe the source of his sanctity, thereby clarifying the Dharma-King’s transformation throughout his single lifetime.
This is the meaning of the beginning and end of the ritual; it is by means of this that he manifests traces to deliver sentient beings.

As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha as a Wheel-Turning King) states: "I recall that in the past, when I was a wheel-turning king, I encountered thirty billion Buddhas. Thus it is the same.
He was named Śākyamuni Tathāgata; he encountered eight hundred million Buddhas. He was named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata; he encountered three hundred million Buddhas.
He was named Puṣya Tathāgata; he encountered ninety thousand Buddhas. He was named Kāśyapa Tathāgata; he encountered sixty thousand Buddhas.
He was named Pradīparāja Tathāgata; he once made offerings to eighteen thousand Buddhas. Furthermore, there were ten thousand Buddhas named...
There were ten thousand five hundred Buddhas named Tathāgata Able to Cross to the Other Shore;
two thousand Buddhas named Tathāgata Kauṇḍinya; six thousand Buddhas named Tathāgata Nāga; one thousand Buddhas named Tathāgata Purple Banner;
five hundred Buddhas named Tathāgata Lotus Superior; and sixty-four Buddhas named Śaṅkha.
There was a Tathāgata named Keśin. There was another Buddha named Samyakcaryā Tathāgata. Furthermore, there were eight thousand koṭis of pratyekabuddhas.
There was one Buddha named Kalyāṇamitra Tathāgata, and another Buddha named Upadeśaketu Tathāgata. In the land of those Buddhas, I was a wheel-turning monarch named Drumila.
There, I first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, and practiced with diligent effort day and night.

He made a vast vow, saying: "In the future, when I have attained Buddhahood, may there be sentient beings who are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas, ignorant of the distinctions between kin and strangers or the hierarchy of high and low within the family, and who do not believe in the causes and conditions of the three periods of time or the fruits of karma."
He practiced only greed, hatred, and delusion, and was fully possessed of the ten non-virtuous actions.

Out of compassion for those sentient beings, he taught the Dharma and transformed them, bringing great benefit. He rescued and protected sentient beings, delivering them through loving-kindness and compassion so that they might be freed from all suffering.
Later, he made offerings to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, who prophesied that he would become a Buddha.
The *Sutra on the Cause and Effect of Purchasing Flowers to Offer to the Buddha* states: "In the past, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a seer named Shanhui (Good Wisdom).

At that time, the crown prince of King Dengzhao was named Puguang (Universal Light). He requested his father’s permission to leave the household life and attain the path of Bodhi. Initially, Shanhui [was accompanied] by five hundred..."
The non-Buddhist teachers excelled in their doctrinal debates, and each offered them silver coins as a reward.

As he was parting from the non-Buddhists and heading toward the Buddha Dīpaṃkara to offer his alms, he saw the king’s servant carrying seven stalks of lotuses passing by. He asked, "Are these flowers for sale?
The servant replied, "They are to be sent to the royal palace; they are intended to be offered to the Buddha. Sumati then gave five hundred silver coins [to purchase them].
He purchased five stalks of flowers to offer to the Buddha. His servant, dressed in blue, followed his command and presented two of the flowers to the Buddha on his behalf.

At that time, the King and his ministers prostrated before the Buddha and scattered flowers, but all their flowers fell to the ground. The five flowers of Sudhana, however, all remained suspended in mid-air and transformed into a flower pedestal.
When he subsequently scattered the remaining two flowers, they stayed at either side of the Buddha. The Buddha praised Sudhana, saying, "You shall surpass the Arhats..."

After incalculable *kalpas*, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Śākyamuni. When Shanhui saw that the ground was muddy and wet, he immediately removed his deer-skin garment to spread it upon the earth and untied his hair to cover it, waiting for the Buddha to pass over. The Buddha then bestowed this prediction upon him:
"You shall later become a Buddha; you shall deliver all devas and humans in the world of the five turbidities.

At that time, Suprajñāta sought to leave the household life to become a monk. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! His hair and beard were shaved off, he donned the kāṣāya robes, and immediately became a śramaṇa.
He then joined his palms and praised the Buddha with a verse: "Now I behold the Guide of the World, who has caused me to open the eye of wisdom. For my sake, you have preached the pure [Dharma]."
The Dharma is free from all attachments; now that I have encountered the Honored One among gods and humans, I have attained the state of non-arising.
May I obtain the fruit in the future just as the Honored One among bipeds has.

Regarding his rebirth above in Tuṣita, the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having upheld the prohibitive precepts under Kāśyapa Buddha and maintained pure brahma-conduct, after the end of his life, was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven with right mindfulness. Thus, as for his first...
Bodhisattvas who are born in the stage of being destined for Buddhahood are mostly reborn in this heaven. Their wisdom is perfected, and their hearts are filled with joy.
The gods in the lower heavens are often given to negligence, while the gods in the higher realms possess great power of meditative concentration;

however, their tranquility is weak, and they do not seek rebirth below, but merely experience pleasure. It is not so for the Bodhisattva; he is born there solely for the sake of teaching and transforming the gods and humans of the celestial realms.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, the multitude of devas and humans called him the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha.
Having been born in that heaven, the palaces of the devas were brilliantly illuminated and naturally adorned; furthermore, there were immeasurable objects of adornment.
Even when the Bodhisattva beheld the most excellent and sublime pleasures of the five desires, his mind was not deluded, and he never lost his right mindfulness or original nature.
As for the conditions: he dwelt in Tuṣita Heaven for a full four thousand years, manifesting the characteristics of phenomena to those devas and causing them to develop world-weariness.
The Bodhisattva then used his divine eye to observe from afar the lower realm, seeing that the sentient beings among humans were creating all manner of evil karmas.

Oppressed by the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, there is no time of liberation. Desiring to be born among humans to rescue all sentient beings from their various sufferings,
for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all beings, and desiring to teach and transform sentient beings by expounding various dharmas,
I shall now descend to be born among humans, leave the household life to study the Way, and attain Buddhahood.
[They shall attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, deliver all sentient beings,
extinguish all sufferings, and accomplish the unsurpassed Way.

Regarding the noble clan of Gautama, the *Śākyapraśasti* states: From King Samavartin at the beginning of the kalpa down to King Yima, the son of King Mahākuśa, the king abdicated the throne in favor of his younger brother and studied under a Brahmin.
He was given the surname Gautama, and he received these words: "You must depart from kingship."
His robes were like those I wear, and he had taken the surname Gautama. Having entered the deep mountains, his appearance and attire were so extraordinary that no one could recognize him.
He established a vihāra within a sugarcane grove. At that time, some bandits passing through the fields followed their tracks and captured the Young Gautama.
They impaled him with a wooden stake, shot arrows at him, and set him up as a target; blood flowed [from him].

The great seer Gautama saw this with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). He flew there by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). "What crime have my followers committed that such cruelty has been inflicted?
Take the blood from among the men and form it into lumps. He brought them back to his monastery; he placed the blood from the left into a vessel on the left, and likewise for the right.
Then the seer Gautama made this prayer of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*): "If this be sincere, may the devas..."
There was a sage who caused his blood to transform and become human. After ten months, that on the left became a male and that on the right became a female;
they were named Gautama, or alternatively Ikṣvāku. Reaching King Siṃhahanu, four crown princes were born:
first, Śuddhodana; second, Śuklodana; third, Droṇodana; and fourth, Amṛtodana. There are four clans distinguished in India.

The Kṣatriya royal caste, the Brāhmaṇa pure-conduct caste, the Vaiśya merchant caste, and the Śūdra butcher caste—the former two being noble lineages and the latter two being lowly lineages—arise according to what is esteemed at any given time. The Buddha was born among them;

Śākyamuni appeared in an age of fierce strength, relying upon the royal lineage to manifest his majesty. His distant ancestor, King Śuddhodana, renounced the kingdom to practice the path. He... [received].
The Gautama clan was a noble lineage for generations. According to the *Ciyinyuan jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Holy King Śuddhodana):
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprabuddha’s meritorious practices were perfected, and his rank had reached the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). He resided in..."
He was born as one destined for the place of succession (ekajātipratibaddha), drawing near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Born in the Tuṣita Heaven, he was named Ārya-Sudhīmat.

For the sake of the various celestial lords, he expounded the practice of one destined for the place of succession. He also manifested various bodies in the lands of the ten directions, preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs.
As the time for his destiny to be fulfilled drew near, he was about to descend to become a Buddha, manifesting five kinds of auspicious omens. The first was the emission of...
1. A great radiance. 2. The great earth shakes in eighteen ways. 3. The palaces of Māra are obscured. 4. The sun and moon lose their light. 5.
The devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all tremble. Furthermore, one contemplates five matters:
first, one contemplates that the conditions of sentient beings have ripened; second, one contemplates that the time has arrived; third, one contemplates which among all lands is the most [suitable].
"Excellent. Fourth, he observes which of the various clans is most noble. Fifth, he observes the past causes and conditions to see who is most authentic and fit to be his father and mother.
He then reflects to himself: 'In the kingdom of Magadha, although the mother is authentic, the father is not true.
The kingdom of Vatsa is subject to the authority of others. The kingdom of Vaiśālī is prone to much strife. As for the kingdom of Bhadraśilā...'"
All movements are delusive. One should not be born in other countries or borderlands;

rather, one should be born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu within this trichiliocosm, specifically here in Jambudvīpa, which occupies the very center. Among all clans and lineages, the Kṣatriya is foremost;
he is of the Gautama lineage, a descendant of the noble kings. King Śuddhodana is preeminent among all those in the world.
His feet are pure; his nature and conduct are benevolent and virtuous; he is intelligent and wise; he is a true husband and wife; they are fit to be parents.
He shall thus be born into that royal lineage.
The *Māyādevī-prasūti-hetu-phala-sūtra* states: At that time, when the Bodhisattva Śubhamati descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb,
Queen Māyā, at the transition between sleep and waking, saw the Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant, soaring through the air.
He came and entered through my right side; his body appeared on the outside as if within lapis lazuli. My body felt peaceful and joyful, as if I had consumed ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Looking back at myself, I was like the sun or moon shining. Having seen this sign, I awoke with a clear realization and went to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"In the interval between sleep and waking, I saw a dream of the Bodhisattva riding upon a six-tusked elephant."

"A white elephant has entered my right side. What kind of omen is this? At that time, the King immediately summoned a Brahmin skilled in physiognomy and asked him to explain whether the Queen’s dream portended misfortune or good fortune. The Brahmin performed his divination and said: "The Queen will certainly conceive a prince.
This is an auspicious and wondrous sign; it cannot be described in full detail. Now, for the sake of the King, I shall speak of it briefly. Thus he spoke to the King.
People will surely cherish this holy son; he will certainly bring glory and distinction to the Śākya clan.

At the time of his descent into the womb, he emitted a great radiance, while the gods, Śakra, and Brahmā attended upon him and surrounded him. These signs must be the auspicious omens of Perfect Enlightenment.

If he does not leave the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King who rules over the four continents, with the seven treasures appearing spontaneously and a full thousand sons at his command. At that time, Queen Māyā—
Ever since this person was in the womb of the Bodhisattva, they have daily cultivated the meritorious practices of the six pāramitās with diligence.
Heavenly food and drink arrived spontaneously; they no longer took pleasure in the flavors of the human world.
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all those suffering from illness were completely healed. The various grains and crops naturally became abundant.
The harvest was bountiful, and the kingdom was in great peace and happiness.
The *Sūtra on the Original Acts of Birth Under the Tree* states: When the noble mother Māyā was nearly ten months pregnant and about to give birth, she led forth all...
The court ladies strolled through the Lumbinī Garden, a site of great auspiciousness, walking with composed and slow steps as they gazed about in every direction.
Within the garden stood a great tree named Pāṭala, its branches supple and drooping low. The Lady then raised her right hand and grasped a branch of that tree;
immediately, the Prince was born, emitting a great radiance that instantly pervaded all the heavens and the world.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wrapped his own exquisite and fine Kāśika cloth around his hands to receive the Prince.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings held the Prince in their arms before his mother. Without anyone supporting him, he immediately walked seven paces in each of the four directions.
As he lifted his feet, great lotus flowers emerged; he gazed toward the four quarters and spoke these words himself: "Heaven..."
Above the heavens and below, I alone am supreme. All the devas and humans of the world pay him homage and offer worship.
Suddenly, from the earth, two ponds naturally emerge—one cold and one warm—filled with pure fragrant water.
Furthermore, nine dragons from the void spout water to bathe the Prince’s body. The devas play music and rain down exquisite incense and flowers as an offering to the Prince. Ten.
At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways, and all sentient beings experienced supreme bliss.

This occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhou Zhao’s reign, the year of Jiayin. On this day, the rivers overflowed, and the mountains, rivers, palaces, and halls trembled.
A light of five colors pierced through the Taiwei Palace. The King questioned his ministers and the Grand Astrologer Suyou.

The奏 (memorial) stated: "A sage has been born in the West; a thousand years hence, his teachings shall arrive here. The King ordered that this be engraved upon stone and buried at the southern outskirts to mark it.
According to the *Benxing jing* (Sutra on the Past Deeds), as he was returning from the garden to the city, a high minister stood outside the Lumbinī Garden and saw a woman emerge in haste.
Overjoyed and leaping for joy, he reported upon seeing her: "The Queen Mother has given birth to a prince; you now..."
"You may now return to the Great King and report this joyful news. The minister, having prepared the horse, traveled as swiftly as the wind and arrived before the King.
First, he beat the drum of joy. King Śuddhodana was seated upon the jeweled palace, with ministers and officials administering the affairs of state.
Suddenly hearing the sound of the drum of joy, the King asked in alarm. The minister replied, "Great King, sir—"
The Prince born into this world was like a celestial being; his body was the color of gold and he emitted a great radiance.

Upon hearing these words, the King immediately went to the garden to see the Prince. Having arrived at the garden, he said to the Queen, "One should perform auspicious rites for the place where the Prince dwells;
I wish to behold the Prince face-to-face. At that time, there was a woman holding [the infant].
Holding the Prince, they proceeded toward the King’s residence. At that time, King Śuddhodana reflected within his mind:
"What kind of palanquin shall the Prince use upon entering the city? Then the celestial Viśvakarman manifested a palanquin made of the seven precious jewels.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings each transformed their bodies, all appearing as youths with conch-shell topknots, handsome and pleasing to behold; they personally bore the Prince’s precious palanquin.
They proceeded by palanquin. At that time, King Śuddhodana ordered the young boys to dress in yellow robes;
with their left hands holding golden vases and their right hands grasping jeweled staffs, they escorted the Prince, walking in attendance before him.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable celestial maidens, each holding various divine incense burners made of diverse jewels, burning all kinds of subtle and wondrous incense as an offering to the Prince.
The son led the way as they proceeded.
The *Siddhārthacarita-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately summoned the physiognomists to observe and divine the auspiciousness or misfortune of the Prince."
The physiognomists and others gazed intently at the Prince’s physical form and, each according to the treatises of the ancient sages, replied:
"This Prince possesses great and magnificent virtue; having now been born into a royal family, his body bears the thirty-two marks.
Within this world, there are two possibilities for him: if he remains at home and enjoys worldly pleasures, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin)."

He was fully endowed with the seven treasures. If he were to renounce his royal throne and leave home to study the Way, he would attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame would spread far and wide, filling the world.
Furthermore, the seer Asita came to King Śuddhodana’s palace seeking an audience with the Prince.
Out of great compassion, the Great King wished to show him [the child], so the Queen took the Prince in her arms and presented him to the seer.
The ṛṣi took the prince in both hands, placed him upon his head, and then set him upon his knees. He then addressed the king, saying: "This prince now has a body of golden hue;
his head is rounded and his nose is straight; his feet are full and his arms are long, like a golden statue.
He is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics. He will certainly leave the household life to study the Way and attain the state of an Arhat."

Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. You shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, and you will be able to proclaim the True Dharma among all devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; those who hear this Dharma shall all attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, the rishi reflected: "Now a Buddha shall appear in the world;
I lament that in my old age I have failed to encounter the Tathāgata, remaining forever in the long night of ignorance and constantly deluded regarding the True Dharma.
Thereupon, weeping with grief and distress, sobbing and choking with emotion, he departed through the air.

The *Mahāvaipulya-buddhacarita-samgraha-sūtra* states: At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed his ministers, saying, "O you ministers, for the sake of my crown prince, I shall grant a general amnesty;
all prisoners confined within the kingdom shall be released and set free."
He was released; even all the birds and beasts were likewise set free. He then addressed the state preceptor, the Brahmin, saying:
"If you know of any place where diligent Brahmins, whether numbering a hundred or a thousand, have gathered..."

"Whatever they require, provide it all as alms. Have all the celestial temples and shrines repaired and maintained, and perform sacrifices according to the Dharma for the sake of my crown prince, so that he may obtain great merit.
At that time, the state preceptor and the brahmins, following the king’s command, summoned thirty-two thousand brahmins from the four quarters and had them enter daily.
In the palace of King Śuddhodana, all possessions were offered as alms for a full seven days and nights.

All resulting merit was dedicated to the Prince, with the wish that his virtues might increase. He then spoke these verses: "King Śuddhodana’s heart was filled with great joy because he had given birth to a son of such merit.
All the ministers gathered together, and throughout the land, all prisoners were released by his grace."
Since the birth and upbringing were already in accordance with his original intention, he wished to perform a rite for the sake of their longevity.
He took hundreds of thousands of milch cows and calves, all with horns gilded in gold and hooves adorned with silver; they were all mature in age, their coats brilliant, each followed by its calf.
Their bodies were full and fleshy, yielding much milk; from each head, ten *śoṇas* could be obtained with a single milking. Furthermore, there were immeasurable numbers...
Various rare treasures, money, grain, silk, and all manner of miscellaneous goods were bestowed upon those brahmins for the sake of increasing the prince’s merit;
thus was he nurtured by his maternal aunt.

The *Sūtra of the Original Deeds* (*Lalitavistara-sūtra*) states: At that time, when seven full days had passed since the Prince’s birth, Lady Māyā’s body became emaciated, and she subsequently passed away. She was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Remaining in that heaven, she thought longingly of the Prince, surrounded on all sides by her celestial maidens, each holding exquisite heavenly incense and flowers, [emerging] from the void...
Gopā descended from the sky to where the Prince was, scattering flowers everywhere as she gradually approached the royal palace.
She spoke to King Śuddhodana, saying, "In the past, when I was pregnant, I experienced joy for the full ten months; now that I have been born in the heavens, I again experience joy.
I pray that you do not give rise to great sorrow and suffering on my account. Having said this, she immediately vanished from sight and returned to that celestial realm.
In the palace, King Śuddhodana then entrusted the Prince to his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī, saying:
"You are the Prince’s maternal aunt; you should nourish him. You must protect him well and cause him to grow. Bathe him with milk at the proper times.
Furthermore, he selected thirty-two other women to assist in his upbringing: eight to hold him, eight...

He was bathed; eight women were made to suckle him; eight women were made to play with him. At that time, his maternal aunt respectfully followed the king’s command and did not dare to deviate from it.
The aunt nurtured the prince just as the sun and moon grow from the first day to the fifteenth day until they are pure and full;
the nurturing of the prince was likewise so. Furthermore, it was like the *nyagrodha* tree.
Having obtained excellent ground, it gradually grew and later became a great tree. From the time the Crown Prince was born,
all the wealth, gold, silver, precious gems, cattle, sheep, elephants, and horses within the house of King Śuddhodana increased day by day,
never lacking anything.

The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* (Great Adornment Sūtra) states: After the Bodhisattva was born, his Śākya kinsmen went to King Śuddhodana and said, "Great King, you should now take the Prince to visit the temple of the gods to pray for ultimate auspiciousness. The King immediately granted their request.
King Śuddhodana said to Mahāprajāpatī, "I wish to take the Prince to the celestial temple.
He then commanded the palace attendants that they must all prepare themselves with adornments and decorate the Prince with various precious garments.
At that time, King Śuddhodana personally took the Prince in a carriage and set forth, accompanied by the ministers and the Śākya kinsmen who escorted him from front and rear. They burned...
Incense wafted and flowers filled the streets and roads. Elephant-mounted, horse-mounted, and chariot-mounted troops in infinite numbers held aloft banners and canopies.
Countless courtesans followed in procession, playing drums and music and singing and dancing. From the midst of the void, immeasurable devas scattered various celestial flowers.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, with dignified and solemn deportment, proceeded to the temple of the gods. Having arrived at the temple, the King—

He personally took the Prince and entered the celestial temple. As his feet crossed the threshold, all the images of the devas rose from their seats to welcome the Prince and stood before him with bodies bowed in reverence.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of devas within the assembly were filled with great joy, and the city of Kapilavastu shook in six ways; the images of the devas each manifested their original forms.
He spoke in verse: "Noble son, you are like the sun and moon, and also like the vast ocean; you are equal to Mount Sumeru. It is not fitting that you should pay homage to me.
Those who possess merit, wisdom, and majestic power, and those who prostrate, obtain great benefit. If a person abandons arrogance, they will be reborn in heaven and realize nirvana.
When the Prince manifested his entry into the celestial temple, immeasurable devas and people resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[He] aroused the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The *Pūrvayoga-sūtra on Sporting in the Gardens* states: "At that time, King Śuddhodana fashioned for the Prince various jeweled necklaces and exquisite flower garlands."
The Prince was adorned with a jeweled crown and a jeweled girdle. Then Mahāprajāpatī took the Prince in her arms, placed him upon her lap, and sat within a precious palanquin.

Countless boys and girls, all their bodies decorated with various jeweled necklaces and ornaments, held various flowers in their hands and led the way before the Prince as he proceeded toward the garden. At that time, Śākya...
Various kinsmen—both boys and girls—each holding deer-carts and sheep-carts, as well as various boats and vessels;
various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and harps; oxen, sheep, lions, elephants, and all manner of bird-shaped figures, along with every kind of weapon, were arrayed before the Prince.
They were allowed to play and sport at will. Furthermore, a ram was provided with a saddle made of pure gold, and the Prince was invited to mount it and proceed to the garden.
He played within [the palace]. Those youths also mounted goat-carts to accompany the Prince in his play.
The boys and girls each laughed with joy; everyone clapped their hands, sang, danced, and shouted. Some gathered sand to build stupas, scattering flowers and prostrating themselves.
They allowed the Prince to indulge in his play as he pleased. Thus he enjoyed himself for eight full years, and the Prince grew.
His wisdom grew. Unlike worldly infants who discharge impurities through weeping, he had no excrement or filth;
nor did he wail, groan, or contort his face. He felt neither hunger nor thirst, and the nurses who raised him were always filled with joy.
At that time, there was a deva within that garden named Vimalā. This deva remained in the sky, concealing half of her body.

Māyādevī then took various celestial flowers and scattered them over the crown of the Prince’s head. Her maternal aunt then took the Prince in her arms, seated him upon a precious chariot, and returned to her own palace.

Regarding the study of writing and arithmetic, the *Biexing jing* (Sutra on the Different Practices) states: King Śuddhodana, knowing that the Crown Prince was already eight years of age, addressed his ministers:
"You should know that you must seek throughout the kingdom for one who is foremost in wisdom and capable of serving as the Crown Prince’s tutor to instruct him."
When they were reading books and other various treatises, everyone remarked that Viśvāmitra was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras and capable of instructing the crown prince;
the young sons of the Śākya clan also followed the prince to study. Just as the prince was about to ascend to the lecture hall,
Viśvāmitra saw the Crown Prince from afar and rose to prostrate himself before him, feeling a sense of shame within.
He beheld the various heavenly kings and deities in the air protecting the Prince and scattering celestial flowers upon him.
As the Prince had just begun his studies, he asked his teacher, "Teach me the Brāhmī script and the Ṛṣi script; if there are any such scripts as these—"
"There are sixty-four kinds. I do not yet know which script my venerable teacher has taught me.
At that time, Viśvāmitra asked the Prince for the name of this script; he then felt private shame and, having subdued his arrogant pride, spoke a verse before the Prince:
"O rare one, person of pure wisdom, who so skillfully accords with all the worlds!"
Regarding the intermediate arts: you have already mastered all treatises and yet come again to enter my school.
Such writings as I do not know, you now recite and uphold them all. You are one spoken of as a great and honored being among gods and men;
yet now you wish to seek a teacher once more. At that time, the Śākya youths entered the school together to read and write, and the Prince—
By the power of his majesty and virtue, and further through the protective empowerment of various devas, all the Śākya youths attained mastery in writing,
arithmetic, scriptures, and treatises,
as well as in the exposition of martial arts.

The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states: At that time, King Śuddhodana again assembled his ministers and said, "O ministers, who among you knows where there is a teacher most skilled in martial arts who is capable of instructing the Crown Prince?
They replied, "Kṣāntideva is capable of teaching the Crown Prince the methods of military arts;
he has mastered twenty-nine such disciplines and is thoroughly proficient in them all. The King then sent for him.
There was a park intended for recreation. Devadatta was about to lead the Prince into the park to instruct him in martial arts and skills;
however, upon seeing them, the Prince discarded them all, saying, "I already understand these; there is no need to learn them further. Devadatta then instructed the other Śākyas.
As for the Prince, why would he need instruction in any of these various skills? Furthermore, [Devadatta] wished to train him in the arts of kingship.

Essential arts include: astronomy, sacrificial rites, divination, archery, prognostication of past events, cryptic speech, knowledge of the cries of birds and beasts, mastery of phonology, the performance of various crafts, providing answers based on those crafts, incantations, and miscellaneous matters—these comprise more than ten categories.
All the ancient and primordial treatises on governance were taught to the Prince; likewise, he was instructed in the Śākya traditions concerning both himself and others.

Furthermore, regarding those various arts and all the treatises that worldly people study over many years and months—whether they achieve mastery or not—the Prince was able to master them all in a single moment, as were the other Śākyas, without the need for further practice or study.
He has attained complete mastery and possesses all sovereign powers. At that time, Deva spoke these verses for the Prince:
"In your youth, you studied with composure; without requiring great effort, you understood everything in an instant."
Having studied for only a few days and months, he surpassed those who had practiced for many years; the skills he acquired were all such that his accomplishments exceeded those of others.
Deva was filled with shame and, in turn, paid homage to the Prince.
The *Sūtra on the Past Causes and Effects of the Prince’s Consecration* states: At that time, King Śuddhodana assembled his ministers and deliberated together, saying, "The Prince is now grown;
he is fully endowed with wisdom, courage, and vigor. It is now appropriate that we [employ] the four..."

The waters of the great ocean were poured over the crown of the Prince’s head. Furthermore, an edict was issued to the other minor kings, commanding them all to assemble on the eighth day of the second month to perform the consecration of the Prince’s head.
When the eighth day of the second month arrived, all the other kings, as well as the rishis and brahmins, gathered like clouds.
Silken banners and canopies were suspended, incense was burned, flowers were scattered, and bells were struck.
Drums were beaten and various musical performances were staged. The waters of the four oceans were collected in vessels made of the seven precious gems;

the assembly of sages each took one upon their heads and presented it to the brahmin. In this manner, the process continued until it reached all the ministers, who each took one upon their heads and passed it on to the king.
Thereupon, the king immediately poured water over the crown of the prince’s head and bestowed upon him the seals of the seven precious gems. Furthermore, drums were struck...
The great drum resounded loudly as it proclaimed: "Now Śākyamuni Siddhārtha is established as the Crown Prince.
At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others in the void performed celestial music, praising him with one voice: "Excellent!"
When the Crown Prince was installed in Kapilavastu, eight other kings likewise installed their own crown princes on that same day.

The Crown Prince requested the King’s permission to go out for a stroll in the gardens; the King granted him leave. Accompanied by his ministers and attendants, he traveled through the fields and countryside.
Upon seeing the farmers at work, he conceived great compassion and immediately reflected upon transcending all sensual desires. The King—

Upon hearing these words, his heart was filled with anxiety and distress. Fearing that he might renounce the household life, he thought it best to arrange a marriage immediately to please him, and further increased the number of female entertainers to provide him with diversion.

Regarding the excursion to observe agricultural labor, the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states: At that time, the Prince had grown to maturity. He requested permission from his father, the King, and went together with the ministers to tour the villages.
There he observed those engaged in plowing, toiling in their labors; he saw the earth being turned by the plow, and insects emerging from the soil as it was turned.
Crows and birds sought to peck at him. Upon seeing this, the Prince gave rise to a heart of compassion and sighed with sorrow over the world’s such suffering.
He lamented that human life is unstable and brief; his anxieties and fears were immeasurable. As the days and months pass by, one cannot guarantee that the next breath will lead to the next life.
From the beginning to the end of existence for devas and humans, the sufferings of the three evil realms are beyond description, as are the cycles of birth and death within the five destinies.
The cycle of rebirth is boundless; submerged within it, one remains unaware, and its suffering is beyond comparison. Furthermore, he saw in the garden a Jambu tree with luxuriant branches and leaves.
Beneath that tree, he sat cross-legged, single-mindedly contemplating in meditative absorption and the correct reception of samādhi.
He was considered the foremost; five hundred celestial immortals flying through the void could not surpass him.
At that time, the various seers descended and stood upon the ground. Observing the Bodhisattva sitting in meditative concentration, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Then the sun shone and the trees bent down to cover the Bodhisattva’s body; all the trees bowed their branches toward the Bodhisattva. [The] ministers...

Having seen this, he went quickly to inform the king. When the king heard it, he proceeded to the foot of the tree and immediately beheld the Prince’s majestic power and auspicious splendor, which were sublime and immeasurable.
He then spoke these verses: "Like a fire upon a mountain peak, like the moon among the stars."
Manifesting his body beneath a tree in meditation, his majestic radiance shone everywhere without exception. At the moment of his birth, he sat in meditation by himself;
the divine light of his physical majesty was clear and penetrating, illuminating all things universally. By means of this, the devas and humans of the ten directions were brought to salvation.
Thereupon, he accompanied the Prince in a grand procession back to the palace.
Regarding the princes' contest of strength, the *Bodhisattvacaryānirdeśa-sūtra* states: King Śuddhodana, together with the great minister Sahadeva, exhorted the young Śākya youths.
"Among those skilled in martial arts, who is the most excellent? A steel drum was placed upon the arena.
Devadatta shot and pierced three drums; Nanda then shot and likewise pierced three drums. The official presented the bow, and the Prince tested the bow.
Because the strength of his bow was weak, he was ordered to take a fine bow from the inner treasury that had been used by the ancestral kings.
The Prince drew it back until it pressed against his chest and released an arrow; it pierced through seven iron drums and traveled ten *krośas*.
Furthermore, seven iron boars were set up separately; with a single arrow, the Prince pierced all seven, and the arrow entered the earth, forming a well.
The well is still commonly called Arrow Well by the people today. At that time, the various devas each took celestial flowers and scattered them before the Prince.
Śakra took the arrow up to heaven and erected a stūpa there to make offerings to it.

When King Śuddhodana saw that the Prince’s skills were in every way superior to those [of his rivals], he ordered a white elephant to be brought for the Prince to ride. Devadatta entered the city first.
Seeing this white elephant, he asked, "Where are you going? It replied, "I am intended for the Crown Prince’s mount. At that time, Devadatta’s pride was at its peak;
with his left hand he seized the trunk and with his right hand he struck its forehead. With a single blow, it fell to the ground and immediately died.
It blocked the city gate so that passage to and fro was impossible. Nanda arrived next; seeing the elephant blocking the road, he seized the elephant's trunk and pulled it.

Having departed from the city gate, the Prince saw it; he lifted the elephant with his left hand and caught it with his right, then hurled it through the air to a distance of one *krośa* outside the city.
When the elephant fell to the ground, it immediately formed a great pit. To this day, the people have handed down the tradition that this place is called "Elephant Pit."
The *Siddhārtha-bhāryā-upādāna-hetu-phala-sūtra* states: At that time, King Śuddhodana assembled his various ministers and deliberated together, saying, "The Crown Prince has now reached adulthood;
it is fitting that he should take a wife. The ministers replied, "There is a Śākya Brahmin named Mahā..."

“Nama,” she replied. “There is a girl named Yaśodharā, whose countenance is upright and beautiful, who is intelligent and wise, whose virtuous character surpasses that of others, and who is fully endowed with proper etiquette.
Possessing such qualities, she is worthy to be the Crown Prince’s consort. The King said, “If she is as you describe, then marry her.
The King returned to the inner palace and immediately commanded an experienced palace lady, “Go to Mahānāma.”
The householder wished to observe the girl’s appearance and her deportment and etiquette; he requested that she stay there for ten days.
Having received the king’s command, the woman went to the householder’s home to observe the girl and returned to report to the king, saying: "I have observed this girl’s countenance;
she is upright and beautiful, and in her majestic bearing and every movement, there is no one who can equal her. The king immediately dispatched a messenger to speak with Mahānāman.
The Elder Māṭhara said, "The Crown Prince has reached an age where he desires to take a consort; your daughter is virtuous and refined, and is well-suited for this undertaking.
At that time, the Elder replied to the messenger, "I respectfully accept your command.

The King immediately ordered his ministers to select an auspicious day and dispatched a carriage with full ceremonial rites to go and welcome her. Once she had arrived at the palace, the marriage rites for the Crown Prince were performed in their entirety.
He performed the rites. Furthermore, he added two more consorts: the first named Gopī and the second named Mṛgajā. Together with various court ladies, they provided entertainment for the Prince.
Because he had three consorts, he constructed palaces for the three seasons. At that time, the Prince was constantly with his consorts whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
yet he possessed no worldly intent. During the stillness of the night, he practiced only meditative contemplation, never [engaging in other activities].
The consort embodies the way of husband and wife.

Regarding the enjoyment of the five desires, the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states: "At that time, King Śuddhodana established three grades of palaces for the Prince, with three thousand court ladies."
The Crown Prince was attended by the maidens of the first palace during the first watch of the night, those of the second palace at midnight,
and those of the third palace during the last watch of the night. At that time, King Śuddhodana,
mindful of what the seer Asita had prophesied, provided various musical instruments by the thousands for each [palace] and maintained them constantly within the palace.
Day and night within, the Prince remained among his court ladies, enjoying every pleasure; there was no need for him to travel far beyond the palace walls.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, in order to increase the Prince’s various merits, established himself in ascetic practice.
Having severed all unwholesome and evil dharmas, they practiced every form of goodness, bestowed various gifts, performed manifold meritorious deeds, and fully engaged in ascetic practices;
dedicating these roots of virtue to the Prince for the sake of increasing his various merits.

"I pray that you do not renounce the household life. While the Prince remains within the palace of his father the King, let him alone possess the five desires, enjoying himself in leisure and play to his heart's content. Let ten full years pass without him ever renouncing the world.
King Śuddhodana then had a separate inner city constructed around the perimeter of the palace where the Prince resided, providing it with only a single gate and installing guards there.
It was triggered by a mechanical device; at the time of opening or closing, five hundred men had to support and guard it before it could be opened or shut.
The sound of the gate resounded for half a yojana. Inside and out, brave warriors were stationed to guard the palace, their bodies clad in armor as they protected the inner chambers.
Such was the strictness and severity that they feared the Prince might abandon the harem, scale the walls to leave home, and wander at will in pursuit of pleasure.
He no longer took pleasure in amusements.
As the *Sūtra on the Exhortation of Original Conduct by the Voice from Space* states: "At that time, there was a son of heaven in space named Kumbhakāra (Pot-Maker) who saw this Prince."

For ten years you have dwelt in the palace enjoying the pleasures of the five senses; do not allow yourself to become intoxicated by craving, nor to fall into delusion and abandon yourself to overflowing passion.
A hundred years pass in rapidity, yet time does not wait for anyone. Bodhisattva Rāhula, you must now exercise discernment;
you ought to renounce worldly life and leave the home early. If I do not first manifest signs of world-weariness for him, he will remain immersed in indulgence.
"He has not yet awakened to the mind of renunciation. I should now assist him in this matter. He then spoke these verses from mid-air: "Excellent, O worthy one!
While you are in the prime of your youth, you should quickly renounce the world to fulfill your vow. You ought to bring benefit to devas and humans;
those who indulge in the five desires find no satiety. It is difficult to abandon the drowning within the realms of the six sense objects. Only...
There is supramundane conduct and great wisdom that can bring about weary detachment from these five desires; therefore, O Benevolent One, you should now renounce them.

Sentient beings suffer greatly from the afflictions of defilement; you should act as a great physician for them, proclaiming the various wondrous medicines of the Dharma-king, and swiftly lead them to the shore of Nirvāṇa. Those obscured by the darkness of ignorance are caught within the nets of various views.
"Quickly kindle the great lamp of wisdom; let gods and humans swiftly obtain the pure eye.
After the deva in the sky had spoken this verse, his majestic power moved all beings to create the causes and conditions for exhortation.

Furthermore, by the power of the Prince’s roots of goodness and merit from past lives, the sounds produced by the maidens residing within the palace no longer accorded with the affairs of the five desires.
He transmitted only the sound of the subtle dharmas that sustain the realization of *nirvāṇa*, desiring to cause the prince to grow weary of and detach from the world,
so that his mind might give rise to awakening;
thus he appeared in the king's dream.

The *Sūtra on the Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states: At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra, desiring to inspire in the Prince the resolve for renunciation, used his supernormal powers to manifest seven kinds of dream-omens to King Śuddhodana during that very night. First, he dreamed that the banner of Śakra emerged from the eastern gate.
Second, he dreamed that the Prince mounted a great white elephant and departed through the southern gate of the city. Third, he dreamed that the Prince yoked [the elephant]...
1. He dreamed of a carriage drawn by four horses exiting through the western gate of the city. 2. He dreamed of a great wheel-city adorned with various jewels exiting through its northern gate.
3. He dreamed that the Prince was in the middle of the main street of the city, holding a mallet in his hand to strike a large drum.
4. He dreamed that the Prince sat atop a high tower scattering precious treasures; people from all four directions came and took the treasures away. 5. He dreamed of the city.
Outside, six men not far away raised their voices in great lamentation and rolled about upon the ground. The King had seen this omen in his dream; his heart was filled with great terror.
The next day, he summoned the dream-interpreters and recounted the dream as described above. They replied that they did not know its meaning, and the King fell into further sorrow.
At that time, the Deva Kumbhakāra manifested as a Brahmin and said, "I am well able to interpret dreams. The Great King summoned him in and spoke of the seven...

He saw seven kinds of dreams. The Brahmin said: "The first is an auspicious sign of the eldest prince’s renunciation; the second is the sign of his realization of the fruits [of the path]; the third is the sign of his attainment of the four fearlessnesses;

the fourth is the sign of his becoming a Buddha; the fifth is the sign of his turning the wheel of Dharma; the sixth is the sign of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the treasure of the Dharma;
and the seventh is the sign of the distress of the six heretical teachers. He then transformed himself into a king to explain these in detail.
Having finished speaking of the dream, he said, "Great King, you should give rise to joy; do not harbor fear, sorrow, or discontent.
Upon hearing this, the Great King further increased the prince's fivefold sensory pleasures, intending to make the prince so attached that he would take no pleasure in leaving the household life.
It relieves my anxieties and brings me peace and happiness.

As stated in the *Lùfénglǎrénběnxíngjīng* (The Sutra of the Elder Encountered on the Road): "At that time, the Devaputra Ghaṭīkāra wished to have the Prince go out toward the gardens to observe and enjoy them."

Through the perception of the pleasant and the unpleasant, he gave rise to a mind of weary detachment (*saṃvega*). He was gradually taught to abandon those five sensual desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), and the groves were praised as being most delightful.
Upon hearing this, the Prince resolved his mind and ordered that a fine carriage be quickly adorned and prepared for him to go and view and enjoy himself in those groves.
The charioteer reported this to King Śuddhodana, who issued a decree ordering that everything be swept clean and sprinkled with water. At that time...
The Crown Prince ascended his precious chariot and departed through the eastern gate of the city.

At that moment, the Devaputra Ghaṭīkāra manifested a transformation, appearing as a decrepit old man with a hunched back and bowed head, his beard and hair like snow, his four limbs trembling and his gait unsteady.
Relying solely on the strength of a staff, such was his appearance as he walked along the road before the Prince.
Upon seeing that old man’s body so extremely emaciated and marked by decay, the Prince immediately asked the charioteer, "What kind of person is this?
The charioteer replied to the Prince, "This is an old man. The Prince asked again, "What is meant by 'old'? The charioteer answered, "Generally speaking, it is called..."
"The old man is oppressed by various decrepitudes; his faculties gradually fail and he has no perception.
It may be morning or evening before his life comes to an end. The Prince asked again, "Must this body of mine also undergo such signs of old age?"
He replied, "Prince, although the noble and the lowly differ, all who have come into existence are subject to old age. Even now, the human body possesses these marks of aging;
they have simply not yet manifested. The Prince spoke again, "I shall not go to the gardens for recreation now.
You should quickly turn back the carriage and return to the palace, where I will reflect within my heart upon what expedient means might allow me to escape this."
He left the household life to study the Way upon seeing the signs of old age and decay.

Regarding his vision of one lying ill on the road, the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra of Past Deeds) states: "At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhaka again observed and reflected: 'The Bodhisattva is within that palace.'"
Attached to the five desires, they have long been dissolute and indulgent in their passions. The world is impermanent, and the prime of youth is easily lost;
you should therefore leave the palace early to renounce the world, so as to awaken them and cause them to quickly develop weary detachment.
Due to the causal conditions of the Bodhisattva’s past merits, he suddenly resolved to go out for a stroll. The Prince then summoned his charioteer and said, "Prepare a magnificent carriage."
The carriage departed the city for a pleasure excursion. The Prince mounted the carriage and exited through the southern gate, gradually proceeding toward the groves.
The Devaputra Kumbhakarṇa manifested as a sick man before the Prince’s path;
his body was emaciated, his complexion was jaundiced, his breathing was feeble, and his life hung by a thread. Having seen the sick man, the Prince asked the charioteer: "What is this?"
"Who is this person? The charioteer replied, "This is a sick man. He asked again, "What is meant by 'sick'? He answered, "This person is not at ease;
his vital energy is exhausted; he is gravely ill and lacks strength; the time of death is approaching and there is no place for him to turn for refuge.
This person will soon naturally reach the end of his life. To seek to live on would be impossible. He asked again:
"Is it only this person who is subject to this? He replied, "It is not only this person; all devas and humans alike have not yet escaped it.
The Prince said, "If this body of mine cannot escape this disease and is difficult to deliver from, then I shall no longer resort to the pleasure gardens for diversion.
I shall immediately rein in the chariot and return to the palace to sit in meditation, focusing my mind with single-minded concentration."
[The Buddha] reflected: "Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana will remember the words of the prophecy given by the seer Asita as being certain and true, and he will think:
'May the Prince not again abandon me to go forth into homelessness.'"

Regarding the sight of a corpse on the road, the *Sūtra of the Original Deeds* (*Bodhisattvapūrvacaryā-sūtra*) states: At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakarṇa again had this thought: "The Bodhisattva is enjoying himself to his heart's content within the palace.
I should now cause him to become weary of the five desires so that he may leave the household life early; let him depart from the palace toward that garden."
At that time, the Prince said to the charioteer, "You may quickly harness the precious carriage drawn by four horses;
I wish to go out of the city to the park for recreation. Seated in the carriage, the Prince departed through the western gate of the city and went toward the park to view the gardens and groves.
The Devaputra Kumbhakarṇa manifested as a corpse on the road before the Prince. When the Prince saw it, he asked:
His heart was filled with profound sorrow, and he said to his charioteer, "Whose body is this lying upon the road?
The charioteer replied, "This is called a corpse. The Prince asked the charioteer again, "What is a corpse?
The charioteer answered, "Prince, this person has already abandoned their worldly life; they possess no majesty or virtue and are now like wood or stone, having cast aside all kin."
All one's consciousness and knowledge depart; only the spirit alone proceeds toward the next world.
From this moment forth, one shall no longer see parents, brothers, wife, children, or kinsmen. Such relatives are separated by birth and death and shall never be seen again;
therefore, it is called a "corpse. He asked the charioteer again, "Do I also have this death? The charioteer replied, "Yes, Great [King]."

"Even though you honor this body, it cannot escape the law of death. Among all people in the world, regardless of noble or humble status, and without distinction between the wise and the foolish, none are exempt from death. Upon hearing this, the Prince was displeased in spirit;

he turned his carriage back to the palace, sat upright in contemplation, and remained silent with focused mindfulness. "Whether one is noble or humble, when the merit one has received is exhausted, impermanence arrives."
At that time, there was no difference at all.
The *Sūtra of the Great Adornment of the Śramaṇa* states: "At that time, the Prince addressed his charioteer, saying, 'Today I wish to go to the gardens for recreation.'"

"Play with him; you may prepare the carriage. The charioteer reported this to the King. The King said to the charioteer, "Previously, when the Prince went out through the three gates, he saw old age, sickness, and death, and was filled with sorrow and displeasure. Today, you should have him go out through the northern gate.

Decorate the roads with incense, flowers, banners, and canopies, making them twice as magnificent as before. Thereupon, the Prince, accompanied by his various officials and attendants leading and following him, departed from the city.
At the North Gate, at that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested as a bhikṣu, wearing dyed robes and with his hair and beard shaven.
Carrying a *khakkhara* staff, he walked with slow steps; his appearance was dignified and his deportment solemn. When the Prince saw him from afar, he asked who this person was.
Then, by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), the Śuddhāvāsa deva caused the charioteer to reply to the Prince as follows: "As..."
"This is what is called a renunciant. The Prince immediately alighted from his carriage, paid his respects, and asked him:
"What benefit does one gain by renouncing the world? The bhikṣu replied: "I see that for those living at home, birth, old age, sickness, and death are all impermanent;
they are all phenomena of decay and instability. Therefore, I have abandoned my kin and dwell in seclusion, applying myself with diligence..."
He sought expedient means to escape this suffering. That which I have cultivated is the untainted Noble Path; practicing the True Dharma, I have subdued my faculties.
Arousing great compassion, I am able to bestow fearlessness; my mind acts with equanimity as I protect and mindfully regard all sentient beings.
Unstained by the world, I have attained eternal liberation. Therefore, this is called the Dharma of renunciation. Having heard this, the Prince was deeply [moved].
He gave rise to joy, thinking: "Among gods and humans, this alone is supreme. I shall certainly practice and study this path.
Having seen this, he mounted his carriage and returned.
The *Yaśodharā-svapna-pūrvacaryā-sūtra* states: At that time, the Crown Prince’s consort Yaśodharā suddenly perceived that she was pregnant during that very night.
Then, while she was sleeping in extreme exhaustion, she saw twenty kinds of terrifying things in a dream. Suddenly—
Then, starting up in alarm, she reported to the Prince, saying: "I have dreamed that the great earth shook all around;
the banner of Śakra collapsed to the ground; all the stars in the heavens fell down; the largest parasol was carried away by Chandaka; my topknot was severed by a sword;
the jeweled ornaments of my body were swept away by water; and my physical form gradually..."
I became ugly; my hands and feet fell off naturally of their own accord. This body of mine suddenly became stark naked. The couch upon which I sat collapsed to the ground of its own accord.
The four legs of the bed on which I lay broke and snapped. The great mountain of various jewels crumbled and fell to the earth.
The great trees within the palace were blown down by the wind. The full, bright moon suddenly vanished. The crimson...
The sun’s radiance suddenly turned to darkness; fires erupted from the palace walls and courtyards, spreading toward the city gates.
The guardian deities of the city walls suddenly wept aloud. Kapilavastu was instantly transformed into a desolate wilderness; the flowers and fruits of the groves all withered and fell.
The armored guards ran about in every direction, reporting to the Prince: "I have seen twenty such evil dreams."
His heart was filled with great terror, alarm, and unease. He wondered, "Is my own life coming to an end?

Or is it that I must be separated from the Prince with whom I share such affection? Upon hearing these words, the Prince reflected within his mind, "I shall soon renounce the world and leave the household.
He then comforted Yaśodharā, saying, "Do not harbor grief because you have seen such a bad dream; you should simply..."
He was at peace and free from further afflictions.
The *Sūtra on the Adornment of the Initial Ordination* states: "In the stillness of the night, the Bodhisattva reflected thus: 'If I do not inform my father, the King, [and depart] in secret...'"
Since his renunciation, he has acted contrary to the teachings and not in accordance with worldly principles. Departing from his residence, he went to the palace of his father, the King.

Emitting a great radiance, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the King, saying, "I wish to renounce the world. Upon hearing these words, the King wept and would not grant permission.
He spoke again to his father, saying, "There are four kinds of wishes that must be severed before one may renounce the world: first, the wish for no aging; second..."
First, they are always youthful; second, they are always free from illness; third, they are always immortal. The king then declared, "This vow is extremely difficult.
Among both sages and worldly men, who can escape old age and death? The king summoned his kinsmen and spoke these words: "Last night the prince came to request permission to renounce the world.
If I grant him this, the kingdom will have no successor. By what means can we cause him to turn back from his resolve? All [the kinsmen]...
The kinsmen addressed him, saying, "We shall together protect the Crown Prince. By what power could he possibly leave the household by force?
The King commanded his relatives to station five hundred Śākya youths outside the eastern gate of the city—youths of heroic majesty, valorous and robust, invincible in battle.
Each youth was provided with five hundred chariots for combat as a formidable guard. Five...
Hundred-powerful warriors held halberds before him. At the southern, western, and northern gates, it was as described above.
Around the perimeter of that city, five hundred stalwart men were stationed; clad in armor and bearing spears, they patrolled day and night without a moment’s rest.
The Queen Mother Mahāprajāpatī gathered the court ladies within the royal palace and said: "From this very night onward, [no one shall...]"
Put him to sleep. Bar the windows and double the locks, firmly holding the keys; guard the Prince without negligence, lest he renounce the world and leave us all without a protector.
The *Rātrī-vyūha-sūtra* states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upright within the Hall of Music and reflected: "All Buddhas of the past have made four kinds of great vows.
First, they vowed: 'In the future, may I personally realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Regarding the self-nature of phenomena...'"
Having attained the status of Dharma King, one uses the wisdom of diligence to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the suffering and afflictions of the triple world’s bonds of craving.
Second, there are sentient beings enmeshed in this dense forest of the darkness of birth and death, afflicted by the cataracts of ignorance and folly;
using emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as a lamp and as medicine, one shatters all dark delusions and removes their heavy obstructions, thereby bringing them to fulfillment.

Regarding such gateways of skillful wisdom: third, there are sentient beings who erect the banner of arrogance, giving rise to notions of "I" and "mine," with inverted thoughts and views that lead to false attachments; for their sake, he preaches the True Dharma so that they may attain awakening and understanding.
Fourth, he perceives sentient beings dwelling in a state of non-quiescence, transmigrating through the three periods of time like a whirling firebrand or like a ball of thread unwinding.

Bound by their own fetters, I shall preach the Dharma to them so that they may attain liberation from those bonds. The Prince said to Chandaka, "Chandaka, you must harness Kanthaka and bring him here.
Chandaka replied, "It is only midnight; why do you need to harness the horse? The Prince spoke again, "I am now leaving the household life;
do not oppose my intent. Then the devas of the Pure Abodes caused all those soldiers and court ladies to fall into a deep slumber.

While everyone remained in sleep without any awareness, Chandaka finished harnessing the horse. Once the Prince had mounted, as he took his first step, the great earth shook in six ways, and they ascended into the sky and departed.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings supported the horse’s hooves with their maces, while Brahmā and Śakra escorted them along the path.
Upon reaching the forest of austerities where the ancient seer Bhārgava practiced, he immediately dismounted.
He sat with dignified composure.

Regarding the shaving of the hair with golden scissors, the *Zhuangyan jing* (Sutra on Adornment) states: "The Bodhisattva reflected thus: 'If one does not shave off the beard and hair, it is not the Dharma of renunciation.'"
He then took a golden razor and shaved his own hair, making this vow: "May I sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) as well as the obstacles of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-āvaraṇa*).
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately caught the hair in the air with a celestial robe and returned to the heavens to make offerings to it.
The Bodhisattva observed that he was still wearing jeweled garments upon his body and thought to himself: "The robes of one who has left the home life should not be like this."
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a hunter. Wearing a *kāṣāya* robe and holding a bow and arrows, he stood there in silence.
He said to the hunter, "What you are wearing is the very garment of the Buddhas of antiquity;
why, then, do you wear it for the sake of committing a transgression? The hunter replied, "I wear this robe to capture herds of deer. When the deer see this garment..."
"He will not avoid me; only then shall I be able to kill him. The Bodhisattva said, "You wear the *kāṣāya* robe solely for the purpose of killing.
If I am now to attain liberation, I must do so. I shall give you this *kauśeya* garment; you may give me your coarse and tattered clothing.
At that time, the hunter immediately removed his *kāṣāya* robe and handed it to the Bodhisattva. At that moment, a thought arose in the Bodhisattva's mind.

Rejoicing, he immediately gave him the *kauśeya* garment. At that moment, the Śuddhāvāsa deva, by means of his supernormal powers, suddenly manifested his original form, flew up into the void, and returned to the Brahma Heaven. Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva felt even greater reverence for the saffron robe.
Thereupon, as the Bodhisattva’s body was clad in the saffron robe and his appearance had been transformed, he spoke these words: "I now..."

This was truly called "leaving the household life. Thereupon, he proceeded with calm and steady steps to the forest of asceticism where the seer Bādarāyaṇa dwelt, seeking the Way with single-minded devotion.
Regarding the passage on Chanda’s departure and return from the *Zhuangyan jing* (Sutra on the Adornment): When the Prince had reached the mountain forest, he consoled Chanda, saying:

"Among the people of the world, there are some whose hearts follow [a path] while their bodies do not; others whose bodies follow [a path] while their hearts do not. Now, both your heart and your body..."
"Everyone follows me. When people in the world see those who are wealthy and noble, they vyingly come to serve them;
when they see those who are poor and lowly, they abandon and distance themselves from them. I have now renounced my kingdom and come here, and you alone were able to follow me.
Now that I have reached this secluded and open place, I shall immediately undress myself, take my ornaments, and return to the palace. He then offered [them].
The father king spoke thus to him: "The Prince now has no further desire for worldly dharmas;
he does not seek to be born in heaven to enjoy the five sensory pleasures, nor is he unfilial. He harbors no heart of anger, resentment, or malice.
Rather, seeing that sentient beings in the world are deluded regarding the correct path and submerged in birth and death, he seeks to uproot and rescue them."
"I am indeed leaving home. I only pray that my father, the King, will not harbor any anxiety.
If you think that I am too young to leave home, you should use my words as a pretext to petition him: 'Are birth, old age, sickness, and death ever subject to fixed timing?
