Though one may be in the prime of youth, who can escape them alone? Furthermore, take off all my other ornamental garments and say to Yaśodharā: 'A person..."
"Born into this world, one must inevitably face separation through worldly attachment. It is for the sake of severing all such sufferings that I have now left the home life to study the Path.
Do not give way to groundless grief out of lingering attachment. He then addressed the various court ladies within the palace and informed the young princes of the Śākya clan:
"I now wish to shatter the net of ignorance; therefore, I vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment. Once my task is accomplished, I shall return to you."
Seeing this, Chandaka wept in secret and turned back. According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*,
at that time Chandaka led the white horse and took with him the necklaces and various articles of adornment.
As he was about to enter the royal palace, the sound of the horse’s neighing was heard within the inner quarters.
Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and all the court ladies gathered together and said to one another, "Could it be that the Prince has returned to the palace?
After Chandaka had entered the palace gate, his maternal aunt, the Queen, and the court ladies saw only Chandaka.
They hid themselves so as not to see the Prince and wept together. They immediately asked, "Where is the Prince now?
Why have you returned alone? Chandaka replied, "The Prince has renounced the five desires in order to seek the Way;
he is currently in those mountain forests wearing dyed robes, having shaved off his hair and beard. Upon hearing this, the maternal aunt wailed aloud and rebuked Chandaka, saying, "I..."
"What wrong have I done to you now? You have taken my noble son and sent him to that mountain forest, where fierce beasts and venomous insects are most terrifying.
Now he dwells there alone; upon what shall he rely? Chandaka said, 'The Prince entrusted me with his white horse and various precious jewels, commanding me to return quickly.
Before I left, the Prince charged me: "When you reach the palace, pay homage to my maternal aunt and convey my earnest regards. "
He exhorted her, saying, "Do not give rise to grief; before long you shall behold me having attained perfect enlightenment, and we shall meet again.
Yaśodharā rebuked Chandaka, saying, "Why have you now brought harm upon me?
Chandaka replied, "It was solely through the supernatural power of the devas that those guarding him were all put into such a deep sleep that they remained unaware; thus the Prince departed."
The palace was like the sun rising in the heavens, emitting a great radiance; the various devas supported the horse’s hooves as it departed.
This was not a matter for Chandaka.
He questioned the forest seer.
The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states: At that time, the Prince arrived at the grove of the rishi Bhārgava. Birds and beasts gazed upon him with fixed eyes.
Seeing the Prince from afar, the rishi took him to be a celestial deity; together with his disciples, he welcomed the Prince and invited him to sit.
The Prince observed the conduct of the rishis: some wore soft grass, others wore tree leaves as clothing, and some ate grass.
They [worship] trees, flowers, and fruits; or they eat once every day, once every two days, or once every three days; or they serve fire and water;
or they revere the sun and moon; or they stand on one leg; or they lie upon dust, soil, thorns, and brambles; or they lie beside fire and water.
The Crown Prince asked them the reason for this. The rishis replied, "It is because we wish to be born in the heavens.
The Crown Prince told the rishis, "Though the heavens are pleasant, when one's merit is exhausted, one falls. Wandering through the six realms of existence ultimately results in a mass of suffering.
I now study the Way in order to sever the root of suffering. As the Crown Prince and the various rishis engaged in this discussion, back and forth in dialogue, it reached [this point].
At sunset, the Prince stayed there for one night. At dawn the next morning, he took his leave. There was a seer well-versed in the science of marks who said to the people:
"This noble person is now endowed with all the marks; he will certainly attain the knowledge of all modes and become a teacher of gods and humans.
The path we study is different, so I dare not detain him. If this noble person departs," [he continued].
"You may travel north. There is a great seer there named Ārāḍa Kālāma; you should go to him and engage in discussion with him.
However, from my observation, it seems you will likely not remain with his doctrine. Thereupon, the Prince immediately traveled north.
When the assembly of seers saw the Prince depart, they were filled with grief and distress; joining their palms, they saw him off as far as the eye could reach.
Only after he had ceased looking back did he return.

Regarding the exhortation to return to the palace, the *Nidāna-kathā* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states: At that time, King Śuddhodana dispatched the Prince’s preceptor and his ministers to the seer Bhārgava.
While in the forest of asceticism, the Teacher questioned a seer: "Has the Prince, who has left the household life to study the Way, ever come to this forest?
The Great Seer replied, "A youth entered into discussion with me and has now gone to the abode of the seer Ārāḍa Kālāma.
The Teacher took his leave and went immediately to that seer’s location; there he indeed saw the Prince. The Teacher then addressed the Prince, saying: "Great..."
The King has long known that the Prince deeply delights in leaving the household life; this intention is difficult to turn back.

Nevertheless, the King’s affection for the Prince is profound, and he entreats him to turn his carriage around and return to the palace, so as not to allow the Prince to completely abandon his spiritual practice.
He asks, "Why must a place of mental tranquility be among the mountains and forests? The Prince replied, "How could I not know that my father's affection is deep? It is only that I fear..."
"It is for the sake of severing the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death that I have come here.
I shall now cultivate the Path and shall never return. The Master reflected to himself: "I accepted the King's command and came to invite the Prince, yet I was unable to change the Prince's resolve.
I have been lingering by the roadside, unable to return on my own. They consulted with one another, saying: "Since we are the King's envoys, and yet [the mission has failed]..."
"Regarding our efforts, how can we now return empty-handed and offer a proper response?

We should leave behind these five men who followed us—those who are intelligent, wise, gentle of mind, and by nature loyal and upright—and have them secretly observe his movements and provide him with protection and service.
He said to Kauṇḍinya, "Can you five all remain here? The five replied:
"Excellent! We shall guard you closely according to your command. The master and his ministers took their leave of the Prince and returned, weeping with grief.
Regarding the subduing of the two sages, the *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states: When the Prince arrived at the abode of Ārāḍa, he asked: "What is the root of birth and death?"

"What must be abandoned? The seer replied: "By maintaining the precepts, practicing patience, and cultivating meditative concentration, one attains the first dhyāna with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).

By eliminating directed and sustained thought, one enters the second dhyāna born of concentration, characterized by joy (prīti). By relinquishing joy, one attains the third dhyāna, endowed with mindfulness and the faculty of bliss (sukhendriya).
By abandoning both suffering and bliss, one attains the fourth dhyāna, characterized by pure mindfulness and equanimity (upekṣendriya), and thus achieves the state of non-perception."
[The attendant] replied. The Prince asked again: "In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is there a self? Or is there no self?
If one says there is no self, one should not call it 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception. If one says there is a self, does that self possess cognition? Or is that self without cognition?
If the self were without cognition, it would be identical to grass and trees; if the self possessed cognition, it would involve grasping at objects. Since—
Where there is an object of clinging, there is defiled attachment; therefore, it is not liberation. You have exhausted the coarse fetters but do not realize that the subtle fetters still remain.
For this reason, you claim it is the ultimate state. However, as the subtle fetters grow, you will again undergo rebirth in the lower realms.
Because of these causes, you have not crossed to the other shore. If one can eliminate the self and the notion of a self, everything will be exhausted.
"Abandoning [them], this is what is called 'direct liberation'. The seer remained silent, reflecting within his own mind:
"What the Prince has spoken is truly subtle and profound. At that time, the Prince took his leave and departed in search of the supreme Dharma.
The seer said, "If you attain the Way, I pray that you will deliver me first. The Prince replied, "So be it. Next, he went to the place of Kālāma.
The place where he dwelt was likewise the site of debates and inquiries. The Prince then took his leave;
the Rishi escorted him until they were out of sight, after which he returned.
For six years, he practiced asceticism.
The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states: At that time, the Prince reflected thus: "For six years I have manifested the practice of great diligence and asceticism.
By means of this, I shall now manifest the four dhyānas and count the inhalations and exhalations, causing my mind to attain liberation through non-conceptualization and non-attention.
Free from all expectations, wherever my mind reaches, it shall have no dependence. I wish to manifest in the world in order to open and transform [sentient beings]."
He taught various categories of practices to those of external studies and instructed the devas, showing them their transgressions and blessings.

Those of external studies and heterodox arts calculate that death is a total severance and that the spirit is not reborn; some claim there is permanence, while others say there are no transgressions or blessings.

For their sake, he explained in detail the retribution for meritorious deeds, teaching that one’s body, speech, and mind should practice purity, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat daily for six years.
He practiced and established difficult and arduous deeds. He was free from the karmic debts of past lives. For six years, he sat in the full lotus posture;
his majestic deportment and movements were never lacking, nor did he ever have anything to cover himself. He did not avoid wind or rain, nor did he rise to perform walking meditation.
He neither bends nor stretches when attending to the necessities of nature; he does not lean or recline, but remains sitting upright throughout spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
Even when encountering various hardships, he never raises his hands to shield himself, and his sensory faculties remain undisturbed.

His eyes did not look askance, and his mind was free from fear. A magpie nested in a tree, brooding over its eggs and feeding its fledglings; though the bird’s droppings soiled his body, he did not cast it away.
The devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings beheld this with their own eyes, seeing how the Bodhisattva’s meritorious achievements and moral virtue were most majestic.
They came and went by his side to make offerings and serve him. The Prince sat in meditative concentration for six years, manifesting ascetic practices;

he taught and transformed devas and humans, establishing them in the Three Vehicles. For this reason, he sat for six years. Having realized the Unsurpassed Way, he extensively delivers all sentient beings.
Regarding the provisions for his journey, the *Sūtra on Cause and Effect* states: When the Prince reached the forest of asceticism at Mount Gayā, he sought the path of true and correct awakening.
He practiced austerities, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat per day. Kātyāyana and the others also practiced austerities to serve and attend upon the Prince.
Having seen this, he immediately dispatched one person back to inform the royal preceptor, detailing the deeds the Prince was performing.
The royal preceptor then went to the King and reported the matter as described above. When King Śuddhodana heard these words, his heart was greatly distressed and his entire body trembled;
he said to the royal preceptor: "The Prince has thus renounced the status of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin), and furthermore—"
Out of affection for his parents and kinsmen, he departed for the distant deep mountains to practice asceticism.
Now, unfortunate as I am, I have lost this son. Furthermore, based on what the messenger said, I related these matters to Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, along with his paternal aunt and Yaśodharā, each prepared five hundred chariots.
He instructed Chandaka to deliver the provisions for the journey to the Prince, providing them at all times so that he would never lack for anything.
Taking the carriage, Chandaka departed with great speed; upon reaching him, he saw the Prince’s form emaciated and wept aloud as he spoke.
"Great King, please remember the Prince. He has sent me to deliver these provisions as a gift for his journey.
The Prince replied, "I have left my parents and abandoned my kingdom to come far away to this place in search of the Ultimate Way.
How could I possibly accept these provisions again? Having heard this, Chandaka thought to himself, "Since the Prince now refuses to accept them, I shall..."
"Seek out another person to lead the supply wagons back to the King's presence. I shall remain here to attend upon the Prince, never leaving his side.
[She then prepared] the milk-rice of the cowherd woman.
The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states: At that time, the Great Sage thought to himself, "I have now been manifesting the practice of asceticism on Mount Gayā.
Eating but one sesame seed and one grain of barley per day, my body has become emaciated like a withered tree.
I have completed six full years of practicing these austerities. If I were to attain the Way with this frail body, those various non-Buddhists would [speak ill of me]."

He thought, "To speak of self-starvation as the cause of parinirvāṇa—though I now possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa in every limb, I shall not attain the fruit of the Path by this means. I must accept food before I can deliver sentient beings.
Having formed this thought, he went to the bank of the Nairañjanā River and sat down on the open ground. At that time, there were two cowherd girls outside the forest.
There were two men, one named Nanda and the other named Pāla. At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven exhorted a cowherd woman, saying, "The Prince is now in the forest;
you should make an offering to him. Upon hearing this, the woman was filled with great joy.

She immediately selected a fat and healthy cow, bathed it in the river, and personally took its pure milk. She boiled it according to the prescribed method and then placed the milk-rice into a vessel.
Filling her golden bowl, she went to the Prince’s location, prostrated with her head at his feet, and offered it to him.
The Prince then accepted the girl’s gift and pronounced a blessing over it: “May this food now offered cause those who eat it to obtain sufficient strength;
may it cause the giver to obtain beauty, power, renunciation, and joy, and to remain secure, free from illness, and preserve their lifespan and wisdom until the end.”
Endowed with wisdom, he then spoke these words: "I accept this food for the sake of liberating all sentient beings.
Having completed the ritual prayer, he partook of the food; his body became radiant and joyful, his physical strength was fully restored, and he was fit to attain Bodhi.

The *Sūtra on the Adornment of Bathing in the River of Dhyāna* states: At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought: "Having practiced austerities for six years, my robes have become worn and tattered.
Seeing some discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*) in the Śītavana forest, he intended to take them. Thereupon, the Earth Deity addressed him:
The deity of space said: "The Prince of the Śākya clan has renounced the rank of a wheel-turning monarch and has taken up these discarded robes of rags.
Having heard this, the deity of space announced it to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and so on, until the news reached the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The Bodhisattva held a garment of discarded rags and spoke these words: "Where is there water to wash this robe?
A celestial deity pointed to the ground with her finger, and immediately a pond was formed. He then thought: "Where is there a stone to wash the robe?"
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately placed a square stone at the edge of the pond. Upon seeing the stone, the Bodhisattva proceeded to wash his clothes there.
Śakra addressed him, saying, "I shall wash these clothes for the Bodhisattva; I pray that you will grant me permission.
However, because the Bodhisattva wished to ensure that future communities of bhikṣus would not have others wash their robes, he did not allow Śakra to wash them.
Having washed his clothes himself, he finished and entered the pool to bathe. At that time, Māra Pāpīyān transformed the bank of the pool, making it exceedingly high and steep.
On the bank of the pool there was a tree named Asana; at that moment, the tree deity pressed down the tree, causing it to bend low.
The Bodhisattva grasped a branch and reached the riverbank. While the Bodhisattva was bathing, the various devas scattered [flowers].
Flowers covered the riverbanks everywhere. When the Bodhisattva had finished bathing, the devas vied with one another to take this water back to the ponds in their celestial palaces.
Having drunk this water, the aquatic beings were reborn in the heavens. For the sake of benefiting them, the Bodhisattva manifested the act of bathing to deliver these aquatic beings.
The *Sūtra on the Robe Offered by Śakra* states: At that time, the Prince went to the Nairañjanā River. Having washed his old robes and bathed in the water, there was a great tree by the riverbank;
beneath it, he put on his old robes himself. At that moment, a devaputra from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven named...
Vimalaprabha offered a saffron robe of proper measure for a śramaṇa to the Bodhisattva, who then accepted and put it on.
At that time, the local deity of the village told Sujātā, "You should prepare delicious food to offer to the Bodhisattva."
Then the daughter of Sujātā immediately filled a golden bowl with milk-rice and offered it to him. The Bodhisattva accepted it.
At that time, a nāga queen named Nairañjanā emerged from the earth and, holding a magnificent and exquisite jeweled throne in her hands, offered it to the Bodhisattva.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva sat upon it and took [the bowl] from Sujātā.
The milk-rice offered by the woman he ate with full satisfaction until nothing remained.
After the Bodhisattva had consumed the milk-rice, his physical marks and signs were restored to their original state. He then cast the golden bowl into the river;
at that time, the Dragon King was filled with great joy, retrieved the golden bowl, and enshrined it for worship within his palace. Thereupon, Śakra-devānām-indra immediately transformed his form.
He became a garuḍa and snatched the golden bowl from that nāga king, returning to his own palace where he erected a stūpa to make offerings to it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat; the nāga queen took back the bed and throne she had offered and returned to her own palace, where she erected a stūpa to make offerings to them.
By the power of his merit and wisdom, the Bodhisattva finished eating the milk-rice, and [was endowed with] the thirty-two marks and the eight...

The ten marks of excellence and the halo extending one fathom became increasingly brilliant. With right mindfulness, the Bodhisattva proceeded to the site of enlightenment and attained perfect awakening.
He proceeded to the site of enlightenment.

The *Sūtra of the Array of Adornments* states: When the Bodhisattva, with right mindfulness, approached the Bodhi tree, there was a deity who presides over wind and rain, who swept and sprinkled everywhere until all was perfectly pure and serene.

The Bodhisattva’s body emitted immeasurable radiance, which universally shook infinite buddha-fields. Furthermore, immeasurable devas played celestial music and rained down various heavenly flowers that completely covered the ground.

There were immeasurable, rare, and auspicious signs of good fortune. As the Bodhisattva was about to proceed toward the Bodhi tree, that night the Great Brahma King addressed the assembly of Brahmās, saying: "You should know that the Bodhisattva has donned the armor of diligence;

with wisdom firm and steadfast, he has accomplished the practices of a bodhisattva, mastered the gates of the pāramitās, attained great sovereignty within the bodhisattva stages, and dwells [therein]."
Regarding the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, he transcends all demonic realms; he is able to self-awaken to all wholesome dharmas and attains enlightenment not through another.
Protected by the great supernormal powers of all Tathāgatas, he shall expound the path of liberation for the sake of sentient beings.
With such immeasurable merits as these, the Bodhisattva proceeds toward Bodhi.
This is for the purpose of subduing all demonic adversaries; for the purpose of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

for the purpose of fulfilling the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); for the purpose of turning the wheel of the true Dharma;
for the purpose of making the great lion’s roar and bestowing the great rain of Dharma so that all sentient beings may attain fulfillment; and for the purpose of causing all beings...
He attained the pure Dharma-eye by birth, so as to cause all non-Buddhists to cease their disputations,
to fulfill his original vow, and to attain mastery over all phenomena; he was unstained by the eight worldly concerns,
just as a lotus flower is not defiled by water.
The *Sūtra on the Past Deeds of Offering Grass by a Deva* states: The Bodhisattva thought to himself, "Now that I have reached the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), what kind of seat shall I use?
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed him, saying, "O Great Sage, O Benevolent One! All Buddhas of the past sat upon seats of grass and attained perfect awakening."

The Bodhisattva reflected, "Who can provide me with such grass? Then Śakra, King of the Devas, transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and stood to the right, neither too near nor too far, mowing the grass.
The grass was green in color, like the feathers on a peacock's neck, soft and lustrous; when touched by the hand, it felt as delicate as fine silk.

The Kāśika cloth was of exquisite blue color and fragrance. Seeing that man mowing such grass, the Bodhisattva gradually approached him and asked with gentle courtesy, "Virtuous one, what is your name? The man replied, "My name is Śrī."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was filled with great joy and reflected: "I now seek auspiciousness;
since the auspiciousness of others is found in their names, and auspiciousness stands before me, I shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Reflecting thus, he uttered a sublime sound and spoke again to the grass-cutter: "O worthy one..."
"Sir, could you give me some grass? The man replied, "I can give it to you. He immediately cut the grass and offered it to the Bodhisattva.
The grass was pure and exquisite; the Bodhisattva then took a handful of that grass and held it himself.
At the moment the Bodhisattva took the grass, the earth shook in six ways. At that time, the Bodhisattva, taking this...
He calmly and slowly walked toward the foot of the Bodhi tree, where he took a seat of grass and attained perfect enlightenment,
benefiting all sentient beings so that they might all attain liberation.
The *Nāgarāja-praśaṃsita-pūrvayoga-sūtra* states: When the Bodhisattva was proceeding while holding the grass, there suddenly appeared in the air five hundred each of blue jays,
*kucīra* birds, peacocks, white cranes, *kalaviṅka* birds, and *saṃjīvaka* birds, all circling him to the right as they flew along with him.
Furthermore, there were five hundred sons of gods and five hundred daughters of gods, each holding precious vases and scattering various fragrant flowers as they circumambulated.

The earth trembled. In that land was a nāga king named Kaca, a long-lived being who had endured through many kalpas and had previously witnessed the passage of former Buddhas. Moreover, for these nāgas, days, months, and nights are exceedingly long.
Not long after falling asleep, he perceived the great earth shaking and heard a thunderous roar.
He immediately woke up in alarm and went out from his own palace to observe. He saw a bodhisattva walking with serene composure not far from his dwelling place.
Upon seeing that bodhisattva, the Dragon King recalled a prior omen, just as when past great bodhisattvas had resolved their minds and were about to set forth.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, there was not the slightest difference. Having seen these signs, he no longer harbored any doubt;
he knew with certainty that this bodhisattva would realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the black dragon king had a dragon queen named Golden Light (*Suvarṇaprabhā*), who, together with various dragon maidens, each held exquisite incense, flowers, and diverse colors.
They offered robes, jeweled banners, parasols, and various kinds of rare treasures as an act of worship.
They played celestial music whose sounds were exquisite, and with palms joined in reverence, they sang praises before the Bodhisattva, prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet.
The Bodhisattva spoke to the Dragon King, saying: "As you have said, I shall now certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He extensively delivers sentient beings.
The *Bodhimaṇḍālaṃkāra-sūtra* states:
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva was proceeding toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there were immeasurable bodhisattvas as well as various devas..."
The assembly each adorned a bodhi tree. Those bodhi trees were lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary, measuring ten billion *yojanas* in height and composed of the seven precious jewels.
There were eighty-four thousand such trees, and for each one, they made a vow that the Bodhisattva would sit beneath it and attain perfect enlightenment.
Beneath each tree, lion thrones were spread according to their respective colors, all fashioned from various jewels.
Adorned. At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested the act of taking grass and spreading it everywhere.
Like a lion king, he was endowed with power, possessed firm diligence, and was free from all faults.

Noble, sovereign, awakened through wisdom, and possessing great renown, he had subdued all Māras and crushed all non-Buddhists. Having fulfilled such various merits, he was about to realize [enlightenment].
Facing east toward Bodhi, he sat cross-legged upon pure grass. With body upright and mindfulness established, he made this great vow:
"If I do not now realize unsurpassed bodhi, my body shall rather shatter; I will never rise from this seat.
At that time, the Bodhisattva ascended the seat of enlightenment and immediately realized the Vaipulya, the Play of Supernatural Powers, and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
He entered a profound concentration. Having attained this concentration, he manifested his body so that each [of the bodhisattvas] sat upon their respective lion thrones;
every single body was adorned with all manner of wondrous marks and signs. Each of the other bodhisattvas, as well as the devas and humans, thought that the Bodhisattva alone was sitting on his seat.
By the power of his concentration, he was able to cause [beings in] the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the world of Yama—

Furthermore, all humans and devas saw the Bodhisattva seated upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). The Bodhisattva emitted a great radiance that illuminated the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
King Māra then had a dream.

The *Sūtra on the Original Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states: At that time, the Bodhisattva emitted a white tuft of light from between his eyebrows, which illuminated the palace of the Māra-king and eclipsed all the lights of the various Māras. While King Pāpīyān was asleep, he experienced thirty-two kinds of evil dreams;
in these dreams, he saw the palace shaking violently, suddenly bursting into flames, and its walls collapsing until they were reduced entirely to shards.
The ground was strewn with gravel; dust and soil were scattered in disorder, filled with filth and impurity. Elephants and horses lay dead, and the feathers of birds fell out.

Springs and wells had dried up, and trees were broken and shattered. Their bodies suffered from alternating cold and heat, their complexions became sallow and emaciated, their throats were parched, and their labored breathing could not cease.
Their garments were stained with grime, and their celestial crowns fell away. The Lord of Devas wailed aloud, and the demonic armies were filled with grief and distress. The sons of Māra...
He cried out, and the māra subjects fled and dispersed; his weapons were lost and his musical instruments shattered.

His attendants withdrew from him, and friends became enemies. The celestial maidens stood naked, and all the women wept. His mind was clouded with confusion, and he was filled with terror and distress.

Seers spoke ill omens and spirits sang of inauspiciousness. He ran in every direction, finding no place of refuge or autonomy. When the Māra King encountered these signs of misfortune, [he was overcome].
In a dream, his heart was filled with dread and his mind became unsettled.
He summoned all the hosts of Māras and their retinues to assemble, and recounted to them the events he had seen in that night’s dream: "Before long, I shall surely lose this place;
I fear that someone of even greater merit and virtue will come to be born here. He then immediately called forth the terrestrial devas and the various hosts of Māra’s armies.
The various classes of beings, including the nāgas and yakṣas, were commanded by him, saying:
"Now there is a son of the Śākya clan who desires to attain bodhi. Let us go together to that place and sever such a courageous resolve."
"Do not allow him to attain the realization of Bodhi.

The *Sūtra on the Original Conduct of the Demon Prince’s Admonition to His Father* states: At that time, the elder son of the Māra King, Śreṣṭhidāraka, addressed his father, the King, saying: "Now, O Father King..."
They wish to become enemies with the Bodhisattva Siddhārtha, fearing only that later they may regret it when it is too late. The Māra King said to his son, "Ho!
You childish, ignorant, shallow, and limited one! You have never known my transformative supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*), nor have you ever beheld my sovereign majesty and power.
The Prince of the Śākyas replied to his father, "It is not that I do not know the supernatural powers and majesty of my royal father."
[He possessed] power. Yet, the father-king did not yet fully know the vast supernormal powers, merit, and majestic might of the Bodhisattva Siddhārtha.
Nevertheless, when the father-king arrives there, he shall see for himself. Māra Pāpīyān did not heed his son’s words;
instead, he immediately summoned the fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—in the hundreds of thousands of myriads.
A hundred million celestial deities, ghosts, and spirits, their forms terrifying, all grasping bows, arrows, swords, blades, and various weapons;
lifting mountains and wielding pestles, they manifested great ferocity. The Māra King led his host toward the foot of the Bodhi tree.
From afar, the Māra’s army beheld the Bodhisattva seated upon the lion throne—neither startled nor terrified, neither wavering nor shaking; his body radiant, like [the sun].
The Golden Mountain emitted a great radiance beyond all comparison. The hosts of Māra’s army were completely dispersed and fled.
Upon seeing this, the King of Māras was seized with great terror; yet, still harboring pride, he refused to retreat. He again addressed his troops:
"Do not be startled, do not be afraid, do not fear, and do not run away! This is merely my testing of his mind. Behold how I shall now further console and pacify him."
He observed that she had departed from beneath the Bodhi tree, lest she cause the Bodhisattva to fail in attaining perfect enlightenment while at this very spot under the Bodhi tree.
The demoness then employed her seductive charms.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*) states: The Māra Pāpīyān did not heed the counsel of his eldest son, Śreṣṭhidāraka.
He addressed the daughters, saying, "You daughters, you should go to that son of the Śākya clan and observe whether his heart possesses any lustful desire.
Having received the King’s command, the māra-daughters together proceeded calmly toward the Bodhisattva’s location and manifested themselves before him.

They manifested various forms of feminine allure, flattery, and deceitful behavior; they further scattered fragrant flowers over the Bodhisattva and entreated him with all manner of the five sensual desires to look upon them.
As he observed their hearts and minds, he perceived that their postures were those of desire.
When the demonesses saw that the Bodhisattva’s profound mind was in deep meditative concentration, fundamentally pure and without [defilement], [they were overcome].
They were free from defilement; their faces were as pure as lotuses emerging from the water, unstained by it.
They were as firm and immovable as Mount Sumeru, having well-restrained their sense faculties and disciplined their minds.
When those [women] saw the Bodhisattva in such a manner, they all felt shame and remorse. For these魔女 (māra-dārikās) were well-versed in the illusions of women.

These delusive phenomena further display amorous gestures and increasingly manifest seductive postures to adorn their bodies; they present themselves with beautiful voices and clever, artful words to come and entice.
The Bodhisattva replied: "By virtue of merit in past lives, you have obtained this celestial body, yet you do not contemplate impermanence as you practice such seductive charms.
Though your physical forms are beautiful, your minds are not upright. You have come on purpose to disturb people."
“O you of evil intent! You are not of a pure lineage; you are like a leather bag filled with filth. Why have you come? Begone! I have no need of you.

Why have you come here in vain, now that your mother and the others are no longer at ease in the heavens? The Buddha pointed his finger, and the demoness was transformed into an old woman, her hair white and her face wrinkled, unable to restore herself.

The *Mārajana-pratyudgamana-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Defeat of Māra’s Army) states: At that time, the King of Māras said, "This man cannot be deluded by the five desires. Rather, employ sweet words to comfort and persuade him so that he will depart.
This venerable śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, has been [in this world] since childhood; I have never seen him engage in combat with weapons."
It is terrifying. Furthermore, O Benevolent One, do not form enmity with others through the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion;
you should depart at once. The Bodhisattva observed this clearly and resolutely refused to comply. He neither moved his body nor shifted from his seat, and addressed the Māra King, saying:
"I have now sat upon this adamantine, firm, and stable full-lotus posture (paryaṅka), which is extremely difficult to destroy. Having heard this, the Māra King...
Speaking with words of wrath, he led a fourfold army consisting of various troops—elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots—along with banners, standards, streamers, pennants, and canopies.
There were many yakṣas who all ate human flesh and were highly skilled in divine archery;
each grasped leather-bound bows and held sharp arrows, spears, lances, swords, halberds, blades, clubs, vajra-staffs, battle-discuses, iron axes, and various other weapons.
Accompanied by their mounts, thousands of millions of elephants, camels, horses, and chariots let out a great roar that filled the void of space.
Furthermore, immeasurable dragons, each riding upon a mass of great black clouds, released flashes of lightning and hail that fell in a chaotic downpour.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, grasping a sharp sword in his hand, said to the Bodhisattva, "I shall cut your body to pieces. The Bodhisattva replied, "You..."
Māra Pāpīyān and his hosts, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, are all like your own body.
Even if they were to come here with all their might, they could not move even a single hair of mine; how much less could they obstruct me by attempting to hinder my bodhi by cutting up my body?
"May I not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I shall never rise from this place to sit beneath another tree.
As he spoke, the hosts of Māra dragged away his water jar.
The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states: At that time, the Tathāgata sat majestically and uprightly beneath the Bodhi tree.
The evil Māra Pāpīyān, leading ten billion followers of desire, came intending to destroy the Buddha. Upon reaching the Tathāgata’s presence, he spoke these words:
"Prince Siddhārtha, how can you sit here all alone? You should rise and depart. If you do not leave, I—"
"Seize his feet and hurl him beyond the sea! The Buddha said, "I observe that in this world there is no one capable of hurling me beyond the sea.
The Buddha told Pāpīyas, "In a previous life, you merely served as the master of a single monastery and observed the eight precepts for a single day."
Because you gave a single bowl of food to a Pratyekabuddha, you were born as a great Māra in the sixth Brahma Heaven;

whereas I have extensively cultivated merit for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, and likewise making offerings to countless Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Pāpīyān said: "Prince, you speak of my past single [act]..."
I have maintained the precepts daily and offered food to pratyekabuddhas; I believe in what is true and real. As for you who claim this for yourself, who can bear witness?
The Buddha then pointed to the ground with his hand and said, "This earth shall bear witness that I speak these words.

At that moment, the entire great earth shook in six ways, and immeasurable earth deities surged forth from the ground. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and joined their palms.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I bear witness that what the Buddha has spoken is true and not false.
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas, "If you can first move this pure pitcher, only then will you be able to hurl me beyond the seas.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas and his assembly of eight billion beings exhausted all their supernatural powers, yet they could not cause the pure pitcher to move. King Māra—
The entire host of soldiers retreated and dispersed.
As the *Sūtra on the Original Acts Witnessed by the Earth Deity* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva pointed at the earth with his right hand and said: 'This earth can give birth...'"
"All things are without marks; this is the practice of equanimity. This serves as my testimony that I shall never speak falsely.
I pray only that you will speak the truth before me. At that time, the Earth Goddess suddenly emerged from beneath the earth.
Kneeling on her right knee with palms joined and bowing in reverence, she addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "O Great Being, I bear witness for you; I know you."
In ages past, throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he had performed unobstructed assemblies of giving.
Having spoken these words, the earth throughout the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways; like the ringing of a bell, it resounded with eighteen signs such as trembling and roaring.
The hosts of Māra’s army were all scattered and dispersed; their strength broken and defeated, they each fled in haste, naturally [vanquished].
Terrified and unable to find peace of mind, at that time some elephants stumble and fall, while camels and horses lie down exhausted.
Some chariot axles break, and bows, arrows, swords, and spears naturally fall from their hands to the ground.
Solid armor shatters and is torn away from their bodies as they flee in frantic competition. Some cover their faces and collapse to the ground to sleep; others run to take refuge in the mountains.
Some entered underground caves; they all lost their original minds, becoming dazed and falling prostrate on the ground.
Others turned their hearts back toward the Bodhisattva, entreating him for protection and care for them. Those who relied upon the Bodhisattva did not lose their original minds.
At that time, Pāpīyān heard the sound of the great earth; his heart was filled with great terror, and he fainted and fell to the ground, losing all sense of direction.
Pāpīyān heard a voice from the sky saying, "Extinguish them all! Do not let Pāpīyān go!
Thereupon, the hosts of Māra’s army fled away in competition with one another.

The *Māraputra-kṣamāpanā-pūrvacarita-sūtra* states: The eldest son of the Māra Pāpīyān was named Śreṣṭhin. He immediately prostrated with his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva and, seeking to offer repentance, addressed him, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous Noble Son, I pray that you will grant my father leave to offer his words of apology."
I am a fool of shallow understanding, like a small child devoid of wisdom.
I have now suddenly come to disturb the Noble Son, manifesting various forms with my hosts of māras to terrify him. Previously, I once consulted my father, saying:
Because of his upright and impartial mind, even a wise man skilled in all arts could not subdue Prince Siddhārtha, let alone someone like me.

I only pray that the Noble Son will forgive my father; my father was ignorant and did not understand the Way, and thus he terrified the Great Holy Prince. How could such a Great Holy Prince be taken as a husband?
"May the vows made by the Benevolent One be swiftly fulfilled; may you quickly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and immeasurable, boundless other devas filled the entirety of space.
All beheld the Bodhisattva subduing the Māras and their demonic hosts, and they were all filled with great joy. With this joy...
With mind and mouth, they uttered these words: "Excellent! How rare! The sound pervaded the four quarters, and the resonance of their voices shook the void.

They performed celestial music and sang hymns of praise. Furthermore, taking various celestial wonderful flowers and the fine powdered incense of celestial sandalwood, they scattered them over the Bodhisattva.
Joining their ten fingers in palms-together salutation, they prostrated themselves before the Bodhisattva and spoke these words: "Now..."
"This noble one will certainly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having prostrated to the Bodhisattva and praised him, the Māra-son Śreṣṭhidāraka departed.
Thus, the Bodhisattva subdued Māra.
The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* states: The Bodhisattva reflected that this Māra Pāpīyān would not accept the admonitions of others and was performing various kinds of deeds.
The Bodhisattva said to Pāpīyān: "When I reach the foot of the Bodhi tree, I shall spread a handful of grass and sit there."
I fear that Pāpīyān will become my enemy; through strife and contention, he will commit various evil deeds without a single thought of virtue.

I now wish to sever this enmity and extinguish these evil karmas. If you harbor a heart of resentment and malice, know that the Bodhisattva sits beneath this tree, using grass as a mat and wearing robes of discarded rags; it is for such matters that your mind is filled with envy and jealousy.
"You, Māra Pāpīyān, first steady your mind. If I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall later take all such matters as these and entrust them to you.
I pray that you will turn your heart and give rise to great joy.
Māra Pāpīyān, within your own heart now there is also a vow: 'We must certainly cause [him] to be terrified.'"
Bodhisattva, rise from this seat now and depart without lingering. Furthermore, I have a vast and great vow:
while my body sits upon this seat, even if for some cause or condition my body should be shattered here like fine dust and my life-span extinguished, if I do not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I—
I shall not rise from this place until my life’s end. O Māra Pāpīyān, we shall observe this sequence:
who possesses the strength of courageous resolve and vows to be the first to fulfill this aspiration?
Whether it be I, you, Māra, or your host—if the power of my merit, karma, and roots of goodness is strong, I shall surely fulfill such a vow as this.
This is indeed true and not false.

The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance of the Attainment of Equal and Right Enlightenment) states: "The Bodhisattva sat beneath the tree; having already subdued the demonic adversaries, he attained perfect and true enlightenment and established the Great [Dharma]."
The Dharma-banner delivers beings across the three realms. Sitting in silence beneath the tree, he manifests the four dhyānas to serve as a path for future students seeking the Way.
With his mind already purified, he accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna. Remaining tranquil and guarding the One with an unwavering focus, he accomplishes the practice of the second dhyāna.
Having attained pure vision of reality, he accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna. His mind neither relies on the good nor clings to the evil; there is no suffering.
The aspiration for joy is precisely within this. To remain tranquil and undergo transformation into the four dhyāna practices is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Way that transcends the world abandons the root of evil; lust, anger, and delusion are eliminated, and the cycle of birth and death is already removed.

The seeds and roots have been severed, with no remaining sprouts or shoots. What was to be done has been accomplished and wisdom is fully realized. When the morning star appeared, he attained great awakening and realized the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
To attain the supreme, true path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha), to obtain the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas;
to realize the intent of the Buddha-way and all-knowing vision—this is truly subtle, wondrous, and exceedingly difficult to attain.
Long ago, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I was prophesied to become a Buddha named Śākyamuni; now, as a fruit, I have attained it through diligent effort over countless kalpas.

That which I sought with such hardship has finally been accomplished. Reflecting upon my past lives and all that I have practiced—virtue, compassion, filial piety, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, trustworthiness, centrality, and rectitude;

maintaining sincerity, cultivating the sages, being humble, yielding, and pure in mind—I have practiced the six perfections of giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom.
I have practiced the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Employing skillful means according to the occasion, he nurtures sentient beings as if loving his own infant. Serving all Buddhas, he accumulates immeasurable merit;
through diligent toil over successive kalpas, his efforts are never in vain.
Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Volume I (1) and Volume I (2),
compiled by the Śramaṇa Baocheng of Baoen Temple.

The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states that the celestial kings of the desire realm, seeing the Tathāgata seated beneath the tree, his supernormal powers having reached fulfillment of his vows,
having subdued the hosts of Māra and enemies, and having raised the great banner of victory— the Great Benevolent One of the Infinite— praised and congratulated him.
The King of Physicians heals the myriad ailments of sentient beings. The Infinite Lion does not experience the bristling of hair on his body even amidst fear.

He harmonizes the mind and extinguishes the three impurities to achieve the three types of penetrating wisdom (*trividyā*). Having crossed the four seas, he holds the single canopy of the Way to rescue and protect the three realms.
A pure brahmin who has cast off all evils is a bhikṣu. What is meant by "removing all ignorance and darkness"?

"O Śramaṇa! You have transcended the six paths and studied extensively without limit; this is called 'vast learning. Your virtue has extinguished worldly toil, and you have become courageous, having crossed to the other shore.
As for what is called 'power,' you have perfected the ten powers and are fully endowed with the treasure of the Dharma.
We see the Tathāgata sitting beneath the tree, having realized the Unsurpassed Way. Thereupon, the gods of the Pure Abodes and the Brahmakāyika gods—

The Brahmā devas, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Yāma devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and the Cāturmahārājika devas, along with the spirits of the void and the great earth, made offerings to the World-Honored One.

They adorned the entire world and its heavens, scattering flowers, burning incense, and raising various banners and streamers. Taking refuge in the World-Honored One, they praised him in verse, saying: "Firm and steadfast."

Like a vajra, his resolve is firm and indestructible. Even if his flesh and blood should waste away until his marrow is exhausted without remainder, if he does not attain the path of Buddhahood, he shall never rise from this seat.
O Lion of Men, your words are upright; you have established your vow and manifested your majestic power.
We, the various devas, have all come to obtain excellent benefit, so that this Most Honored One may illuminate everything without exception. We—
Upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, they all exhorted one another to assist in the path of the Buddha.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Dharma of the Flower Adornment of the Buddha, states: "At that time, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment, he was at the site of tranquil extinction together with forty..."
A Dharma-body Mahāsattva and the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, whose roots had matured from past lives, simultaneously surrounded him like clouds enveloping the moon.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested the body of Vairocana and preached the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*, which is known as the Sudden Teaching (*tóngjiào*).
This sūtra consists of seven locations, nine assemblies, and thirty-nine chapters, and it describes the "Exquisite Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords" (*Shìzhǔ miàoyán*) of the Tathāgata.
The manifestation of the Samantabhadra-samādhi world; the accomplishment of the Flower Treasury (Kusuma-garbha) world; the name of the Tathāgata Vairocana;
the Bodhisattva Awakening to the Light of the Four Noble Truths (Catur-ārya-satya-prabhā-bodhi) inquiring about pure conduct;

the noble Śrī-mukha ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru to praise in verse the merit of the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi), the holy life (brahma-carya), and the arousal of the bodhicitta; and ascending to the Yama Heaven. Yama...
Verses of praise for the ten practices and the ten inexhaustible treasuries. Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven.

Verses of praise in Tuṣita for the ten dedications, the ten stages, the ten concentrations, the ten supernormal powers, and the ten patiences. The dwelling place of Bodhisattvas with an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lifespan.
The ocean of marks and minor characteristics of the Buddha’s inconceivable body. The conduct of Samantabhadra, the appearance of the Tathāgata, transcending the world and entering the Dharma.
Chapter on the Elements and so forth: For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains, then the deep valleys, until it finally shines universally upon the entire earth.
It is only because the mountains have heights and depths that the illumination occurs in succession. The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is likewise:
having perfected such immeasurable and boundless light of wisdom regarding the dharma-realm, he first illuminates the bodhisattvas, and then [illuminates...]

First it illuminates the pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates the śrāvakas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings with determinate roots of goodness, transforming them according to their capacities;
thereafter, it universally illuminates all sentient beings.
The *Bodhivṛkṣavyūha-sūtra* states:
When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, immeasurable devas all praised the Tathāgata’s merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed at the King of Bodhi Trees without blinking for even a moment, taking the joy of dhyāna as his sustenance.

While maintaining the perception of having leftover food, he did not rise from his seat for seven days. Then, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm, each holding a golden basin in their hands and grasping a precious vase filled with scented water, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and requested the Tathāgata to bathe.
Having accepted their request and bathed, the World-Honored One was presented by each of the devaputras with celestial and wondrous offerings.
They offered robes, burned exquisite celestial incense, and scattered exquisite celestial flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata.
Immeasurable devas, nāgas, humans, and others each took some of the water used for the Tathāgata’s ablution and sprinkled it upon themselves; they all resolved their minds on the Way.
The sons of the gods each returned to their celestial palaces, yet the fragrance of the remaining water did not fade; they smelled only the fragrance of the Buddha and no other scent.
With hearts full of joy, they gave rise to the bodhicitta. At that time, there was a devaputra named Samantakusuma who addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, in what samādhi do you abide, such that for seven days you sit cross-legged with body and mind unmoving? The Buddha said:
The Tathāgata dwells sustained by the food of the *prāmodya-samādhi*. By the power of this concentration, he remains seated in the full lotus posture for seven days without rising from his seat.
Because he intends to eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death—which have neither beginning nor end—while dwelling in this place, he gazes at the tree for seven days without rising.
Upon reaching the second week, he walks back and forth for three thousand [yojanas] all around.
Taking the thousandfold world system as its limit, he gazed at the Bodhi tree for twenty-one days without blinking his eyes;
having severed birth and death, he attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The *Bonnōnyūjōhongyōkyō* (Sutra on Entering Samādhi in the Dragon Palace) states: The World-Honored One sat facing the place where Mārīcī was located.
At that time, the Naga King Kāla and the Naga King Mucilinda went to the Buddha’s presence and said: "We have already offered this palace as a gift."
“O Buddhas! Today the World-Honored One has accepted my palace; out of compassion for me, may he dwell here for a short while.

Having accepted and sat therein, the Buddha remained for seven days without rising. During those seven days, clouds arose and rain poured down, and great cold winds blew so that the rain did not cease even for a moment, resulting in a freezing cold. Then the dragon kings emerged from their palaces with their massive bodies.

Sevenfold they encircled and shielded the Buddha’s body. Furthermore, with seven heads, they hung above the World-Honored One to form a great canopy, standing majestic and firm, so that the World-Honored One’s body would not be chilled by cold or dampness, nor touched by insects.
At that time, the Dragon King transformed himself into the body of a young Brahmin. Standing before the Buddha, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not intend to terrify or disturb the Tathāgata. Rather, I fear that cold winds or dust may touch the World-Honored One’s body;
it was with this thought in mind that I covered the World-Honored One’s body. Then the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana:
The Nāga King Mahā-mucilinda said, "Great Nāga King, come and receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, so that you may obtain peace and happiness for a long night.
Then the Nāga King Mucilinda addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the World-Honored One has commanded, I dare not disobey.
Thereupon, the Nāga King Mucilinda received the Three Refuges from the Buddha.
He took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and further received the five precepts;
thus, he was the very first dragon king in the world to attain deliverance.

The *Línjiānyànzuò Běnxíng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Seated Meditation in the Forest) states: At that time, the World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration in the dragon palace.

There was a devaputra possessed of sovereign supernormal powers whose body emitted a most excellent radiance of great color, which illuminated that Nyagrodha tree. By means of this celestial light, he himself...
Jiāozhào Lǎng approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “In the past, I was a shepherd boy.
When the World-Honored One was practicing the six years of austerities as a bodhisattva, I once offered pure milk from my heart as an offering to the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, I broke off branches from a nyagrodha tree to fashion [a seat].”
"In its cool shade. By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, immediately upon my death, I was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as a deva-son of great merit and power.
I have now obtained this retribution; how much more so for the World-Honored One, who has attained unsurpassed bodhi!
I only pray that the World-Honored One will now, for my sake, return beneath that tree and enjoy its shade as you please."
"May you be at ease. Out of compassion for me, World-Honored One, please grant this:

I wish that you would go to the nyagrodha tree where the former shepherd boy sat cross-legged and remain there for seven days, entering meditative concentration without moving, experiencing bliss through the power of liberation. Then, after those seven days had passed, the World-Honored One...
Afterwards, emerging from samādhi with right mindfulness and right awareness, he addressed the devaputra, saying: "Come, O devaputra;
receive from me the three refuges and the five precepts, so that you may attain peace and happiness for a long night.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, that devaputra immediately received the three refuges and the five precepts. At that time, in the world... [the most...]
In the first heaven, he became a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

Regarding the four kings' offering of the bowl, the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states: "The World-Honored One reflected that all past Buddhas had likewise carried bowls to receive their food."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings each brought four golden bowls from the four directions and offered them to the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One did not accept them.
They then brought four silver bowls, which the World-Honored One did not accept. Four lapis lazuli bowls were likewise not accepted.
Four crystal bowls were also not accepted. Four agate bowls were likewise not accepted. Four musaragalva bowls were also not accepted.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the other heavenly kings, saying:
"I recall that in the past, the blue-colored devas brought a stone bowl and offered it to us, saying: 'O virtuous ones, you may now use this stone bowl to receive food and eat.'"
Furthermore, a certain devaputra came and said to me: "Be careful not to accept food in this stone bowl; it should be honored as if it were a stūpa.
In the future, when a Buddha appears in the world named Śākyamuni, you may take this bowl and present it to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the Four Heavenly Kings quickly returned to their palaces, each taking a stone bowl and filling it with celestial flowers.
Having anointed their bowls with incense, they came to where the Buddha was and together offered the four bowls to him, saying, "We pray only that the World-Honored One will accept these stone bowls.
The World-Honored One then reflected: "These Four Heavenly Kings, with hearts of pure faith, have offered me these four bowls."
"It would also be improper for me to accept and keep four bowls; if I were to accept them from one person, the other three would harbor resentment.

I shall now accept the bowls of the Four Heavenly Kings collectively. At that time, after the World-Honored One had accepted the bowls of the Four Heavenly Kings, he arranged them one upon another in succession.
Having received them with his left hand, he pressed them down with his right hand; by means of his supernormal power, they merged into a single bowl, which was firm and durable.
The four boundaries are pure and clearly defined.
Regarding the two merchants who offered food, the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states: "In Northern India, there were two merchant leaders: one named Tiri-pu-po and the other named Ba..."
Licchavi, while traveling along a road not far from the Milk Grove with five hundred ox-carts, both the carts and the oxen refused to move forward.
At that time, the forest-guardian deity said to the caravan leader, "There is a Buddha here who has newly attained perfect enlightenment.

It is most appropriate for you now to go before him and offer a portion of roasted flour as an offering. Thereupon, the caravan leader and his followers each took a lump of roasted flour mixed with curds and honey.
Arriving before the World-Honored One, they prostrated at his feet and said, "We pray that you will accept this offering of parched grain, curd, and honey for our sake.

The World-Honored One reflected: "All Buddhas of the past have accepted food using alms bowls. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings each brought a stone bowl and offered it to the World-Honored One, saying it could be used to receive the food. Having accepted the bowls, [the World-Honored One] from the two merchants...
The caravan leader received a lump of parched grain mixed with curd and honey; he then offered a blessing and ate it according to the Dharma.

Having finished eating, he addressed those two caravan leaders, saying: "Come, receive from me the refuge in the Buddha, the refuge in the Dharma, and the refuge in the Sangha, and further receive the five precepts.
This shall bring you peace and happiness for a long night and secure for you great and wholesome benefit. When the caravan leaders heard this, they...
They immediately addressed him together, saying, "We shall not contravene the holy teaching of the Buddha.

Thereupon, they together received the three refuges and the five precepts, becoming the very first in the human world to attain deliverance. The merchant leader addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that you will grant me one thing to fashion a stūpa for my offerings.
The World-Honored One then gave the two merchants hair and nail-clippings from his own body and said to them, "If you see..."
"This object is no different from my own. Having received the hair and nails, the merchant leader prostrated to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, took his leave, and departed.
Brahmā then made his formal request.
The *Sūtra of Adornment* states: At that time, the Great Brahmā King, together with sixty-eight koṭis of Brahmā followers, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
"World-Honored One, Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, you seek unsurpassed enlightenment."
"Now that you have attained Buddhahood, I pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma. The World-Honored One remained silent. He observed the world and thought:
"I have realized the Dharma of tranquil Nirvāṇa; yet if I were to expound it for others, they would all be unable to understand it.
For this reason, I remain silent. At that time, Great Brahmā Deva-king, Śakra Devendra, and even those of the Heaven of the Thirty-three...
Having prostrated to the Buddha, the assembly of devas requested the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma. The Buddha addressed the Brahmā King, saying:
"I have realized a most profound and subtle Dharma, which is supremely tranquil, difficult to see and difficult to awaken to;
it cannot be understood through discursive thought, but can only be known by the Buddhas. For this reason, I remain silent. At that time, the Great Brahmā...
The King observed that in the kingdom of Magadha there were many non-Buddhists who recklessly fabricated speculative theories regarding earth, water, fire, wind, and space;
they clung to false views, mistaking them for the true path. Although those sentient beings practice such heterodox paths, there are among them those ready to be delivered whom he must now deliver.
"I only pray, World-Honored One, that for the sake of these sentient beings, you shall turn the Wheel of Dharma. The world...
The World-Honored One, observing all sentient beings with his Buddha-eye, perceived their superior, middling, and inferior faculties; he gave rise to great compassion and turned the wheel of Dharma.
Having heard this, the Heavenly King suddenly vanished from before the Buddha. At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Space Deity, proclaiming:
"The Tathāgata has now accepted the Brahma King’s exhortation to turn the wheel of Dharma. Upon hearing this, the Space Deity expanded [the proclamation].
It was transmitted in turn up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

The *Sūtra on the Causes and Effects of Turning the Sublime Wheel of Dharma* states: "The World-Honored One went to the country of Vārāṇasī and arrived at [the place where] Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāma, and B..."
At the dwelling place of Pāṭali, Aśvajit, and Bhadrajit, five people came of their own accord to attend to his needs.

The Buddha observed that the faculties (*indriya*) of these five were capable of receiving the Path. The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya and you others, you should know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are a mass of suffering:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks."
"One should not suffer the suffering of losing prosperity and happiness. All sentient beings do not know the root of suffering and thus all wander in saṃsāra.
Kauṇḍinya, suffering should be known, its origin should be abandoned, its cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated. Thus the World-Honored One addressed those five men.
"Welcome, bhikṣus! As soon as he spoke, their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.
Then the World-Honored One asked those five men: "Bhikṣus, do you know whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent or impermanent?"
"Is this suffering or not suffering? Is this empty or not empty? Does it have a self or is it without a self?
When the five bhikṣus heard the Buddha speak thus of the impermanence of these five aggregates, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated;
they attained the fruit of arhatship and immediately replied: "World-Honored One, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are truly impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self."
The earth deity, filled with joy, proclaimed: "Today, the Tathāgata turns the sublime Wheel of Dharma here!

This cry was passed on in succession until it reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Thus, for the first time in this world, the Three Jewels appeared: the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, as the Buddha Jewel;
the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths as the Dharma Jewel; and the five Arhats as the Saṅgha Jewel. For the sake of all...
The *Dulufulun benxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of Pūrṇa) states:
"In the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was a great brāhmaṇa who served as the royal chaplain for King Śuddhodana."
The Master’s family was immensely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and treasures. He had a son named Pūrṇa, who was foremost in intelligence and fully mastered the Vedas and other treatises.
He was born on the same day as Prince Siddhārtha; by nature, he felt a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
Resolved to seek liberation, he saw the Prince renounce the world and immediately went with thirty companions to the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) to practice austerities and seek the Way.
Through courageous and diligent effort, he attained the four *dhyānas* and the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Using his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he beheld from afar the World-Honored One in the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) preaching the Dharma to devas and humans. He said to his companions, "We should go to see the Buddha."

They practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Their companions replied, "We obey your command. Thereupon, together with thirty others, they descended from the Snowy Mountains to the place where the World-Honored One was.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and requested ordination, saying, "May the World-Honored One deliver us.
The Buddha said, "It shall be according to your intent and as you wish. Having thus obtained ordination, they requested the reception of the precepts. Each...

Each applied their minds to walking and sitting alone, practicing with courageous diligence and never being negligent. Constantly dwelling in secluded places with a correct mind and correct faith, they sought the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Having exhausted all desires and perceived the characteristics of all phenomena, and desiring to cultivate the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they immediately realized those dharmas.
Having severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they attained the realization of the holy life; having completed what was to be done, they were no longer subject to further existence.
He will receive a future existence. Because his mind has attained all liberations well, he shall become one of great virtue;
he will be fully capable of performing great deeds to benefit sentient beings. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Pūrṇa possesses inexhaustible eloquence;
among those who preach the Dharma, he is the foremost."

The *Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Rishi Seeking Deliverance* states: In the kingdom of Āpantī, there was a very wealthy Brahmin of the Mahākātyāyana clan who served as the royal preceptor to King Ugrasena.
His second son was named Nārada; his father ordered him to study the Vedas.
When the various incantations and arts were discussed, the second son replied to his father before long: "I have already mastered and understood the Vedas and all the treatises;
you may now assemble for me all those who understand the Vedas and possess various skills. His father immediately gathered a great assembly.
Nārada understood all the treatises. When the eldest brother heard that his younger brother was able to master all the treatises, an evil thought arose in his mind.

He intended to take his life. His father sent his second son to the hermitage of the seer Asita on Mount Vinataka, where he thoroughly mastered all treatises, attained the four dhyānas, and was endowed with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Before long, the seer passed away.
Nārada, however, became attached to worldly gain and honors; lacking right mindfulness, he did not believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha. There was...
The Nāga King Elāpattra and the Nāga King Śaṅkha spoke in the language of the yakṣa Kiñjalka.
In that city there was previously a verse which said: "By what does one have mastery? What is called 'defilement'? How is one purified?
Why is one called 'deluded'? For what reason is a deluded person confused? What makes one a wise person? After what kind of meeting and separation is one said to have reached 'exhaustion'?"
Regarding the causal conditions: the Dragon King went to the hermit Nārada and asked about the meaning of this verse, but he could not explain it.
Nārada then went to the Buddha’s presence and inquired about this matter. The Buddha immediately expounded and explained various dharmas for him.
[The Dragon King] was filled with great joy and requested ordination. The Buddha said, "Welcome! Enter my Dharma and cultivate the holy life. Because of his lineage...
The clan name of his original surname was Mahākātyāyana.
The *Sūtra on the Boatman’s Repentance for His Past Deeds* states: "The World-Honored One proceeded calmly and gradually from the city of Saṃkasya to the bank of the Ganges River. The river..."
The floodwaters rose until they levelled with the banks. The World-Honored One, wishing to cross over, went to the boatman and said to him, "I beg you, ferry me to the other shore.
The boatman replied, "Venerable One, you must give me a fare for crossing; only then shall I ferry you across.
The World-Honored One replied to the boatman, "Where could I possibly have a fare for crossing now?"
"But I have renounced all wealth and treasures; were anyone to see me now, they would view me no differently than a piece of tile, stone, or clod of earth.
For this reason, I have no fare for crossing. The boatman spoke again: "Venerable One, if you cannot give me the fare for crossing, I will certainly not ferry you across.
Suddenly, the World-Honored One saw a flock of geese flying through the air from the southern bank of the Ganges.
He came toward the north and spoke these verses: "The flocks of geese crossing the Ganges Never asked the boatman for a fare.
Each exerting its own strength, they flew freely through the air To wherever they wished to go.
I should now, by means of my supernormal power, Soar through the sky like those geese. When I reach the southern bank of the Ganges, I shall dwell there in peace and stability."
Like Mount Sumeru. At that time, having seen the Buddha pass by, the boatman felt great remorse in his heart, thinking:
"I beheld the Great Sage, a field of merit, yet I did not know to give alms so as to cross over to the other shore. Having thought thus, he fainted and fell to the ground.
After a long while, he regained consciousness and rose from the earth. He immediately went to King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, and reported these matters to him. The king...
Having heard this matter, he immediately commanded the boatman: "From this day forward, whenever any person who has left the household life seeks to cross, do not accept any payment."
The *Yaśas-causality-and-fruition-sūtra* states: There was a son of a householder named Yaśas, who possessed great eloquence, keen intelligence, and wisdom.
During the middle watch of the night, he saw a radiance in the sky; following the light, he went to the Deer Park and beheld the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Possessing the eighty minor marks, he prostrated before the Buddha and said, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will rescue and deliver me.
The Buddha said, "Do you know that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self? He replied, "Truly so.
Upon hearing these words, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and became an Arhat. He then requested ordination. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," and he immediately became one.
"Śramaṇa! At that time, Yaśas’s father sought his son Yaśas and went to where the Buddha was. By means of his supernormal powers, the Buddha concealed Yaśas and preached the Dharma for him, saying:
'Noble son, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, empty, suffering, and non-self.'"
"Do you know? When Yaśas’s father heard this, he was distanced from and freed of dust and defilement, and he perceived the path.

The Tathāgata asked him, "For what reason have you come here? He replied, "I am searching for my son. The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and father and son saw one another; their hearts were filled with great joy.
The Buddha then conferred upon him the three refuges, making him the first *upāsaka*.
Furthermore, fifty sons of elders who were friends of Yaśas, having heard that Yaśas had left the household life, went together to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested to go forth.

The Buddha said, "Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; do you understand this? Upon hearing this, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated. The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣus! You have immediately become śramaṇas. At that time, there were fifty-six arhats for the first time.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "You are capable of serving as the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. You should each travel to various regions to teach and transform others, delivering all sentient beings with a heart of compassion."
The *Sutra on the Causes and Effects of Subduing the Fire Dragon* states: The World-Honored One thought to himself, "Uruvilvā Kāśyapa has great renown;
I shall go to him and instruct him with the True Dharma. He immediately went to seek him out. As the sun was about to set, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "I wish to..."
He stayed in the stone cave for one night. Kāśyapa said, "There is a venomous dragon within this stone cave; I fear it may harm you.
The Buddha said, "Even if there is a venomous dragon, I shall simply borrow its dwelling. Kāśyapa said, "If you can stay, then do as you please."
At that time, the Tathāgata entered a stone chamber, sat cross-legged, and entered into *samādhi*.
Then, the venomous dragon emitted smoke from its entire body. The World-Honored One immediately entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi), and the Buddha likewise emitted smoke.
The dragon became greatly enraged and fire issued from within its body; the Buddha also emitted fire. The two fires blazed together, consuming the stone chamber. Kāśyapa rose in the night.
Seeing the entire chamber ablaze, he was struck with terror and lamented in sorrow: "This great śramaṇa is so handsome and noble, yet he did not heed my words;
