now he is being consumed and harmed by a fire-dragon. He immediately ordered his disciples to douse it with water, but the fire could not be extinguished;
instead, the flames grew even more fierce. At that moment, the World-Honored One used his supernormal powers to subdue the venomous dragon and granted him the Three Refuges.
He placed it within his almsbowl. At dawn, he took the bowl containing the dragon and went out.
Kāśyapa and his disciples said, "World-Honored One, has the dragon’s fire caused you injury? The Buddha said, "I am inwardly pure; I can never be harmed by external calamities such as that.
That venomous dragon is now inside this bowl. He then lifted the bowl to show it to Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa...
When the teacher and his disciples saw that the fire did not burn them in the presence of the World-Honored One, and that he was able to subdue the venomous dragon and place it within his alms bowl,
Kāśyapa rejoiced and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Furthermore, he witnessed the violent torrent of water being divided and severed.
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* (*Puyao jing*) states: When the World-Honored One arrived at the Nairañjanā River, the current was swift and turbulent.

The Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the water to cease its flow and remain still, parting it asunder. He walked through the midst of the waters. Seeing this, Kāśyapa feared the Buddha would be swept away;
he immediately ordered his disciples to take a boat to retrieve him. The Buddha then passed through the bottom of the boat from within the water, yet there was no trace of a hole.
Kāśyapa prostrated himself and requested to become a śramaṇa. The Buddha said, "Return for now and inform your disciples.

Kāśyapa, having received these instructions, told his disciples, "I have received the Buddha’s precepts and wish to become a śramaṇa. His disciples said, "We pray that we may all follow you so that we too may become śramaṇas.
Thereupon, master and disciples removed their garments, furs, coarse wool, water-pots, staffs, sandals, and all implements used for tending the sacrificial fires.
Having cast everything into the water, they all went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and said: "Now we five hundred people all possess the aspiration for faith and wish to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha said, "Welcome. Kāśyapa and his five hundred followers shaved off their hair and beards and all became śramaṇas.
Kāśyapa’s two younger brothers—the elder named Nadī and the younger named Gaja—each had two hundred and fifty [disciples].
The ten disciples were at a hut by the water’s edge when they saw the fire-worship implements of various brahmins being carried downstream.
Fearing that their elder brother and five hundred men might be swept away by the great flood, they immediately ordered five hundred disciples to go upstream.
Upon seeing that their elder brother and his entire assembly had all become śramaṇas, they asked the elder brother, "In my mind, I considered you to be an arhat, along with the five..."
The hundred men declared with one voice, "We wish to become śramaṇas just as the Great Master has. The Buddha said, "Welcome.

The two younger brothers and their five hundred disciples shaved off their hair and beards, and all became śramaṇas. Thus, the Buddha now had a retinue of one thousand śramaṇas following him as he traveled.

The *Prakīrṇaka-vastu* (Discourse on the Abandonment of Ritual Implements) states: At that time, among the three Kāśyapas, there was a nephew, a brahmin with matted hair named Upasena, who was practicing the way of the rishis together with two hundred and fifty disciples on Mount Asura. He...
Hearing that his three uncles, the Kāśyapas, along with their disciples, had all gone forth under the Buddha and become renunciants, he came before his uncles and spoke this verse:
"Uncles, for a hundred years you have offered fire in vain, And likewise practiced those ascetic penances in vain.
Today you have together abandoned this dharma, Just as a snake sheds its old skin. Upasena said:
"O disciples, I now wish to go to the Buddha’s presence to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). What is your intention?
The disciples replied, "We too shall follow you. Together they went to the Buddha's presence and said, "We now wish to bring our disciples into the Buddha's Dharma to practice the holy life.
The Buddha said, "You should take for yourselves your deer-skin garments and your sacrificial fires."
They cast away all their ritual vessels. The brahmins declared that they would follow the instructions without fail;

they went to their dwellings and discarded and destroyed all the implements for fire sacrifice. Returning to the presence of the Buddha, they requested ordination. The World-Honored One granted his permission.
He then preached the Dharma to them further and, by means of the three types of supernormal power, instructed, benefited, and gladdened them. At that time, the assembly...

Having exhausted all outflows through unconditioned dharmas, their minds attained liberation. At that time, the World-Honored One gathered the assembly of bhikṣus, namely these two hundred and fifty persons together;
they had all gone forth from the household life as brahmins, and were all arhats who stood at the head [of the assembly].
They were the most excellent, the most sublime, the most supreme, and the most venerable, having immediately attained their own benefit. Following...
He attended upon the World-Honored One at the assembly where the Dharma was being preached.
The *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) of the Zhuyuan Monastery states: "The World-Honored One then [accompanied] the three brothers of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and their thousand [disciples]..."
The bhikṣu went to Rājagṛha and approached King Bimbisāra. The king and his hundred officials came out of the city to welcome the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them: "Great King, this body of the five aggregates has consciousness as its root.
Because of consciousness, the faculty of mind arises; because of the faculty of mind, form arises. Yet these phenomena of form arise and perish without staying, just like..."
This observer skillfully understands impermanence. By observing the body in this manner, one does not grasp at the characteristics of the body; thus, form is detached from both "I" and "mine.

If one can observe that form is detached from "I" and "mine," then the arising of form is itself the arising of suffering, and the cessation of form is itself the cessation of suffering. If a person can practice such contemplation, this is called liberation.
Having heard the Dharma, the king’s ministers and the people attained the pure Dharma-eye. At that time, the king said:
"From this day forth, I take refuge in the World-Honored One and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I shall ensure that the four requisites are never lacking for you.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will dwell in the Bamboo Grove. The Buddha said, "Excellent! The king then commanded his ministers to establish dwellings and build halls in the Bamboo Grove.

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will go and reside there. Thereupon, surrounded by bhikṣus and immeasurable devas, and accompanied by various musical performances, he dwelt with the King at the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the King held a precious vase filled with fragrant water in his hand and, before the Tathāgata, spoke these words: "I now offer this Bamboo Grove to the Tathāgata and..."

"O Bhikṣu-saṃgha, I pray that you will compassionately accept this for my sake. The various kings took the Buddha as their foremost leader, and the various monasteries were the first to be established.
The *Caiguo jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states: In the city of Rājagṛha, there were two Brahmins, wise and intelligent;
one was named Śāriputra and the other Maudgalyāyana. Each had one hundred disciples, and the two men were close friends. To an extreme degree...
They held one another in deep affection and all made a vow together: "If any of us first hears the sublime Dharma, we shall reveal it to one another.
At that time, Śāriputra suddenly encountered the bhikṣu Aśvajit on the road as he was entering the city to beg for alms.
His deportment was composed and dignified, so Śāriputra immediately asked him: "Who is your teacher? What instructions does he give, and what Dharma does he proclaim? The bhikṣu replied:
He said, "My teacher is of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the teacher of gods and humans. In his marks and signs, wisdom, and supernormal powers, there is no one equal to him.
Since I am young and my study of the Way has been brief, how could I possibly proclaim the Tathāgata’s subtle Dharma?
Nevertheless, I shall speak for you according to what I know. He then spoke these verses: "The root of all phenomena arises from causes and conditions; they are without [inherent existence]."

"Lord, if one understands this Dharma, one shall attain the true path. Having heard this, Śāriputra immediately attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement.

Then, as Śāriputra returned to his dwelling, Maudgalyāyana saw that his faculties were serene and composed, and he asked, "You must have heard the sublime Dharma. Śāriputra related [the matter] in full.
As previously described, upon hearing this, Maudgalyāyana attained the pure Dharma-eye. He then led two hundred disciples to the Bamboo Grove.
From afar, he beheld the Tathāgata’s majestic and dignified marks and features; his heart was filled with joy, and he aspired to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome," and ordained him as a śramaṇa. At that time, the World-Honored One was with one thousand two hundred and fifty people in Magadha.
He extensively delivered sentient beings in the kingdom of Videha.
The *Kāśyapa-seeks-Enlightenment Cause-and-Effect Sūtra* states: In the kingdom of Thulakṣa, there was a brāhmaṇa named Kāśyapa who was extremely great...
He was wise and had recited the four Vedas. His family was immensely wealthy and he was skilled in giving alms. His wife was so beautiful that she was peerless throughout the entire kingdom.
Yet, the husband and wife were free from carnal desire; they took no pleasure in the household life and felt weary of and detached from the world.
Contemplating and seeking the way of renunciation, they immediately abandoned their worldly affairs and entered the mountain forests. With mind and speech, they thought and said: "All..."
"The Buddha, the Tathāgata, has left the household life to practice the Way; I too shall now follow the Buddha and leave the household life.
He immediately cast off his gold-threaded robes and donned dyed saffron-colored patched garments, then shaved his own beard and hair.
At that time, the devas in the void, having seen Kāśyapa leave the household life, addressed him, saying: "Kāśyapa, King Śuddhodana of the Ikṣvāku lineage..."
"His name is Sarvārthasiddha; having left the household life to study the Way, he is titled Śākyamuni Buddha.
He currently resides within the Bamboo Grove. Upon hearing these words from the deva, Kāśyapa immediately proceeded to the Bamboo Grove.

The World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa was about to arrive and that it was appropriate to go and deliver him, set out and encountered Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa then prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "You are my Great Master; I am your disciple. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, you should know that the five aggregates and the physical body are a great mass of suffering.
Upon hearing this, Kāśyapa immediately perceived the Truths and eventually attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned with Kāśyapa to the Bamboo Grove. Because this Kāśyapa possessed such great majesty...

His virtue was esteemed by gods and humans; thus he was named Mahākāśyapa. Even until the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he maintained the Dharma and its transformative influence so that it might extend into future ages;
this was due to the power of this man.

Regarding the false accusation of pregnancy, the *Caitra-sūtra* states: Not long after the World-Honored One had first attained the Way of the Buddha, the six heretical teachers flourished. [The Buddha said:
"I have one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, all of whom have attained arhatship and possess the unimpeded six supernormal powers. At that time, there was a woman named Ciñcā-mānavikā...

That woman was a disciple of Ājīvakas such as Gosāla; having received her teacher’s instructions, she came daily to the Buddha’s presence, outwardly manifesting the conduct of a lay follower while inwardly following the teachings of that heterodox master.
She moved about so as to be seen by others, gradually making her belly larger by stuffing it with grass, until later she tied a wooden bowl to her abdomen as if she were about to give birth.
At that time, the false teacher asked the woman, "How did you come to have this body? She replied, "Because I go every day to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama, I have this body.
The teacher immediately spoke in anger, "You have deceived my disciple! This disciple of mine was on the verge of being reborn in the Brahma Heaven;
you have brought disgrace upon my disciple by reducing him to such a state as this. Then the false teacher led his disciples...
The son, together with this woman, went to where the Buddha was. At that time, the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma to an assembly of immeasurable numbers.
When the Brahmin arrived at the Buddha’s place, he cried out in a loud voice: "This śramaṇa Gautama has committed sexual misconduct;
he has truly not attained the Way. The supernatural transformations he performs are all mere illusions and not the true Way," pointing his finger at him.
The woman said, "Do all sentient beings see this? Out of love for me, this girl has caused me to become pregnant.

Having spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a yellow rat. He gnawed the cord of the bowl inside the woman's skirt, causing it to break and the bowl to fall to the ground.
Everyone saw this. With one voice, the multitude reviled them, saying, "You followers of a heterodox teacher! You have slandered the Noble Ones!"
I have committed such sins as these.
In the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*,
it is said that when the father-king heard that his son had attained the Way six years prior, he spoke to Udāyin, saying:
"You should now go and invite the Buddha to return to the kingdom. It has been twelve years since we were parted, and he longs to see you once more.

Udāyin received these instructions and immediately went to the Buddha's dwelling. Having fully conveyed the king's intention, he expressed his wish to become a śramaṇa and attain the path of Arhatship.
The World-Honored One reflected that the king would then return to the kingdom and be able to deliver his parents; he thus spoke to Udāyin.

"You should first go and manifest the eighteen transformations. The King was greatly delighted and immediately commanded his ministers and the common people to travel forty *li* outside the city to welcome the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One’s majestic demeanor was dignified and sovereign. The Father King said, "We have been separated for many years; now we are able to meet again.
The great ministers and hundreds of officials prostrated themselves in salutation. Having seen the various śramaṇas, they were filled with affection...
He selected five hundred men from the prominent clans within the kingdom and ordained them as śramaṇas to attend upon the Buddha.
The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, also became a śramaṇa. Nanda’s attendant was named Upāli, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter. All those of noble rank have abandoned worldly glory, yet my own status is lowly."
"What is there for one of low status to covet or delight in? Only the Buddha’s compassion; may you grant me deliverance and permit me to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said, "Welcome," and ordained him as a śramaṇa. He sat down according to custom. Nanda paid homage [to the Buddha], but when he came to Upāli, he did not pay homage.
The Buddha told Nanda: "The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean; it receives the hundred rivers. The four currents flow into it, and all become of one taste. He then conferred [the precepts upon him].
"Regarding the precepts, they do not depend on whether one is noble or lowly. This body is a provisional name for the harmony of the four great elements;
fundamentally there is no 'self,' so do not give rise to arrogance. Nanda then prostrated himself in worship.
Regarding the recognition of the son and the clearing of doubts, the *Śrī-mālā-devī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: At that time, the Buddha entered the palace and sat upon the throne.

The king, along with his ministers and subjects, daily provided him with a hundred kinds of delicious foods. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, delivering immeasurable multitudes. Yaśodharā then took Rāhula...

They came to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and after gazing upon him and exchanging greetings, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "It has been a long time since we last attended upon you, and our offerings have been neglected for too long.
At present, all the members of the Śākya clan and their kin harbor doubts: 'The Prince left his kingdom twelve years ago;
how could Yaśodharā have conceived and given birth to Rāhula? The Buddha spoke to the King, his father, and the assembled ministers: "Yaśodharā..."
"Your conduct is chaste and pure, free from any blemish. If you do not believe me, I shall now provide proof.
At that time, the World-Honored One transformed all the bhikṣus so that they were exactly like the Buddha, their marks and signs and their radiance being identical and without distinction.
At that moment, Rāhula was seven years old; Yaśodharā then gave him her signet ring as a token.
He spread out [the net] and said to him, "This is for your father; give it to him.
At that moment, Rāhula went directly to where the Buddhas were and offered the seal-ring to the World-Honored One. The king and his ministers were all filled with joy and exclaimed in praise.
"Excellent! Rāhula is truly the son of the Buddha. The Buddha said to the King, his father, and the ministers:
"From this day forward, you should no longer harbor doubts. This is my son; he was born through my miraculous transformation. Do not blame Yaśodharā."

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the king, who immediately attained the Way. The ministers, the myriad subjects, and the ladies of the inner palace all received the precepts;

they observed the six monthly fasts and the three annual fasts, purely cultivating the Brahma-faring. Within the realm, there was peace and tranquility, wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, and the myriad states came to offer congratulations.

The *Baozang jing* (Ratnakoṭi Sūtra), in the section on "Saving His Brother Nanda," states: When the Buddha went to Nanda’s house to beg for food, Nanda paid his respects, took the bowl, filled it with rice, and offered it to the Buddha.
The Buddha did not accept the bowl and followed Nanda to the vihāra. There, the Buddha urged Nanda to shave his head; Nanda constantly desired...
He returned home, but the Buddha would not permit it. He waited for the Buddha to go out and then took a different path back. The Buddha immediately came by that same alternative path.
Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he hid behind a large tree. The Buddha then lifted the tree up into the air.
Seeing that Nanda was about to return to the monastery, the Buddha took Nanda to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and showed him all the celestial palaces. There he saw one palace...
Within it were various celestial maidens, but no celestial youths. Nanda then asked, "Why is it that this palace alone has no celestial youths?
They replied, "Nanda, when you have left the household life and your life ends, you shall be born in this celestial palace. Nanda then wished to remain there immediately.
The celestial maidens told him, "We are devas; you are currently a human being. You must first relinquish your human lifespan and be reborn here."
After a short while, the Buddha took Nanda back to hell. He saw that all the cauldrons were boiling people, except for one cauldron which was steaming empty space.
The Buddha stopped there, and Nanda immediately asked why. The hell-warden replied, "Nanda, by virtue of his renunciation he would have been reborn in heaven;
however, because he abandoned the path out of desire, he has fallen into this hell at the end of his life. For this reason, I am now boiling this cauldron."
As he waited, Nanda became terrified, fearing that the hell-wardens would detain him. He immediately cried out, "Namo Buddhāya!
May the Buddha protect me and lead me back to the vihāra. The Buddha said to Nanda, "You must diligently uphold the precepts and cultivate your heavenly merit."
Nanda replied, "I do not wish to be born in heaven; my only wish is that I may not fall into this hell.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and within twenty-one days, he became an Arhat.

The *Rāhula-pravrajyā-aśrutapūrva-nidāna-sūtra* states: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, the World-Honored One sent Maudgalyāyana to inform his father and Yaśodharā, saying, "Prince Rāhula is now nine years old; he should be permitted to leave the household life. Yaśodharā replied:
She said, "When the Tathāgata was a crown prince, he took me as his wife. Before nine years had passed, he fled to the mountains and marshes and practiced austerities for six years.
Having attained Buddhahood, he returned to his kingdom. Now he wishes to seek out my son to ordain him. How cruel this is!

At that time, Maudgalyāyana used skillful means to instruct and persuade her, but she showed no intention of listening. The World-Honored One then dispatched a devaputra from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven to appear in the air.
He said to her: "Do you recall when you bought five stalks of lotuses for five hundred silver coins to offer to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?

At that time, you requested of me, 'In every lifetime, may I be your wife. I replied, 'A Bodhisattva practices vows throughout many kalpas, practicing all forms of giving and never refusing the wishes of others.
If you can do so, I will allow you to be my wife. You then made a vow, saying, 'I shall follow whatever you give away. He swore this oath.
[She] had no regretful heart. Why then does she now cherish Rāhula and not allow him to leave the household life?
Having heard this, Yaśodharā recalled her past lives as if seeing them yesterday; her maternal affection for her son naturally subsided. She took Rāhula’s hand and entrusted him to Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately assembled the noble clans of the kingdom and commanded each to send one son to follow me.
There were fifty of Sun’s sons who went to the place where the Buddha was.
He ordered Ānanda to shave their heads, and appointed Śāriputra as their upādhyāya and Maudgalyāyana as their ācārya. Rāhula did not take pleasure in listening to the Dharma;
therefore, the Buddha spoke to him of a marvelous causal connection, whereby he received the ten precepts and donned the kāṣāya upon his body. Immediately—
He became a śramaṇa and subsequently realized the four fruits of the path.
According to the *Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish*, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī had a minister named Sudatta. His household was immensely wealthy, and he provided relief to all in need.
Because he provided for the poor and all those who were orphaned or aged, he was named Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute).

When he went to the great city of Rājagṛha to marry his son to a wife, he stayed at the house of the minister Ghoṣila. That family had prepared great offerings and extensively arranged food and drink.
Sudatta asked, "Householder, for whom do you intend to invite tonight as you personally exert yourself to prepare these drinks and foods? He replied, "I am inviting..."
"Buddha and Saṃgha. When Sudatta heard the names "Buddha" and "Saṃgha," his heart and mind were filled with joy. He asked, "What is meant by 'Buddha'?

He replied, "Prince Siddhārtha, son of King Śuddhodana, immediately took seven steps at the time of his birth. Raising his hand, he declared: 'In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored.
Having witnessed the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, he left the home life to practice the Way. For six years, he engaged in ascetic practices."

Because he has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he is called a Buddha. Again, it was asked: "What is meant by 'Saṅgha'? He replied: "After the Buddha had attained the Way, Brahmā entreated him to preach the Dharma.
For the sake of the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths; their outflows were exhausted and their fetters were untied."
He thus became a śramaṇa, capable of serving as a fertile field of merit for sentient beings; therefore, he is called the Saṃgha.
Having heard this, Sudatta immediately conceived faith and looked forward to going to see the Buddha at dawn. At dawn, he arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was.

Knowing that Sudatta had come, the World-Honored One went outside to practice walking meditation. Sudatta saw the Buddha, who was like a mountain of gold, with his marks and signs and majestic countenance.
He stood with solemn dignity, his joy redoubled; he prostrated himself, knelt with palms joined, and inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him—the subtle and wondrous Four Noble Truths of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and was immediately imbued with the noble Dharma, attaining the stage of Srotāpanna.
Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
Volume I (2) / Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Volume I (3).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Baocheng of Baoen Monastery.

Regarding the story of covering the ground with gold, the *Xiányújīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) states: Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying, "I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to visit Śrāvastī, so that the sentient beings therein may abandon evil and turn toward the right path.
The World-Honored One replied, "There is no vihāra there. Sudatta said, "Your disciple is able to build one."
"I pray that you will grant me your permission. The World-Honored One remained silent. The Buddha then commanded Śāriputra to go together with him to inspect various sites.
They found that only the site of Prince Jeta’s garden was truly suitable for the construction of a vihāra.
Upon reaching the prince’s residence, he said to him: "I now wish to erect a vihāra for the Tathāgata. Your garden is excellent; I now wish to purchase it."
The Prince said, "If you can cover the ground with gold such that no space remains empty, I shall indeed give it to you.
Sudatta sent men who loaded eighty *krośas* of gold upon elephants; in a short while, they were nearly finished, lacking only a small portion of ground.
The Prince said, "I am weary of this expense; let it be. Sudatta replied, "No. He thought to himself, 'What treasure of gold could ever suffice? The Prince [continued].
He thought to himself, "The Buddha must possess such great virtue that he can cause this man to regard wealth so lightly as to command him to stop and not produce the gold.
He then said, "The garden grounds belong to you; the trees belong to me. I shall offer them to the Buddha and together we shall establish a vihāra. Sudatta agreed to this.
Even as they were constructing and erecting the vihāras, building halls for the Buddha and separate rooms for his residence, there were twelve hundred people across one hundred and twenty sites.
He then reflected, "There is a king above; I ought to inform him. He immediately went to report to the king, saying, "I only pray that Your Majesty will dispatch an envoy to invite the Buddha.
Having heard this, the king sent an envoy to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha. At that time—
The World-Honored One emitted light and caused the earth to tremble as he traveled to Śrāvastī. For the great assembly gathered there, he preached the sublime Dharma;
according to their past affinities, each attained the fruits of the Path, and Yuyé received his instruction.
The *Yujie jing* (Sūtra of Yujie) states: The householder Anāthapiṇḍada took a wife for his son; the woman’s name was Yujie.

She did not serve her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband with the propriety due to a daughter-in-law. The householder and his wife deliberated, saying, "Our son's wife is disobedient; only the Buddha can transform her."
He then invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his home. Everyone came forth to pay homage to the Buddha, but Yuye fled and hid away, refusing to prostrate before him.

The Buddha immediately performed a miraculous transformation, causing the walls of the elder’s residence to become like the color of lapis lazuli and crystal, so that the interior and exterior could see one another.
Yuye then emerged to pay homage to the Buddha and repent. The Buddha said to Yuye: "You must not treat your husband with contempt."

Within the body of a woman there are many evils. When first born and falling to the ground, her parents do not rejoice. In raising her, they find no pleasure; their minds are constantly fearful of others.
Her parents perpetually worry about the dowry for her marriage. From birth, she is separated from her kin. She is always in fear of her husband. Childbirth is exceedingly difficult.
In youth, she is scrutinized and controlled by her parents; in middle age, she is constrained by her husband; in old age, she is rebuked by her children and grandchildren.
The way of a wife is to lie down after [the husband] and rise before him, attending diligently to her tasks. Whenever there is food or drink, she must not eat first.
She must not harbor resentment if her husband scolds or reviles her. She must not engage in illicit sexual conduct. When her husband goes abroad, she shall manage the household affairs.

She constantly dwells upon her husband’s virtues and does not dwell upon his faults. She serves her husband with humility and obedience to his commands; rising early and retiring late, she is reverent and diligent in carrying out his instructions.
Her mouth utters no idle words and her body performs no idle deeds. When there is merit, she attributes it to others; when there is fault, she takes it upon herself.
She was instructed with benevolence and kindness to encourage the practice of goodness. Her heart was upright and her mind single-minded, free from any improper gaze;
she directly cultivated the virtues of a wife until the end, never failing or neglecting them. In her conduct and etiquette, she held harmony as most precious. Yuye addressed the Buddha:
"From this day forward, I shall serve my parents-in-law and my husband."
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (Xiányújīng) states: At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling toward the city of Vaiśālī and sat down not far from the river Līyuè (Lohitya).
At that moment, a fisherman caught a fish in his net; five hundred men pulled at it but could not bring it out. He then called out...
A thousand cowherds together hauled out a fish that had a hundred heads on its body.
Upon it were various kinds of beings such as donkeys, horses, camels, tigers, wolves, pigs, dogs, monkeys, foxes, and raccoon dogs.
The World-Honored One went to where the fish was and asked it, "Are you Kāpilī? It replied, "Truly I am. Ānanda addressed the Buddha.
"For what reason is this fish like this? The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the past, there was a brāhmaṇa who had a son named Kāpilīya.
He was intelligent and profoundly learned. His mother asked her son, 'My son, you are naturally brilliant; is there anyone more excellent than you? He replied, 'A śramaṇa.
His mother said, 'Why do you not go to study under him and learn his dharma? Following his mother's instruction, he immediately—"

In the past, he studied and mastered the meanings and principles of the Tripitaka. Whenever he engaged in discussion with the bhikṣus, if his reasoning was deficient or he was outwitted, he would immediately revile them, saying:
"You fools are devoid of discernment; you are worse than beasts! What dharma do you know?
He compared all manner of hundred-headed animals to them. Due to the retribution of these actions, he now suffers the body of a hundred-headed fish. At that time...
The fishermen and cowherds simultaneously sought ordination as monks under the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma to them with various exhortations on the nature of suffering;

their outflows were exhausted and their fetters severed, and they immediately became śramaṇas. At that time, Ānanda and the great multitude, hearing what the Buddha had said, were despondent and unhappy.
Grief and sorrow filled their hearts, and with one voice they spoke these words: "Body, speech, and mind—"
One must be careful in one's conduct.

The *Moonlight Sutra on the Elder’s Son Moonlight Admonishing His Father* states: There was an elder named Shenri (Śin-ni) who believed in and followed the six heterodox teachers, including Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
The son of [Devadatta], named Candraprabha, remonstrated with his father, saying: "The Buddha is a Great Sage, the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Formerly, on the day the World-Honored One sought the Way, the sixth celestial Mara, seeing the Buddha’s divine sanctity, felt vexed and poisonous in his heart.
He thought that once the Buddha’s Way was perfected, he would surely surpass him, and thus he plotted [the following]."

They devised a stratagem. They summoned their ghostly armies, raising troops and gathering a multitude. Clad in armor and wielding spears, their banners and standards eclipsed the sun, obscuring the heavens.
Of strange forms and diverse species, they underwent a thousand transformations; some carried mountains and bore stones, while others spat fire from their mouths and eyes.

With a single voice they roared and shouted toward the World-Honored One. The Buddha, with a mind of compassion, raised his hand and pointed at them; the host of ghosts and evil soldiers naturally [subdued].
They retreated and dispersed. The Māra-king prostrated and vowed to take refuge. At that time, the Tathāgata subdued the evil that filled the heavens and made him a disciple.
With the poison of Mount Sumeru or the fires of a great trichiliocosm, even swords, spears, and blades could not move a single hair of the Buddha’s body.
Now, he seeks to harm the Buddha with a pit of fire and poisoned rice; it is, for example, like this:
It is like the power of mosquitoes and gadflies wishing to topple Mount Tai, or the wings of flies and gnats wishing to obstruct the sun and moon;

they merely bring themselves ruin and exhaustion, yet it would be better to repent and confess one’s transgressions early on to escape punishment. The body of the Tathāgata is the adamantine essence of virtue.

I pray that my father will reform and repent, taking refuge in the World-Honored One. Elder Shenri, obscured by the canopy of his own sins, finds his mind unenlightened; he says to his son: "The Buddha..."
One who possesses supernormal powers perceives what has not yet occurred; they should have foreseen that I would prepare a fire pit and poisoned rice, and now accept my invitation.
Judging by this, he certainly lacks foresight.
The *Moonlight Youth Sutra on Śreṇika’s Poisoned Meal* states: At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation of the elder Śreṇika, but it was not like his usual practice.

He manifested his majestic spiritual power to move the ten directions, causing them to submit with heartfelt devotion so as to widely transform beings without limit, and he also transformed the six heretical teachers.
Together with nine thousand six hundred non-Buddhist practitioners, he emitted a great radiance that reached the very limits of the Buddha’s realm.

Upon arriving at the elder’s gate, the fire pit was instantly transformed into a pool of water, from which a great lotus flower emerged. When Shenri saw this, his heart stirred and his spirit was struck with alarm;
trembling with fear and agitation, he thought to himself: "The transgressions and evils I have committed are most unrighteous. He then looked toward the Six Masters and said: "I am now like..."

At this, the six masters were struck with terror and shame; they immediately fled and hid themselves. Shenri (Śroṇa) prostrated himself and said, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will forgive my ignorance and folly.
Relying on evil words, I gave rise to a mind of malice. Fortunately, I have relied upon your compassionate transformation;

I beg you to pardon my transgressions. Within the food and drink, he had placed poison throughout. He requested, "Please wait a moment while I cook more food. The Buddha said, "Bring the food here at once."
"There is no need for further preparation. Greed, lust, anger, hatred, ignorance, and false views are the world’s most grievous poisons;
I possess none of these poisons. These poisons have already been extinguished; they cannot harm me. As Shenri served the food, its fragrance permeated the ten directions.

Shenri addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Buddha possesses great compassion and takes pity on sentient beings, rescuing me from this mire of suffering. The Buddha told Shenri, "You are able to awaken yourself."
Enlightened! Your heavy sins shall surely be eradicated. I shall extensively proclaim the principles of the Way for you, so that your mind may attain liberation.

I shall expound at length immeasurable Dharma teachings: the eight liberations, the four truths, the three deliverances, and the six perfections—the profound essentials of the Path and subtle practices.

I shall explain the emptiness of the triple world and the causal conditions of all phenomena; I shall prescribe remedies according to the ailments, like a physician selecting medicine, and shall extend my teaching by preaching the Dharma as is appropriate.
Upon seeing [the Buddha], his mind was awakened, his doubts were resolved, and he was freed from affliction.

The *Buddhāvadāna-śraddhā-prasāda-kṛta-mūḍha-buddhi-saṃbodhana-sūtra* states: In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the son of a chief minister named Aśoka (Unafflicted). He was valiant and possessed...
His strength was such that he could match a thousand men. His father sent him to a Brahmin teacher, who instructed him:

"Within seven days, you must sever the heads of a thousand men and take a finger from each to fashion a garland for adornment; Brahmā will come to welcome you, and you shall certainly be reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
Without hesitation, he received the instruction, took up his sword, and ran outside. Whenever he saw a person, he would kill them; everyone called him Aṅgulimāla.
He traveled about committing these killings until the morning of the seventh day, at which point he had obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine fingers, lacking only one.
Everyone hid and fled, with no one daring to go near him; they searched everywhere but could not find him. In the midst of these seven days, his mother took food and went there in person.
When the boy saw his mother from afar, he ran toward her, intending to kill her. His mother said, "Why do you harbor such rebellious intent as to wish to harm me?
The boy replied, "I have received my teacher’s instruction that within seven days I must obtain a full thousand fingers. He was born [into this state].
Brahmā, when the days were nearly complete—lacking only one finger—he desired to kill his mother. At that time, the Buddha manifested as a śramaṇa walking along the side of the road.
Upon seeing him, the son felt no more distress and abandoned his mother, hurrying quickly toward the monk. Seeing him approaching, the Buddha walked slowly away.
Aṅgulimāla ran with all his might but could not catch up. He called out from afar, "Śramaṇa, stop for a moment! The Buddha replied from a distance, "I always abide in stillness;
it is only you who do not abide. Aṅgulimāla asked again, "In what way do you abide while I do not?"
The Buddha said, "My faculties are tranquil and stabilized, and I have attained mastery. You, however, have received false teachings from a heterodox master;
your mind has been transformed and cannot abide in stillness. Day and night you commit slaughter and create boundless offenses.
Upon hearing this, Wunao’s mind was awakened, and he went forth as a monk under the Buddha.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Subduing of the Six Heretics* states: The Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, King Bimbisāra had already attained the first fruit [of the path], and his heart of faith and reverence became doubly profound. In the kingdom...
There were six teachers, such as Pūraṇa and others, who previously in that kingdom had spread false views and perverse doctrines, deceiving and deluding the myriad people.

Those who were mired in ignorance believed in these heterodox teachings; their followers proliferated extensively, and their evil faction filled the land. At that time, the king had a younger brother who venerated these six teachers.
Deluded by their heterodoxy and perversity, he believed they possessed the Way and exhausted his family’s wealth to provide for them without lack. His elder brother—
King Bimbisāra earnestly and skillfully exhorted him to take refuge in the Buddha. However, the younger brother clung to heterodox principles and did not follow his elder brother’s advice.

The younger brother said to his elder brother, the King: "I already have my own teacher; I shall no longer serve the Buddha. He then sent a messenger to summon the six heretical masters, who all came together to deliberate on this matter.
Once the six masters had assembled, they each spoke in council: "Our skills and talents are no less than [those of the Buddha]."
The Buddha immediately went to the king’s location and personally described his own wisdom, spiritual transformations, and miraculous arts. He invited the king to test him.

The king led the six masters to the Buddha’s location and declared that the six masters wished to compete in their arts; he prayed only that the World-Honored One would exert his divine power to convert and subdue the wicked.
At that time, the Buddha ascended the seat; Śakra attended on his left, and Brahmā attended on his right, while the king sat before him.

Surrounded by myriads of followers, the Buddha slowly extended his arm and caught the seat with his hand. Immediately, five great spirit-kings (mahārājika) crushed, struck, and dragged the bodies of the six teachers.
Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Keeper, grasped a vajra-pestle; from the head of the pestle, fire burst forth as he raised it to threaten the six teachers.
The six teachers were struck with terror and fled in haste. The disciples of the six teachers sought mercy and repented. For...
A disciple of the Buddha aspired to become a śramaṇa.
Holding a sword, he sought to harm [the Buddha].
The *Píngděngjīng* (Sūtra on the Equal Treasure) states: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, there was a brahmin minister who was violent and impetuous by nature.
She did not follow the path, and her wife’s wickedness and flattery were likewise no different. The husband said to his wife, "The Śramaṇa Gautama is within this kingdom;
if he comes, do not open the door. One day, the Tathāgata suddenly stayed in their house.
When the Brahmin woman saw him, she remained silent and did not speak to him at all. The Buddha then said to her: "You..."
The brahmin was foolish and held false views; he did not believe in the Three Jewels. When his wife heard these words, she was seized by great anger.
She stripped off her pearl necklaces, put on soiled garments, and sat upon the ground. When her husband returned from outside, he asked, "Why are you like this?
She replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama has insulted me, saying such things as: 'You, O brahmin, are a heretic.'"
Seeing this, he did not believe him. The man said, "Wait until tomorrow. On the following day, he opened his gate and waited for the Buddha to arrive.

Later, during midday, the Buddha appeared at his house. The Brahmin immediately seized a sharp sword and struck at the Buddha, but the Buddha manifested supernatural powers so that [the sword] could not reach him.
Seeing the Buddha in the midst of the air, he felt deep shame and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray only that the World-Honored One will descend and accept my repentance.
The Buddha immediately descended and accepted his repentance, preaching the essentials of the Dharma for him. Both husband and wife attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

At that time, when the people heard that the Buddha had thus converted such an evil person, they each said, "The appearance of the World-Honored One in this world is most marvelous and extraordinary. The Buddha told the assembly:
People say: "It is not only today that you have subdued and transformed such evil persons; in the past as well, you once tamed and transformed such evil persons.
Thus, the Buddha saved the Nirgranthas.

The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Tathāgata subdued the six heterodox teachers of wrong views and their followers, causing them all to be utterly defeated.
The five hundred Nirgranthas then thought to themselves, "Our entire assembly has been completely shattered and dispersed.
It would be better for us to burn our bodies and thus ensure our passage to the next world. They immediately gathered firewood and...
Desiring to burn his body, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, wished to uproot their suffering so that the fire would not ignite.
The Buddha stood by his side and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi). When the Nirgranthas saw the great mass of fire, they felt joy in their hearts and spoke these words:
"We have no need for fire; let us all cast ourselves [into it]. Once they reached the mass of fire, their bodies became cool and they experienced supreme bliss.
Seeing the Buddha in its midst, they were redoubled in joy and sought to leave the household life. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained arhatship.
Their hair and beards fell away, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
In the past, there was a caravan leader who entered the sea to gather treasures. Favorable winds carried him directly to the place of jewels.
The merchants, driven by greed, took up precious gems until their ship was filled to capacity. The caravan leader warned them, "Do not overload yourselves with treasure, lest you lose your lives."
At that time, the merchants would not listen to his words; they would rather die with their treasures than reduce their load.
The merchant leader immediately cast the treasures from his own ship into the sea and took the other merchants onto his vessel.
Because those treasure ships were so heavily laden, they all sank into the sea, while only the merchant leader’s ship rescued the merchants, and they all reached safety.

He returned home. At that time, the merchant leader felt profound compassion and sought to save the merchants; he now employed various skillful means to preach the Dharma and deliver the non-Buddhists.
He first established the precept platform.

The *Jietan tu jing* (Sutra on the Diagrams of the Precept Platform) states: While the Buddha was in the courtyard of the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, Lohita Bodhisattva requested the Buddha to establish a precept platform for the purpose of formulating and receiving the precepts.

At that time, the Tathāgata granted his consent according to these words and established three platforms to the east of the gate of the Buddha’s courtyard, naming it the "Precept Platform for the Buddha to Formulate Precepts for Bhikṣus.
To the west of the gate of the Buddha’s courtyard, the Buddha [established the platform] for the bhikṣuṇīs...

The Bhikṣuṇī established the boundary for the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*). To the south of the eastern gate of the outer enclosure, he established a platform for the monks to confer the precepts upon bhikṣus.
The ordination platform rises from the ground and is characterized by three tiers, symbolizing the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma.
Since ordinary delusions cannot be dispelled without emptiness, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, offered a covered cauldron and placed it upon the platform to serve as a vessel.
Śāriputra, the Great Brahmā King offered a priceless precious gem and placed it atop the lid of the urn as an offering to the śarīras;
this constitutes the fifth layer, symbolizing the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya). The precious gem offered by the Great Brahmā King was as large as a five-sheng jar.
Those with great merit and virtue saw its light illuminating eight hundred yojanas, while those with meager merit and virtue saw it as if it were [a mere glimmer].
The ink gathered. Once the altar was completed, at that time the Buddhas of the ten directions, immeasurable bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all assembled like clouds.
The Buddhas ascended it and together deliberated upon the characteristics of the gravity of the precepts, their observance and violation, and so forth.

They further deliberated on the matter of ordaining bhikṣuṇīs and the signs of the extinction of the True Dharma. The Buddhas deliberated collectively, saying: "In antiquity there were four divisions [of the Saṃgha]; why is it that now there is none alone? At first...
Even though the True Dharma has been extinguished for half its duration, because the nuns observe the Eightfold Respectful Conduct, they shall remain for another thousand years.
Therefore, these two platforms are ascended by the Buddha alone to perform buddha-work together with him. The outer enclosure is the ordination platform for monks;
it is the platform where monks confer the precepts upon bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Regarding the proclamation of the Dharma of the precepts, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "At that time, Vairocana Buddha sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower and emitted a great radiance.
He addressed Śākyamuni Buddha on the thousand-petaled calyx, saying: 'The Diamond Jewel Precepts within the Mind-Ground are the original source of all Buddhas.'"
The seed of the Buddha-nature of Bodhisattvas: all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
At that time, after Śākyamuni Buddha had first attained perfect enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:

"One should be filial toward one's parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem. Filial piety is the dharma of the Ultimate Way. Filiality is called the precept, and it is also called restraint. Thus spoke the Buddha.
He immediately emitted immeasurable rays of light and, for the sake of the great assembly, expounded the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas. The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"All you sons of the Buddha, the great assembly of bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on enlightenment, you should receive and uphold them.
Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Those who receive the Buddha-precepts—whether they be kings, princes, ministers, high officials, or bhikṣus—"

Bhikṣuṇīs, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the six heavens of desire, commoners, eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves, the eight classes of spirits and deities, Vajrapāṇi, animals, and even transformed beings—all who understand the words of the Dharma Master may fully receive the precepts.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of inexhaustible treasury precepts. The first is not to kill living beings. The second...
1. Not stealing property. 2. [Not taking what is not given. 3. Not engaging in sexual misconduct. 4. Not speaking falsehoods. 5. Not drinking intoxicants. 6.
Not speaking of the faults of householders or monastics. 7. Not praising oneself and disparaging others.
8. Not being stingy with wealth and goods. 9. Not harboring anger. 10. Not holding wrong views or slandering the Triple Gem.
O Jewel, you should uphold this with a reverent mind.

Regarding Mahāprajāpatī’s request for ordination, the *Zhongbenqijing* (Sutra of the Middle Arising) states: When the Buddha entered the kingdom of Kapilavastu, his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to the Buddha.
She said: "I have heard that a woman who exerts diligence can attain the four stages of a śramaṇa.
I wish to receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya and leave the household life to practice the Way. The Buddha said: "Stop for now. If women enter my Dharma and Vinaya and don the dharma-robes..."
"You should practice the pure Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) for as long as you live. The aunt pleaded with him three times, but the Buddha would not grant her request.
Standing outside the gate, she wept and sobbed. Ānanda then asked his maternal aunt why she was so distressed.

She replied, "I am grieving because I am not permitted to go forth [into the religious life]. Ānanda said, "Please compose yourself for a moment; wait while I inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Stop, stop!"
Ānanda spoke again: "My aunt has many virtuous intentions. When the Buddha was first born, she personally nurtured him until he reached adulthood.
The Buddha said: "She has indeed shown me great kindness. Seven days after I was born, my mother passed away; she then raised and nourished me until I grew up.
Now that I have become a Buddha in the world, I likewise owe much gratitude and virtue to my maternal aunt. However—"

"Because of me, they are able to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and to uphold the prohibitive precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no lying, and no drinking alcohol.
The Buddha said, "If a woman wishes to become a śramaṇī, there are eight rules of respect that she must not transgress;
she must study and practice them for as long as she lives. If she can truly uphold these eight rules of respect, she is permitted to become a śramaṇī, Ānanda."
He then explained the Buddha’s injunctions to his maternal aunt. His aunt assented, saying, "So be it.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If women were allowed to become śramaṇīs, my True Dharma would decline by five hundred years. Why is this?
It is simply because there are five conditions that women cannot fulfill."
The *Sūtra on the Former Deeds of the Woman Bhadrā* states: At that time, the World-Honored One permitted women to leave the household life.
Mahākāśyapa, observing with his divine eye, saw that the woman Bhadrā-Kapilā had departed from the place of the Pāṣaṇḍaka heretics.
While she was training in the path at home, [the Buddha] immediately commanded a bhikṣuṇī endowed with supernatural powers to go to that woman’s place and say:
"Your husband Kāśyapa has gone forth from home with me as our common teacher to train in the path and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
You too may now go to his place to practice the holy life. The woman Bhadrā asked the bhikṣuṇī: "Who is your teacher?"

He replied, "My teacher is Śākyamuni Buddha. He is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and great loving-kindness and great compassion;
his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are all complete. His disciples are likewise so. The woman Bhadrā said, "If it is so..."

"I shall follow you. Then, together with the girl Bhadrā, the bhikṣuṇī traveled by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling in the time it takes to bend or stretch one's arm.
She prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said, "World-Honored One, please grant me permission to go forth (*pravrajyā*).
The World-Honored One told Mahāprajāpatī: "This girl is permitted to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Bhadrā...
Not long after the Licchavi woman had gone forth, she went to a secluded place to dwell alone in tranquility. Remaining far removed from all defilements, she practiced with diligent austerity;
her mind and body were unremitting as she dwelt in contemplation. She cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and attained the vision of the Dharma in this very life.

Having personally realized the supernormal powers and attained a state of peaceful dwelling, she proclaimed aloud: "Birth and death have been severed; the holy life has been established; that which was to be done has been accomplished."
"His task is accomplished; he shall not undergo further existence.
[The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Forest at Kapilavastu and addressed Udāyin: 'You..."
"You may enter the city and inform the King, your father. Udāyin, by means of his supernormal powers, flew through the air to the residence of King Śuddhodana.
When the King saw him from afar, he asked, "Great Teacher, where have you come from? He replied, "I have come to beg for alms on behalf of the Tathāgata.
The King said, "You should return quickly to the Buddha's presence and offer this food to the Buddha; I, too, shall now go to see him."
“World-Honored One, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he first manifested auspicious signs. When King Śuddhodana saw these signs, he commanded his ministers, saying:
‘Quickly prepare excellent vehicles, incense, flowers, banners, and canopies, and proceed to the place where the Buddha is.

At that time, for the sake of converting the king, the World-Honored One rose above the level of humans and traveled with sovereign ease through the midst of the void. Mahābrahmā and Śakra-devendra...”
Śakra-devānām-indra, Suyāma-deva, Tuṣita-deva, Nirmāṇarati-deva-king, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin-deva-king each held incense, flowers, banners, and streamers to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
The devaputras of the Cāturmahārājika-heaven and the Trāyastriṃśa-heaven scattered celestial incense and flowers from mid-air to make offerings to the Tathāgata. At that time, King Śuddhodana...
Having seen this, a sense of wonder arose in his heart, and he spoke these words:
"When the Tathāgata was a youth, he felt no lingering attachment to being a Wheel-Turning Sage King over the four continents.
Now, within this trichiliocosm, he acts as the Great Dharma King, sovereign over the wealth and nobility of gods and humans. Now this World-Honored One is the True Dharma King; I now..."

Surrounded by these people, the World-Honored One was attended by devas and humans. At that time, King Śuddhodana, without realizing it, prostrated with his head at the ground to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.

The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that when the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the King, he addressed the King, his father, saying: "The Dharma I have taught is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching; its flavor is also excellent. It is pure and unadulterated, clear and untainted, and is proclaimed with full clarity."

The Dharma of the Brahma-faring: each part shall be analyzed and explained. These are the six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
There are the six bases of contact: the spheres of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness. If one conditions a favorable object, a mind of attachment arises;
if one conditions an unfavorable object, anger and resentment arise; and toward neutral objects, a mind of delusion arises. Thus one acts in accordance with these conditions.
Form gives rise to desire; when one acts in opposition to form, anger arises; when one acts with indifference toward it, ignorance arises.

Thus, these three conditions give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion. Because of greed, hatred, and delusion, one falls into the four evil realms, revolving through birth and death with no prospect of liberation.
Great King, such karmic actions and their retributions are never lost or destroyed; there is no such thing as acting [and not being affected].
"O Great King, there is no one who experiences retribution; it exists only in accordance with worldly convention and not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
You should know, O Great King, that all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent. That all phenomena are empty is the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)."
Emptiness devoid of the characteristic of emptiness is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). If there are no signs, then there is no aspiration;

this is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). All phenomena possess these three gates of liberation. They proceed together with emptiness as the preliminary path to Nirvāṇa;
they are far removed from signs and far removed from aspiration. Ultimately, the realm of Nirvāṇa is definitively like the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all-pervasive.

Pervading the reaches of space, one should know that the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams. When the Buddha preached this Dharma, King Śuddhodana and the others attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha through Retained Images* states: At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Buddha is my son and I am the Buddha’s father.
Now that I am in this world, I behold the Buddha’s physical body; yet I see only its exterior and do not see its interior."
When Siddhārtha was in the palace, the physiognomists all saw the thirty-two marks;
now that he has attained Buddhahood, his radiance is even more manifest, surpassing that of former days by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should sentient beings of the final age contemplate the Buddha’s physical form, color, and marks? How may they know the Buddha’s radiance? I pray only that the World-Honored One will now explain this for me and for the assembly.
He gave rise to conceptual distinctions and delivered this exposition. At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Pervasive Body.
Emerging from this samādhi, five-colored rays of light issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating the crown of the Father King’s head, the vihāra, and the entire Sahā world-system.

It then re-entered through the crown of his head. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause the great assembly to see the Buddha’s physical body with perfect clarity, transformed a vihāra into a mountain of white jade, lofty and sublime in its proportions like Mount Sumeru, containing hundreds of thousands of grottoes and chambers.

Within the various niches and grottoes, images appeared that were indistinguishable from the Buddha himself. At that time, upon the ground before the Buddha, there was a great lotus flower with a thousand petals.
Each petal emitted a thousand rays of light, and from each ray emanated a thousand transformation Buddhas, each attended by a thousand disciples as their attendants.

The Buddha told the King, his father: "After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples can sever all worldly affairs, cast away all evils, and fix their mindfulness in contemplation upon the Buddha’s constant radiance, they may be said to see the Buddha even though he is not present.
Because they have seen the Buddha, all evils shall be extinguished, and according to their vows, they shall attain realization in future lives."
Regarding the three paths to enlightenment,
the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha by the Śākyas* states: At that time, five hundred Śākya sons addressed the Buddha, saying, "We constantly behold the Buddha."
"Their bodies are like charcoal men. What transgressions have we committed in our past lives?
We pray only that the Buddha-Sun may grant us liberation. The Buddha told the Śākya sons: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata.
There was a householder named Candrasūryaśrī who had five hundred sons. They were intelligent and possessed great wisdom; they extensively knew all the worldly arts, astrology,"
He was thoroughly versed in the ancient chronicles and calculations, leaving nothing unmastered. His father, the eldest son, had faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma;

he constantly taught his sons the method of contemplating the Buddha-mind and also expounded upon the twelve links of dependent origination. Having heard these teachings, the sons were filled with doubt and did not believe them, saying, "Our father has grown old and senile;
he has been deluded and misled by those śramaṇas. None of our own books contain such doctrines. Why does our father now [teach this]?"
While searching for them, he found them there. At that time, his sons suddenly fell gravely ill. Observing that his sons' lives could not be sustained much longer, the father said to them:
"You all held wrong views and did not believe in the True Dharma. Now the sword of impermanence cuts through your bodies;
your minds are distressed and agitated—upon whom can you rely? There is a Buddha named Vipaśyin; you should invoke His name. The sons then invoked: "Namo..."
"There is no Buddha. Our sons, upon the end of their lives, were reborn in the heavens because they invoked the name of the Buddha; they were born in this same place together with us.

Because of your wrong views, you have been unable to hear the Dharma. Now, by following the Buddha’s words and repenting of all your transgressions, the eye of your mind shall open, and you will see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
They addressed their father, the King, saying, "We wish today to leave the household life and study the Way within the Buddha-Dharma."
The Father King said, "You yourselves should inform the Buddha. They both informed the Buddha together, saying, "We both wish to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus! and they immediately became śramaṇas.
The *Sūtra on Subduing the Poisonous Dragon and Contemplating the Buddha’s Samādhi* states: The Tathāgata went to the cave of the rākṣasa Nakha-rahasa.
Within it were five rākṣasīs who had transformed themselves into dragon girls and consorted with a poisonous dragon. The dragon further sent down hail, while the rākṣasīs caused chaos and famine.
The pestilence had already lasted for four years. At that time, the king was struck with terror and summoned various mantra-masters to command the poisonous dragons and rākṣasas;

however, his vital energy was so intense that their incantations were ineffective. The king then went to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested that the Buddha subdue them. Having accepted the request, the Buddha departed.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and their retinue of five hundred to transform themselves into a hundred thousand dragons coiling their bodies as a seat.
From the mouths of the dragons, fire was spat forth, which transformed into a golden terrace and a couch of the seven treasures.

At that time, from the crown of his head, the World-Honored One emitted countless rays of golden light, and transformation-buddhas filled the void of space. When the Dragon King saw the World-Honored One approaching, he and his father, along with his retinue of ten...
The six great nāgas arose, and with a great roar like thunder and lightning, they rained down hail; from their eyes and mouths they spat forth fire.
Five rākṣasīs manifested hideous forms, their eyes flashing like lightning, and stood before the Buddha. At that time, the Naga Prince, seeing the Buddhas in the void, said to his father:
"Father King, you are spitting fire, wishing to harm a single Buddha; yet look at the sky, where there are countless Buddhas. Then the Golden...
The Vajra Deity grasped a great mallet; from the head of the mallet, fire emerged and scorched the body of the evil dragon. Terrified, the Dragon King fled into the shadow of the Buddha.
The Buddha’s shadow was cool and refreshing, like the sprinkling of nectar. The dragon was filled with great joy and prostrated before the Buddha.
The five rākṣasī women also paid homage to the Tathāgata. At that time, the Tathāgata was like a compassionate mother caressing her child. Then the Dragon King—
Furthermore, five rākṣasī women and sixteen nāga princes prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, requesting to receive the Buddha’s precepts.
The Buddha expounded for them the Dharma of the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts,
and he transformed the various courtesans.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states: In the city of Śrāvastī, there were many courtesans who seduced men with their charms;
those who stayed for a single night had to pay a fine of two hundred gold coins. There was an elder in the kingdom named Yuludata (Rujuda), whose accumulated wealth reached ten billion.
He had three sons, including one named Huade (Kusumaśrī); the brothers were dissolute and unrestrained, vying with one another to frequent the brothels. On their very first visit—
Each paid a sum of gold coins. At the end of one month, an entire treasury was exhausted. When the elder went on inspection and saw that the treasury was empty, he questioned the keeper.
The treasurer replied, "The three men named Puṣpavanta go every day with money to the house of a courtesan."
The elder immediately went before the king and said, "Great King, there are certain courtesans who have enticed my sons and exhausted all our family wealth.
The king said to the elder, "If even your vast riches and gold treasuries have been depleted, how much more must those of lesser station be in distress?
The elder addressed the king, "I only pray that Your Majesty will swiftly execute these wicked people. The king told the elder, "I have accepted [your request]..."
The Buddha’s precepts do not permit him to harm even an ant, much less to kill a human being. While the Tathāgata was in the world, he transformed all beings.
[The king] went together with them to the Buddha’s dwelling and reported this matter, praying that the Buddha would transform them. The Buddha told the Great King:

"You may dispatch a *caṇḍāla* to summon the courtesans to the assembly hall. The king struck the golden drum to proclaim the edict, commanding the officials and citizens of the kingdom to assemble together.
At the site of the debate, the Buddha commanded one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus to each manifest great supernormal powers (ṛddhi) according to their meditative concentration.
Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kātyāyana, Kauṇḍinya, and the others each performed eighteen transformations of supernormal power;
they leaped into the air, flying through the sky and manifesting miraculous apparitions. When the courtesans saw this, they all conceived faith and received the three [refuges].
Regarding the refuge and the dharma of the five precepts:

the *Ānanda-sor-nu-ru-kuang-fu-jing* (The Sūtra on Ānanda Seeking Milk from the Buddha Ruciraprabha) states: "In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was a brahmin named Māyārī; his family was wealthy and noble."
Lacking faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, she practiced only heterodox paths. The Buddha sent Ānanda to the house of Māyārī to seek cow’s milk.
The brahmin reflected, "If I do not give it to him, people will say I am stingy. Therefore, I shall point out a poor, wicked cow and let Ānanda take it himself;
I will have the cow gore and kill Ānanda, thereby bringing disgrace upon his Way. Thus spoke Māyārī.
He sent the boy to lead [Ānanda] to where the cow was and instructed him, saying, "Be careful not to take the milk yourself; see if Ānanda can obtain it.
Ānanda went immediately to the side of the cow and thought to himself, "My teacher has strictly commanded that I must not take the cow's milk with my own hands.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, descended and transformed himself into a young brahmin, standing by the side of the cow. Ānanda—
The brahmin said, "Please fetch some cow's milk for me. The brahmin then took his vessel and went to where the cow was;
the cow stood still and did not dare move again, allowing him to take as much as he wished. Ānanda took the milk and departed with joy. The brahmin said, "This cow is extremely fierce;
no one can approach her. For what reason today has she become so gentle? Is it because of Gautama’s younger brother?"
"If you, my son, can do such a thing, how much more so the majestic power of the Buddha! The Brahmin was filled with joy and attained faith and understanding in the Buddha-dharma.
Ānanda took the milk and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it and said to Ānanda:

"In a previous life, this cow did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and fell into this state as a cow for sixteen kalpas. Now, having heard the name of the Buddha, she has followed her master to take this milk and offer it to me."
"O Buddha, by virtue of these causes and conditions, he shall attain liberation; when his life later comes to an end, he will never fall into the three evil realms.
Finally, he shall become a Buddha named Kṣīraprabha Tathāgata."

Regarding the method for subduing a drunken elephant, the *Dharmapada* states: Devadatta conspired with King Ajātaśatru to destroy the Buddha. The king issued an edict to the people of the kingdom that they were not to serve the Buddha.
While the Buddha and five hundred arhats were dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, Devadatta went to the king’s residence and said:
"The disciples of the Buddha have now dispersed; there remain only five hundred disciples by the Buddha's side.
Your Majesty, I pray that you invite the Buddha into the city tomorrow. You may feed five hundred great elephants until they are intoxicated and then have them trample him to death.
I shall then carry out the Buddha’s teachings to transform the world. Upon hearing this, the king was delighted and immediately went to invite the Buddha. The Buddha, knowing his plot, replied:
"Excellent! The king withdrew and returned to report this to Devadatta. At the time of the meal the following day, the Buddha entered the city gate together with the Arhats.
The intoxicated elephant cried out and charged forward, crashing against walls and houses until they were all destroyed; the entire city trembled with fear.
Five hundred Arhats flew up into the air, leaving Ānanda alone at the side as the intoxicated elephant lowered its head in unison.

He came directly toward the Buddha. The Buddha raised five fingers, which transformed into five lions; they roared in unison, shaking heaven and earth. The intoxicated elephant prostrated itself on the ground, not daring to lift its head.
The elephant, having regained its senses, shed tears and repented its transgression. The king, his ministers, and the common people were all struck with awe and solemnity.
The World-Honored One walked slowly to the king’s palace, and after he and the various arhats had finished eating, he offered a blessing. The king addressed him:

The Buddha said, "By nature you were not clear-minded, yet you believed those slanderous words and committed rebellious evils. I pray that you will extend great compassion and forgive my delusion and folly.
The Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru and his ministers: "In this world, there are eight matters that give rise to and prolong slander."
All say that these eight names lead to great transgressions. What are the eight? They are gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and contempt, suffering and pleasure.
From antiquity to the present, there have been few who have not been deluded by them.

Regarding the drawing of the bow to harm the Buddha, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, Devadatta constantly harbored evil intentions and desired to harm the World-Honored One.
He therefore hired five hundred Brahmins skilled in archery, ordering them to carry stiff bows and sharp arrows and hide behind trees.
The forest-dweller waited for the World-Honored One’s passage; he went to where the World-Honored One was and drew his bow to shoot at the Buddha.

The arrows he shot were transformed into *kubjaka* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *padma* flowers, and *utpala* flowers. When the five hundred brahmins witnessed this miraculous transformation, they were all struck with great terror.
They immediately cast away their bows and arrows, prostrated before the Buddha to repent, and knelt with palms joined.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; their minds were opened and their intentions were resolved, and they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

They further addressed the Buddha, saying, "We pray that you will permit us to leave the household life. The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus! Their hair and beards were shaved away, dharma robes were donned upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.
The Buddha again preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the stage of *arhat*. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, [Ti...]"
Devadatta constantly sought to harm the Buddha, yet the Buddha always gave rise to great compassion. The Buddha said: "It is not only today;
in the past, there was a merchant leader named Ungrateful who went to sea to gather treasures and returned.

Upon reaching a place of swirling currents, he encountered a water-rākṣasa who blocked his ship so that it could not move forward. There was a great tortoise who, feeling compassion in his heart, came toward the ship."
The boat carrying its cargo reached the shore. At that time, the turtle came ashore to rest and fell into a brief sleep.
One who did not recognize his kindness took up a knife, intending to kill him. The merchants said, "We were saved from disaster and our lives preserved by this turtle;

it would be inauspicious to kill him. The ungrateful one replied, "I am also in desperate need of food; I do not care about your debt of gratitude. He then killed the turtle and ate him. Thus was the ungrateful one.
The one who showed such kindness was Devadatta. According to the *Buddha Huà Lùzhì Jīnglǜ Yìxiàng* (The Buddha’s Transformation of Lu-zhi:
Different Aspects of Sūtra and Vinaya), there was an elder named Lu-zhi in the city of Śobhāvatī who served the Nirgranthas. I...

Desiring to deliver them, I arrived at that city. When the Nirgranthas heard that I intended to go to that city, they thought to themselves, "If Gautama comes here, these people will surely abandon us and no longer provide for us.
They said to Luṭi, "The śramaṇa Gautama now wishes to come here; however, that śramaṇa has abandoned his parents to wander about hither and thither."
