Wherever he arrives, he causes the five grains to fail to ripen in that land, leading to widespread famine and a great many deaths among the people.
Having heard this, Lu-zhi was immediately filled with fear and said, "Great Master, what plan do you intend to employ?

The Nirgrantha replied, "Gautama is by nature fond of groves and clear waters. If there are such things outside the city, they should be cut down; the flowing springs, ponds, and wells should be filled in."
With foul odors and filth, each person shall prepare their weapons and stand ready for defense so that if those [demons] come, they may not advance.
I will employ various arts to cause them to turn back. Those people will then respectfully follow my instructions.
At that time, I will arrive at that city and town, and immediately give rise to compassion and a heart of loving-kindness toward them; all the trees will grow back as they were before.
The rivers, ponds, wells, and springs were pure and their waters filled them to the brim; various kinds of flowers grew there, completely covering their surfaces.
The city walls were transformed into deep-blue lapis lazuli, so that the people within could see clearly through them, and the gates opened of their own accord.
Neither I nor the great assembly could restrain him. The weapons he had arrayed were transformed into various flowers.
The elder Lu-zhi, together with his people, followed one another and came to where I was. I immediately expounded for them the essentials of the Dharma;
they all resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta and collectively received the precepts.

In the *Sūtra on an Old Poor Man Who Saw the Buddha*, it is said: In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an old poor man one hundred years of age who came leaning on a staff, desiring to see the Buddha.
Śakra and Brahmā were attending at the gate and ordered that he not be admitted. The old man cried out loudly, saying: "I..."
"Though I am poor and lowly, I have been fortunate for a thousand years to now encounter the Buddha.

Desiring to inquire about sin and merit and to seek liberation from all sufferings, I have heard that the World-Honored One’s benevolence reaches everywhere and that all things rely upon him, none failing to receive his grace.
For this reason, I have come from afar to beg for a single instruction. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Call him forward. Thereupon, the old man crawled forward inch by inch and approached.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am born into an unfortunate world; impoverished and suffering from hunger and cold, I seek death but cannot find it, and for my life there is no reliance.
Human life is most precious, and I cannot cast it aside myself. Hearing that the Buddha dwells in this world, my heart alone rejoices."

Day and night I have resolved to attend upon Your countenance. Previously, I stood outside the gate for a long time without being able to advance. Calculating that I wished to return, I found my strength insufficient;
yet having no way to proceed or retreat, I only fear that my life will end here, defiling the holy gate and further increasing my transgressions.

Not realizing that the World-Honored One had already grown old, I was moved by compassion and permitted to advance. May my original vow not be thwarted; if I die thus, I shall have no further regrets.
I only pray that you may quickly bring this life to its end so that I may finish my retribution in a future world, and that you will deign to bestow your grace upon me with supreme wisdom.
The Buddha said, "Regarding the birth of human beings, the causes and conditions of birth and death lead to the roots of transgression through manifold causes and conditions.
In your previous life, you were born into a wealthy and noble family; being clever and wise, you used these qualities to act willfully and treat others with contempt.
You accumulated wealth and property but refused to practice charity. Therefore, you now suffer this poverty. The retribution for sin and merit is likewise."
[He] was influenced [by this]. Having heard it, he paid homage and departed.

The *Lao ren chujia xianyu yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of an Elder’s Renunciation and Wisdom or Folly) states: In the city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder named Śrībhūti, who was one hundred years old.
In that year, having heard it said that the merit of leaving the household life is immeasurable, he reflected to himself:

"Why should I not now leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma to cultivate the Way? He went to the Bamboo Grove and asked the bhikṣus: "Where is the World-Honored One, the Buddha, at present?"
He replied, "He is not here. He asked again, "Who is the preceptor’s senior disciple? The bhikṣu pointed to Śāriputra.

[The man] went before him and said, "Please allow me to go forth. Śāriputra observed that this old man was deficient in all three matters—study, meditation, and assisting in the communal affairs—and told him, "Go away; you are too old to go forth. Next he went to Mahā-...
Kāśyapa, Upāli, Anuruddha, and the five hundred great arhats all said, "We are too old to leave the household life.
They returned to the Bamboo Grove and stood outside the gate, weeping with grief and distress, wailing aloud.
The World-Honored One immediately went before him, emitting a great radiance and appearing with his marks and signs of excellence, most dignified and majestic.
The Buddha asked the old man, "For what reason do you weep? Upon hearing the Buddha’s Brahma-voice, the elder’s heart leaped with joy like a son seeing his father.

Prostrating himself on the ground, he wept as he addressed the Buddha, saying, "What sin have I alone committed that I am not permitted to leave the home-life? The Buddha said, "Who has made such a statement? That one is old..."
"He did not permit him to go forth. Śāriputra and the others replied: "At that time, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, consoled the elder, saying:
'Do not grieve or be distressed; I shall now cause you to go forth, and it will not be through Śāriputra.'"
Having cultivated merit for a hundred kalpas through diligent and arduous ascetic practices, he said, "Come, follow me," and immediately followed behind the Buddha into the Buddha’s vihāra.
He then instructed Mahāmaudgalyāyana to grant him the going forth.

Regarding the Ugly Woman’s Transformation of Her Appearance, the *Baiyuan jing* (Sutra of One Hundred Karmic Conditions) states: King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was exceedingly ugly and whose form did not resemble that of a human being.
When she had been raised to adulthood, they sought the son of a wealthy family from a poor lineage to serve as her husband.

He constructed a residence with doors firmly closed, seven layers thick both inside and out. The king summoned his daughter’s husband and said, "If you go outside, take the keys yourself and lock the doors;
do not let anyone see you. The king provided wealth and goods for his son-in-law and appointed him as a high minister.
He joined him in a social gathering with various noble clans. At the time when they held these monthly assemblies, [the following occurred].

Husbands and wives came together and took delight in one another. All those present at the assembly had brought their respective wives to attend the gathering, yet that minister alone did not bring his wife.
The people speculated among themselves: "Is that man’s wife perhaps beautiful, or is she extremely ugly?
The crowd then urged him to drink until he was intoxicated and lay prostrate on the ground; they then took the locks and keys, and sent someone to open the door.
She gazed upon her wife. The woman reproached herself, thinking, "What sin have I committed that I am confined in this dark chamber?

From afar, she paid homage to the World-Honored One, praying for his compassionate pity. The Buddha, knowing her intention, went immediately to her home. When the woman saw the Buddha, she sought refuge and repented.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and her mind was opened and her understanding attained. Her evil features and ugly form suddenly became upright and handsome;

her body was so majestic and dignified that she resembled a celestial maiden. When the man sent to open the door saw how exceptionally beautiful and peerless she was, he returned with the lock and key and fastened them back in their original place. Upon returning home, the man saw his wife’s extraordinary appearance and asked, "Who is this person?"
He replied, "It was your wife. The wife then explained to her husband in detail how she had paid homage to the Buddha, saying, "It is due to the Buddha’s divine virtue that I have become thus.
Her husband accompanied his wife to see the Buddha with the King.
Biographies of the Manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Volume Upper (3);
Biographies of the Manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Volume Lower (1).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Baocheng of Baoen Temple.

The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha to Fulfill the Vows of Queen Vaidehī* states: "In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a crown prince named Ajātaśatru.
Following the teachings of his evil friend Devadatta, he arrested his father, King Bimbisāra, and imprisoned his mother, Queen Vaidehī."
She was confined within the inner palace and not permitted to go out again. Once Vaidhī had been thus imprisoned, she became distressed and emaciated;
bowing toward the Buddha, she spoke these words: "The World-Honored One is majestic and grave, and there is no way for me to see him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Maudgalyāyana, Ānanda, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, came through the air. Vaidhī addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One..."

"What sin did I commit in my past lives to give birth to such an evil son? I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me in detail the place free from sorrow and affliction, where I may be reborn and no longer delight in this five-turbid evil world of Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha emitted a light from between his eyebrows, which shone throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddha said to Vaidehī: "To the west lies the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where resides Amitābha Buddha. It is..."
This is not far away. You should fix your mindfulness and contemplate that land with clarity. Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three kinds of merit:
first, filially supporting one’s parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing while practicing the ten wholesome actions;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, being fully endowed with the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct; third, generating the bodhicitta and possessing deep faith.

Regarding cause and effect: those who read and recite the Mahāyāna sutras and exhort practitioners to progress should single-mindedly fix their attention and contemplate with clarity the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Therein dwell Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, seated upon lotus flowers.
The images of these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all radiate light; that golden light fills the entirety of that land. This...
When this visualization is perfected, one will be reborn in that land.
The *Śuka-praśna-buddha-śata-pūrvakalpa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha was about to depart from the Jeta Grove for the kingdom of Magadha when he encountered a flock of birds. Among them...
The king of parrots, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, soared into the air and went out to meet him on the road.
He said, "I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will, out of compassion and pity, come to my grove to accept my invitation for one night. The Buddha consented.
Knowing that the Buddha had granted his request, the king of parrots returned to his own grove and commanded all the parrots to come forth and welcome them. Thus it was.
At that time, the World-Honored One led the bhikṣus to the Śuka Grove. Each spread out his sitting mat and sat beneath a tree to practice dhyāna and engage in contemplation.
When the king of the śukas saw the Buddha and the bhikṣus sitting in tranquil stillness, he was filled with great joy.
Throughout the entire night, he flew about, circling the Buddha and the bhikṣus, turning back to gaze at them; there were no lions, tigers, wolves, or other predatory beasts present.

Because robbers had harassed the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, when dawn arrived, the World-Honored One proceeded forth with Śuka and Nandika leading the way toward Rājagṛha, and addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"The World-Honored One is now leading the bhikṣus and has arrived nearby; we pray that Your Majesty will prepare various delicacies to welcome him on the road."
They went out to welcome him. When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he issued orders to prepare a feast and to carry banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and musical instruments;
leading his ministers, he went out to meet him on the road to welcome him. At that time, the parrot king passed away during the night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Descending from heaven to repay the Buddha’s kindness, he brought with him incense and flowers.

He made offerings to the Buddha, prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha's feet. The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Thus, the wicked ox was delivered.

The *Śatavarga-vinaya-sūtra* states: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kośala and intended to proceed to the foot of the Laṅgaka tree, he arrived at a marsh where there were five hundred water buffaloes that were extremely fierce and malevolent.

There were also five hundred cowherds who, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar with his bhikṣus traveling along this path, cried out in a loud voice: "We pray only that the World-Honored One will not travel by this way!"
Within the herd of water buffaloes was a large, fierce bull that gored and injured people, making it difficult to pass through.
The Buddha said to the cowherds, "You need not worry. Even if that water buffalo comes to gore me, I shall take care of it myself."
A wicked ox suddenly approached, tossing its tail, lowering its horns, kneeling on the ground, bellowing, and leaping forward.
The World-Honored One manifested five lion cubs at the tips of his five fingers, positioned to the left and right of the Buddha. On all four sides, there were great pits of fire.
At that time, the water buffalo was filled with extreme terror; it ran in all four directions, but found no place to go, save for a small space before the Buddha’s feet.
The empty space became tranquil and cool. He galloped forward with a mind at ease, free from all fear.
He knelt down on his haunches, bowed his head, and licked the World-Honored One’s feet. Then he lowered his head and gazed upon the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Knowing that the wicked bull had been tamed, the Tathāgata spoke these verses: "With a fierce heart you gave rise to evil intent, Desiring to come and harm me. Now you have returned in sincerity, hoping for deliverance."
"Excellent! It has come back to lick my feet. At that time, having heard the verses, the buffalo ceased eating water and grass and immediately passed away, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Descending from heaven, it returned to repay the Buddha's kindness; carrying incense and flowers, it came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha then preached various essential teachings for it, and its mind was opened.
Through mental realization, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
"The World-Honored One entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the house of the young brahmin Māṇava Tuṭṭha, son of a parrot."
Cunda had just left that house when a white dog was on the bed, eating from a dish. Seeing the Buddha approaching, the dog jumped down from the bed and barked.
The Buddha said to the white dog, "It is because of Dhana-pāla that you have fallen into this state. The dog became greatly enraged and lay down in sorrowful dejection.
When Cunda returned home and saw the dog lying on the ground, refusing to rise, he immediately asked, "Who has provoked its anger?"
"Dog! his family members replied, "World-Honored One. Then Dōti, filled with anger, went to where the World-Honored One was.
The World-Honored One told him, "The dog is your father. If you do not believe me, go home and ask the dog; let the dog show you the hidden treasure. He returned home and spoke to the dog:
"If you were my father in a previous life, you should rise up, eat, and show me the hidden treasure. The dog immediately showed it to him.
At the site of the hidden treasure, he used his mouth and feet to pull at the space beneath the bed; he then immediately dug into the earth and obtained a great quantity of precious objects.

Having developed great faith, he asked the Buddha about the causes and conditions of his past karma and its retribution. The Buddha said: "Whether man or woman, those whose lifespan is extremely short have the karmic retribution of killing;
those whose lifespan is extremely long possess a compassionate heart and do not kill. Those who are extremely poor and suffer are those who were stingy, greedy, and thieving."
A thief may possess abundant wealth and jewels and constantly practice giving, yet if he possesses evil wisdom and associates with wicked people, his merit will not ripen.

One who possesses good wisdom and stays close to virtuous friends, however, will see their merit flourish. Dautiya, you should know this: by performing the karma of longevity, one will certainly obtain long life;
by performing the karma of giving, one will certainly obtain wealth; and by extensive study and great learning, one will certainly obtain wisdom. Such causes produce such results.

As for the fruit: all sentient beings, due to their own past actions (karma), receive retribution based on those actions. Conditioned by karma and dependent upon karma, they experience the fruits of retribution according to whether those actions were wholesome or unwholesome.
This is what is meant by "receiving."
The *Huo zhong qu zi jing* (Sūtra on Taking a Child from the Fire) and the *Lü yi xiang* (Dharmas Heterogeneous in the Vinaya) state: In the city of Campā, there was a great elder who had no heir.
He served the six heretical teachers in hopes of obtaining offspring. When his wife became pregnant, the elder went to consult the six teachers as to whether it would be a boy or a girl.
The six teachers replied, "She will certainly be a girl. The elder was filled with grief and distress. A wise friend said to him, "Why do you not ask the Buddha?
The elder immediately went to where the Buddha was and asked him about the matter. The Buddha said, "There is no doubt that it is a boy."
The six teachers were envious in their hearts. They mixed poisonous drugs with mango fruits and brought them to the elder, saying, "When your wife is about to give birth, she may take this medicine;
then the delivery will be without suffering. The elder accepted it and gave it to his wife to take. Once she had taken it, she died immediately.
The elder enshrouded the body outside the city and cremated it. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I wish to go there to destroy false views.
The Buddha and the great assembly proceeded to the place of cremation. The elder spoke, saying, "The Buddha’s words are not false;

yet the mother of my son has already passed away—how could she have given birth to a child? The Buddha said, "At that time, you did not ask whether your mother’s life was long or short; you asked only—"
"What you carry within is either a boy or a girl; Elder, you should know that you will certainly obtain a child. At that moment, the corpse was consumed by fire, its belly split open.
The Buddha said to Jīvaka, "Go into the midst of the fire and bring forth this child. Jīvaka stepped forward into the fire, took up the child, and returned to present him to the Buddha.
The Buddha handed him over to the Elder, saying, "The lifespan of sentient beings is as uncertain as..."

Like bubbles upon the water, if a person’s merit is profound, fire cannot burn them and poison cannot harm them. The elder prostrated himself, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on me, for I am ignorant and deluded to the extreme, having faithfully followed non-Buddhist paths.
From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha and the Sangha."

The *Jianfo shengxin jing lü yixiang* (The Scripture on Seeing the Buddha and Giving Rise to Faith: Various Phenomena from the Sutras and Vinaya) states: There was a king named A-zhi (Ajitavat), whose power and prowess were formidable.

He invaded neighboring countries and unjustly oppressed the virtuous. The people resented him. The Buddha, together with his great assembly, intended to go and transform him. When King A-zhi heard of this—
He immediately conceived an evil intent and, together with the princes, raised an army and gathered his forces. He intended to intercept the Buddha on the great road to resist him.
At that moment, the Buddha stood before them and emitted a great radiance; he delivered King Aśvajit from the midst of the army.
The drums no longer sounded, bows and crossbows were not drawn, and swords and spears were not raised. Elephants and horses stumbled, and the infantry’s sinews cramped.
Heaven and earth became dark and gloomy, and the sun and moon lost their light. The king and his entire army were utterly bewildered; they lost their breath, collapsed, and fled.
When the Buddha reached the royal city, the city gates opened of their own accord. The Buddha proceeded to the royal palace, entered the hall, and sat down. The various devas...

The King surrounded himself with his retinue for protection. When the King and his sons heard that the Buddha had entered the palace, they returned to the palace to meet the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and offered this apology:
"We are base, ignorant, and crude; having studied little since our youth, we knew nothing of ritual propriety and were like beasts or wolves.
In our folly and delusion, we have offended the devas and humans. Yet the Great Sage has not disregarded this remote and small kingdom, and now has deigned to come here."
“World-Honored One, you have come from afar to this humble land where the sovereign and his ministers have been rebellious. We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on our ignorance.

Since you have already bestowed your profound grace in teaching and transforming the people, the King and his sons repent their transgressions and reproach themselves, saying to the Buddha: ‘We beg for the precepts so that we may practice them throughout our lives. The Buddha said:

‘The King should be gracious and trustworthy, benevolent and righteous, compassionate and filial, upright and pure; he should be broad-minded and gentle, patient and enduring, and spread [these virtues].’”
Bestow gifts to nurture the people. Sentient beings are to be pitied and human life is to be cherished; the treasures of the realm are not to be relied upon for support.
As parents of the people, love them as you would your own children.
The *Samyuktāgama Sūtra on Attaining Liberation through a Wife* states: A king from the kingdom of Nanda sent an envoy to the house of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī.
When the elder saw that the envoy was as black and ugly as a ghost, he asked, "What kind of person are you? He replied, "Nanda..."
The king was arranging a marriage for his crown prince. Having heard that the elder’s daughter, named Samajātā, was the foremost among women, he came to seek her hand.

The king sent a letter to inform him of this. The elder then went to the Buddha and said to him, "The King has dispatched a messenger to my home, requesting my daughter on behalf of the king’s crown prince. What should I do now?"

"Why? The Buddha said, "Give it to him. The elder sent his daughter to him. When King Nanda saw that his son’s wife had arrived, he invited his teacher, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, into the palace to provide him with a meal.
The king and the queen called their son and daughter-in-law out to pay homage to the teacher.
Samajika beheld the Nirgrantha as naked, ugly, and black—like a pig, a dog, or a beast.
There was no difference. [The husband] spat from afar at her and immediately closed the door and would not come out. The Master said to the king, "Whose teacher did your wife ask about?
The wife replied, "It was the Buddha. The king asked, "Can the Buddha be seen? She replied, "The Buddha possesses supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
If one burns incense and invites him from afar, he will arrive immediately. The king said, "Excellent! Then Samajja ascended a high platform, burned incense, and paid homage, saying:
"Now the King of Kalinga does not know that there is a Buddha. We pray that tomorrow morning the Buddha, together with his disciples, will condescend to come here.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to each manifest their supernatural powers and transformations at will.
The bhikṣus each mounted dragons, phoenixes, tigers, leopards, oxen, horses, and peacocks, arriving through the air. They then preached the Dharma for the king.
As well as all the Nirgranthas, were fully delivered.

Regarding the blind boy who saw the Buddha, the *Yuēnán jīng* (Sūtra on Overcoming Difficulties) states: "In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was an elder named Yuēnán. His wealth amounted to billions, and he was a man of—"
Being stingy and jealous, he was unwilling to give anything away. He constantly told his gatekeeper not to admit any beggars.
The son of Vena, named Candana, was likewise miserly and greedy. When Vena’s life came to an end, he returned to his own country and became the son of a blind woman.
Her husband said to his wife, "Your body is afflicted by a grave illness and you are now pregnant; since I have no food or drink for you, you may go on your own. The wife then—
He went out, found a large cave in a wall, and took up residence within it. In the ninth month, he gave birth to a son whose two eyes were blind; she begged for food to nourish him.
When the boy reached the age of seven, his mother instructed him, saying, "Now there is someone begging for a little rice from me to satisfy their hunger, as one would quench thirst with rain.
Upon hearing his mother’s words, the boy went out to beg for food and arrived at the house of her son. At that time, the gatekeeper happened to be young.
He went outside and entered the central courtyard. Upon hearing the words, Candana called out to the gatekeeper and questioned him.

Fearing punishment, the gatekeeper immediately seized the blind boy and threw him outside the gate, where he injured his head and broke his arm. Hearing this, the mother ran toward him, crying, "What kind of heartless person is this?
At that moment, the gate deity spoke to her: "The pain you have received is but a minor matter; what is great shall follow later. In your previous life..."
Because he did not give away his wealth at that time, he received this retribution; upon death, he experienced even greater suffering. Those who were watching heard the sound.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "What kind of sound is this? Ānanda explained it in detail. The Buddha went with the great assembly to where the boy was;

he gave him a small amount of food and rubbed his head and eyes with his hand, whereupon they immediately became clear and the broken injuries were healed. Consequently, the boy recognized his past lives. The Buddha asked him: "You..."
"In his previous life, he was the elder named Vatsa. The beggar replied, "It is so. Upon hearing this, everyone conceived faith and made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha;
the old maidservant attained deliverance.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* states: The elder Sudatta had an old maidservant named Vidyā who was diligent and conscientious in her household duties;
he entrusted everything to her, and she constantly managed the storehouse. When Sudatta invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, she provided them with all their necessities.
A sick bhikṣu made many requests. An old maidservant, being stingy and miserly, felt resentment toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and spoke these words:
"The master of my house is foolish and deluded; he has accepted the arts of the śramaṇas and begs without satiety. What kind of path could this be?"
He again gave rise to an evil thought, wondering, "When shall I no longer hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha? When Queen Mallikā heard this, she said:
"How is it that Sudatta, who is like a fine lotus flower, cherishes an old slave girl? She immediately commanded Sudatta to send his wife to her. When the wife arrived, she said:
'An old slave girl in your house has slandered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha with wicked speech; why do you not expel her?'"

The wife said, "The Buddha’s presence in the world brings great benefit and nourishment; how much more so for an old servant girl! Upon hearing this, the lady was filled with great joy and said, "I wish to invite the Buddha;

you must send the girl to come. The next day, when the Buddha arrived, the elder sent the girl, who immediately took gold and silver to assist the royal family in making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
At that time, as the Buddha entered the gate, the old girl saw him, yet no joy arose in her heart.
As she was about to withdraw immediately, the Buddha stood before her. The Buddha raised his ten fingers, and each transformed into a Buddha.

Upon seeing the Buddhas and hearing the sublime Dharma, the old maidservant returned home, yet she remained fearful of encountering the Buddha again. The Buddha said, "This maidservant has no karmic affinity with me."
The Buddha perceived that Rāhula had the karmic affinity to go and transform her. Rāhula, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, traveled through the air and arrived there.
Upon seeing him, the old maidservant was filled with great joy and requested to receive the five precepts. At that time, Rāhula expounded for her the Three Refuges and the five precepts;
having heard them, she immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

The *Sūtra on Exhorting Relatives to Invite the Buddha’s Dharma* states: The elder Sudatta had a relative who served non-Buddhist teachers and did not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma or in medical arts.
At one time, he fell gravely ill. His kinsmen and friends all came to visit and inquire after him, exhorting him to invite [the Buddha].
The Buddha treated his illness, but [the man] remained obstinate and refused, replying to the assembly: "I serve the Heaven and Earth and the divine deities;
I shall never change my resolve. Sudatta said to him: "The teacher I serve is titled 'Buddha. His divine virtue extends everywhere, and those who behold him obtain blessings."
"You may try inviting him to preach the sutras and offer prayers of aspiration. Listen to what he says and observe how his conduct, speech, and progress are;
since you have been ill for a long time and have not recovered, I urge you to invite the Buddha so that you may receive his blessings.
The elder replied, "Then please invite the Buddha and the Sangha on my behalf. Su-datta immediately invited the Buddha to visit his residence. The Buddha emitted a radiance within.
It penetrated through to the outside. When the elder saw the light, he was joyful and felt his body become light. The Buddha told the elder:
"There are three ways in which people meet with untimely death while living in this world. First, having an illness that one does not treat; second, treating it but being negligent;

third, being arrogant, self-indulgent, and self-willed, failing to understand what is contrary and what is compliant—these constitute the three untimely deaths. If one has an illness, one should follow the clear Way and provide peace and care according to the season."
"Ji! First, when the four elements suffer from cold or heat, one must rely on medicine. Second, when confronted by various malevolent spirits and ghosts, one must rely on the scriptures and precepts.
Third, by serving the worthy and holy ones and showing compassion to those in distress, one’s virtue will move the deities and bring blessings to all living beings.
Through great wisdom, one eliminates the veils of the five aggregates. By practicing in this way, one will enjoy peace and security in the present life. Having heard this, the elder—4.
Greatly tranquil, with all afflictions eliminated as if having drunk nectar, his inner and outer being was joyful, his body at ease, and his mind settled;
among the imperial clan and the people of the land, there were none who did not revere and honor him.

The *Fǎbànjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Buddha-Dharma) concerning the feeding of children states: There was a great householder named Śūradatta, whose wealth was immeasurable and who was a devoted believer in the Buddha.
He vowed that he would always invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha on the eighth day of the twelfth month. When the householder was approaching death, he entrusted these instructions to his descendants.
"After my death, you must carry out these instructions without fail. My son’s name is Bhīradvāja. Later, as time passed, he became increasingly poor and had nothing at all.
When the month arrived for which he was responsible, he lacked the funds to provide the offerings and was filled with grief and unhappiness. The Buddha sent Maudgalyāyana to inquire of Bhīradvāja:
'The month for which your father was responsible is about to arrive; what plan do you have? Bhīradvāja replied: 'My father left me instructions when he died.'"
He caused [them] not to dare disobey it. "I only pray that the World-Honored One will have compassion and not abandon me; during the eight days, may you turn your light back to look upon me.
Maudgalyāyana immediately returned and reported this in full. Bīradvāja took his wife to his maternal family's home to borrow a hundred gold coins, with which he returned home to prepare food.
The Buddha, together with the assembly of monks, went to his house to receive the meal and offer blessings. Bīradvāja...
Free from regret, they returned home with joyful hearts. At midnight that very night, the various old treasuries became spontaneously filled with precious objects.
When Vīradatta and his wife saw this at dawn, they were both filled with joy and fear;

fearing that the authorities might see them and ask where they had obtained such things, the couple deliberated together that they should go to question the Buddha. They immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling and reported the matter to him in detail. The Buddha—
I tell you, Bhīradvāja: set your mind at ease and employ him with confidence; do not harbor doubts or difficulties. You have practiced faith and never disobeyed your father’s instructions;

you have maintained the precepts and a sense of shame, remaining single-minded until death. Your seven riches—faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, wisdom, and the path—are fully perfected.

This is the result of your merit and is no portent of calamity. A wise person can practice this regardless of whether they are male or female; wherever they are born, such blessings will manifest naturally.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, their faith increased all the more.
They provided the funds to prepare food.

The *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya) states: "The people of the city of Rājagṛha gathered together and deliberated, each contributing one hundred coins to provide a meal for the Buddha."
And as for the Saṃgha, there was a Kukkuta Brahmin who was poor and lacked the wealth to assist that assembly.

The people said to him, "Since you have no money, you should leave quickly. Kukkuta then returned home in sorrow and said to his wife, "I have no money to assist the assembly in providing a meal for the Buddha; the people have driven me out quickly. His wife replied, "You should go to Puṣyamitra."
The householder Tora borrowed some money from him, promising to repay it within ten days, saying, "If I do not return it, my wife and I shall become your slaves.
The householder then lent him one hundred gold coins. Taking them, he went before the assembly and said, "I have now obtained this money;
please allow me to take my place in the order. The assembly spoke to Kīṭa, saying, "It has already been prepared; you need not [wait]."
[Kṛkī] took the money and returned. The husband and wife went before the World-Honored One, paid their respects with prostrations, and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Kṛkī, "You should invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha. Having received these instructions, Kṛkī proceeded to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
At that time, Śakra Devendra said to King Vaiśravaṇa, "You shall assist this brāhmaṇa in preparing the food. He further spoke to Vai...
The devaputra Śivagamana said, "Venerable One, you may manifest a lofty and vast lecture hall.
Both replied, "We shall receive your instructions. The Buddha told Kīṭa, "You may invite the King for a meal together for one day. He immediately went to the King's residence and addressed him:

"May the Heavenly King accept this invitation tomorrow to assemble at the Buddha’s lecture hall. At that time, the King prepared his carriage and was surrounded by his ministers; the Buddha and the assembly of monks [proceeded].
Protected by devas and nāgas, he proceeded to the lecture hall to receive the *kikidivi* food. Having offered prayers after the meal, he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
the king and his ministers were all filled with great joy.

The *Laoqi yu fo jinglü yixiang* (Heterogeneous Phenomena from the Sūtras and Vinaya on an Old Beggar Encountering the Buddha) states: At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Śrāvastī.

There was a certain brāhmaṇa, aged and with his faculties fully matured, who carried a staff and a bowl, seeking alms from house to house. The World-Honored One asked him, "Why do you act in this way? He replied:
“World-Honored One, I have already provided my wealth for my son’s marriage and have settled all matters. Only then shall I renounce these possessions and take up the alms-bowl to beg for food.

The Buddha again addressed him, saying, “If you can receive and recite a single verse from my Dharma and then explain it to your son, I will grant your request. He replied to the Buddha, “I am able to receive it.
The World-Honored One then spoke this verse: “When a son is born, the heart rejoices; For the sake of the son, one gathers wealth and goods. Furthermore...”
Having been betrothed and married off a wife, you have abandoned me to go forth as a renunciant. You are but a rustic from a remote village, a son who has betrayed his father;
with a human form but the heart of a rākṣasa, you have cast aside your aged sire. Now that the old horse is no longer of use, it is deprived of its beans and fodder.
While the son is young and the father is old, he abandons him to wander for alms; yet the curved staff is the most excellent thing, for it serves as my defense against the wicked oxen. It is able to—
He warded off violent and wicked dogs, supported me as we walked through the darkness, avoided deep pits and empty wells, and relied upon the power of his staff.
At that time, the Brahmin, having received the verses from the Buddha, returned to his house and first addressed the assembly, reciting the verses above.
His son, filled with shame and fear, immediately embraced his father and brought him back inside the house, where he bathed his father’s body, changed his clothes, and stood [in attendance].
At that time, the householder—the brahmin—had this thought: "Today I have received the grace of the World-Honored One;
as stated in the sūtras, he is my teacher. I shall now take these exquisite garments to the World-Honored One, prostrate at his feet, and say to him:
'I pray that you will accept these garments out of compassion for me. The World-Honored One then accepted them and further spoke on various matters.
He taught the various sublime Dharmas, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha came to proclaim the Dharma, the *Dharmapada* says: "In the Jeta Grove Monastery, four bhikṣus deliberated among themselves: 'What in this world..."
The most painful things are: first, sexual desire; second, hunger and thirst; third, anger and resentment; and fourth, fear and alarm. They disputed among themselves without ceasing.

The Buddha, knowing this, went to their location and asked them about it. They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "What you are discussing does not exhaust the meaning of suffering.
Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses having a body. [Suffering arises from] hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, and sensual desire."
Enmity and calamity all arise from the existence of the body. Indeed, the body is the root of manifold suffering and the source of misfortune;

it exhausts the mind and strains the intellect through ten thousand forms of anxiety and fear. That beings within the three realms are restless and constantly harm one another, and that the bonds of self-attachment cause the cycle of birth and death to never cease—all this is due to the body.
Desiring to escape worldly suffering, one should seek nirvana; by restraining the mind and maintaining rectitude, one becomes serene and free from [worldly concerns].
[The Buddha said: "Perception: one may attain Nirvana, which is the supreme bliss. Long ago, there was a bhikṣu who entered the mountains to study the Way.
At that time, four creatures—a pigeon, a crow, a snake, and a deer—clung to his side. During the day they went out to seek food, and at night they returned to dwell with him.

One night, they questioned one another regarding the suffering of the world. The pigeon said: 'Passionate desire is so intense that one has no regard for anything; it endangers the body and brings about its destruction.'"
Life does not fail to depend upon this. The crow said: "In times of hunger and thirst, the body becomes weak and the eyes grow dim; the consciousness is not at peace.
Casting oneself into a net and losing one's body and life—none of these do not arise from this. The snake said: "Once anger arises, one spares neither the near nor the distant;
it can kill others and can likewise cause one's own death. The deer said: "I am constantly afraid of hunters and various wolves and tigers. Wandering...
It was as if there were the sound of someone running along the bank of a pit. From this, it can be seen that fear and terror constitute suffering. The bhikṣu sighed and said:
"Among all the great sufferings in the world, none surpasses having a body."
In discussing the joy of the Buddha, the *Dharmapada-sūtra* states: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, four newly ordained bhikṣus went beneath a mango tree to walk about and amuse themselves. The mango blossoms were in full bloom, beautiful in color and fragrant.
The companions said to one another, "Of all the myriad affairs in this world, what is most enjoyable?
One person said, "In the second month of spring, when the hundred trees are in full bloom, to roam and play upon the plains and fields—this is the greatest joy.

Another said, "When kinsmen gather for a celebration, with cups and goblets clashing and music, song, and dance—this is the greatest joy. Yet another said, "To accumulate vast stores of wealth and treasure so that whatever one desires..."

One said: "To obtain carriages, horses, and finery that differ from those of the common crowd, so that one’s presence is radiant and conspicuous as one enters and exits, drawing the gaze of all passersby—this is the greatest pleasure.

Another said: "To have a wife and concubines of upright beauty, dressed in bright and colorful garments, their bodies perfumed with fragrant incense, allowing oneself to indulge in desires to one's heart's content."
"This is the ultimate bliss. The Buddha, knowing this, went to where they were and addressed them, saying: "What you have been discussing is entirely the way of anxiety, fear, and perilous ruin;
it is not the Dharma of eternal peace and supreme bliss. All things flourish in spring and wither in autumn and winter."

Relatives and kin who rejoice together must all eventually part. Wealth, treasures, carriages, and horses are shared among the five families. Wives and concubines of beautiful form are the root of love and hatred.
Attachment gives rise to sorrow; greed and desire give rise to fear. To understand that there is no greed is to be without sorrow and without fear.
Ordinary people dwelling in the world give rise to resentment and calamity; they endanger their own bodies and destroy their clans, facing immeasurable anxiety and fear.

The myriad forms of suffering in the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions do not all originate from this. When these four newly ordained bhikṣus heard this teaching, their minds were awakened;

they extinguished their worldly intentions and severed their desires. Feeling shame and remorse for their transgressions, they sought the Way with single-minded devotion, setting their will upon non-action and remaining free from greed.
Regarding worldly honors and profit: having attained the path of an Arhat, he offered sacrifices to Heaven.

Encountering a passage from the Buddhist Dharma, the *Jingyun* states: "In a border region there was a king named Hemuka, who served non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) and whose entire nation believed in heterodoxy."

He performed animal sacrifices for the purpose of worship. His maternal grandmother had been ill for a long time without recovery. He summoned a Brahmin and said, "My late mother-in-law has been bedridden with illness for a long duration;
I do not know the cause. The Brahmin replied, "It is simply because the stars and constellations are disordered and the yin and yang are out of harmony.
The King asked, "What method should be employed so that she may be cured? The Brahmin replied, "One must prepare oxen and horses."
"One hundred heads of pigs and sheep must be slaughtered to sacrifice to Heaven, and only then will he recover. The King immediately obeyed the command;

he led one hundred oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep toward the sacrificial altar, intending to slaughter them for the sacrifice to Heaven. The Buddha, harboring great compassion, took pity on the King’s ignorance and delusion.
He went to where the king was. Seeing the Buddha from afar, the king paid homage to him and said to the Buddha: "My mother has been ill for a long time;
I now wish to sacrifice to the heavens to pray for her life, hoping she may recover. The Buddha said: "If you wish to obtain grain and food, you should practice farming.
If you wish to obtain great wealth, you should practice giving. If you wish to obtain long life, you should practice great compassion. If you wish to obtain wisdom—"
Wisdom should practice learning; by practicing these four matters, one obtains the fruit according to what has been sown.
Sacrifices involving sexual license take the perverse for the correct; seeking life through the killing of living beings distances one from the Way of Life.

Even if a person lives a hundred years serving the deities and offering cattle and sheep in sacrifice, it is not as good as practicing compassion. The Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated heaven and earth; the King heard the Dharma.

Upon beholding the light, he immediately attained the stage of the Path (srotāpanna). Feeling shame and remorse, he ceased his sacrifices to the heavens. When his mother heard this, her heart was filled with joy and her ailment was eliminated.
Thereafter, the king placed faith and reverence in the Triple Gem; he loved his people as his own children and constantly practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
The five grains grew in abundance, and his mind was ever joyful and at peace.
The *Dharmapada-sūtra on the Conversion of the Butcher* states: There were five hundred non-Buddhists who constantly sought an opportunity to slander the Buddha.
They deliberated among themselves, saying, "We shall have a butcher kill living beings to invite the Buddha and the Sangha. The Buddha will surely accept the invitation and praise the butcher. We...

They went before him to revile him together. The Buddha accepted their invitation and addressed the butcher, saying: "When fruit is ripe, it falls of its own accord; when merit is ripe, one is delivered of its own accord.
The butcher returned home and prepared food and drink. When the Buddha and the assembly of monks arrived at the butcher's house, the Brahmins, both great and small, all rejoiced together, thinking:
"Today we have finally found an opportunity against the Buddha. If he praises merit... [they intended to]... with... (the text breaks off).
They previously committed the sin of killing living beings and now used it to revile him. If he were to speak of their own sins, they would challenge him by citing the merit of that very day.
Of these two options, they had now found their opportunity. When the Buddha arrived, he sat down and washed his hands before partaking of the food.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One observed the minds of the assembly to see who was ready for deliverance, and immediately extended his tongue so that it covered his face. He then emitted—
A great radiance illuminated the entire city, and from it issued a subtle and wondrous sound that spoke in verse as a prayer of blessing:

"As the True Person teaches one to sustain the body through the Way, the fool envies him and commits evil upon seeing him. By practicing evil, one obtains evil, just as planting bitter seeds yields bitterness.
One's own evil brings its own retribution; one's own goodness brings its own reward. Each ripens for itself and cannot be substituted for another. By practicing good, one obtains good."

Just as when sowing sweet [seeds], the minds of the five hundred brahmins were spontaneously opened and liberated. They immediately came forward to prostrate themselves before the Buddha with their five limbs touching the ground to receive his holy instruction, saying:
"We only pray that you will compassionately nurture us so that we may become śramaṇas. The Buddha immediately granted their request, and they all became śramaṇas.

When the butcher and his family saw the Buddha’s supernatural transformations, there was none among them who did not rejoice; they all attained the fruits of the Path. All the common people praised him as a Sage.
Friend, you shall no longer bear the name of a butcher.
Regarding the fisherman who crossed the net, the *Dharmapada* states: To the southeast of the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great river that was both deep and wide. There were five...
More than a hundred families lived along the shore; they had never heard of the path of moral virtue that delivers one from the world.

They were habituated to violence, making the catching of fish their primary occupation, greedily pursuing profit with unrestrained indulgence and excessive self-satisfaction. The Buddha, knowing that these families possessed the merit to be saved, stayed by the water’s edge and sat beneath a tree.
When the villagers saw the Buddha’s extraordinary radiance, there was none among them who was not struck with awe and reverence.
They went to pay their respects, either bowing, prostrating, or greeting him with inquiries after his well-being. The Buddha bade them sit and preached the Dharma for them;

yet, upon hearing it, the people did not believe in their hearts. The Buddha then manifested a person coming from south of the Yangtze River, who walked upon the water without sinking below the ankles.
When he arrived at the Buddha’s place and bowed his head to the ground in worship, all the people were struck with wonder and asked: [End of excerpt]
The transformed person said, "Our ancestors have lived by this river for generations, yet we have never heard of anyone walking upon the water.
Who are you, and what spiritual arts do you possess that allow you to tread upon the water without sinking? The transformed person replied, "I am a foolish and ignorant man from south of the river.
Hearing that the Buddha was here, I longed for the joy of the Way and its virtue; thus I came to the southern bank, but I was unable to cross."
The Ferryman asked the man from the other shore about the depth of the water. The man replied, "The water reaches only to my ankles.
Believing his words, I crossed over in this manner; there was no other special method involved. The Buddha praised the transformed man, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
Indeed, by holding fast to faith one can cross the abyss of birth and death; what is so remarkable about a river of only a few li? At that time, there was a village on the riverbank...

When people heard the Buddha preach various dharmas, their minds were opened and their understanding awakened; they all gave rise to faith, sought to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and became lay devotees (upāsakas).

The *Dharmapada* on the Conversion of Hunters states: In the kingdom of Rājagṛha there was a mountain. Beneath this mountain lived a man who had grown up in the mountain forests and made his livelihood by killing and hunting.
The Buddha went to his location and sat beneath a tree. The Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated the mountains; the wood and stones were all...
It was made golden. The men of the mountains all went out together to hunt; only the women beheld the Buddha’s radiance.
They came to where the Buddha was and all prostrated themselves in worship. The Buddha then preached to the women on the sin of taking life and the merit of practicing compassion and benevolence.
He taught that though love and affection meet for a time, there is inevitably separation. The women addressed the Buddha, saying, "The mountain folk are devoted to their labors..."
"The hunter replied, 'I subsist on meat. I wish to offer a small gift; I pray that you will accept it. The Buddha said, 'The Dharma of all Buddhas does not involve eating meat;
there is no need to prepare any more. Therefore, I tell you: throughout a person's life in this world, the food consumed is countless.
Why do you not instead prepare food that is beneficial? Instead, you harm living beings to sustain yourself, and upon death, you shall fall into the evil realms.'"

To cause harm without benefit: while humans sustain their lives and prolong their longevity by eating the five grains, those who kill living beings and eat their flesh suffer from many ailments and die prematurely.

To kill another to save oneself results in immeasurable karmic retribution; one who is compassionate and refrains from killing will encounter no misfortune wherever they go. A man returned from hunting.
Seeing that all the women were seated before the Buddha, he became enraged and drew his bow, intending to harm the Buddha. The women admonished him, saying, "This is a holy man;

do not harbor such evil intentions. They immediately repented their transgressions and prostrated themselves before the Buddha. The Buddha again preached for them the blessings of non-killing and the sins of cruelty and injury.
He taught that if a person can refrain from killing and practice great benevolence and compassion, they must have pity for all living beings.
"Universal love saves the multitude; blessings always follow one's person. Whatever benefit one attains in this life, upon death one ascends to the Brahma Heaven.
Having heard this, the hunters were filled with joy and accepted it with faith, and all received the five precepts.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-vicitrakumāra-śataka-pratyaya-sūtra* states: In the city of Śrāvastī, there was the son of an elder whose physical appearance was exceedingly ugly, resembling an evil spirit.
As he gradually grew older, his parents loathed him and drove him away to a distant place; anyone who saw him was struck with terror.
Terrified, he lived among the mountains and forests, subsisting on wild fruits; birds and beasts alike fled from him in fear.

Out of compassion, the World-Honored One led his bhikṣus to the forest intending to deliver him. Seeing the Buddha, [the man] tried to flee, but the Buddha used his supernatural power to prevent him from leaving.
At that time, the bhikṣus were each sitting cross-legged in meditative concentration beneath the trees. The World-Honored One then transformed himself into a hideous person.
His robes were coarse and tattered, and his alms-bowl was filled with food as he approached an ugly man.
Upon seeing him, the ugly man felt joy in his heart, thinking, "This person is truly my companion. He immediately came forward to speak with him and ate from the same vessel.
When they had finished eating, that transformed man suddenly became handsome. The ugly man asked, "Why have you suddenly become so handsome? The transformed man replied:
He replied, "I ate this food while contemplating with a virtuous mind that bhikṣu sitting in meditation beneath that tree, which has made me handsome.
Upon hearing this, the ugly man immediately imitated him; he gave rise to wholesome thoughts and his heart was filled with joy.
He then conceived deep faith and understanding toward the transformed being. Thereupon, the transformed being returned to his original form. When the ugly man saw the Buddha’s thirty-two [marks],...
He was endowed with the [thirty-two] marks and eighty minor characteristics; his radiance shone everywhere like a hundred thousand suns. He came forward and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha immediately preached various teachings for him, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. He then sought ordination before the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu.
His hair and beard were shaved away, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he became a śramaṇa. He then applied himself with diligence to cultivation.
He attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Regarding the rescue of the bandits, the *Jinglü yìxiàng* states: There were five hundred bandits plundering people and property. The King of Śrāvastī commanded his generals...
The officers pursued and captured them, seizing five hundred thieves. The King ordered that they be executed. The thieves cried out to the Buddha. The Buddha instructed Ānanda:
"Go and speak to the King: 'You are a king of men; you ought to love your subjects as your own children. Why do you order the execution of five hundred people at once?
Ānanda went to the King's presence and related the Buddha's words in full, saying: "The sin of killing a single person is great; how much more so for many?"
The five hundred men’s offenses were immeasurable. The king said, “World-Honored One, if you can cause them not to commit robbery again, I shall immediately release them and let them live.
Ānanda returned and reported this in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Tell the king simply to release them; I will ensure that these men shall not commit robbery again.
Ānanda went first to the place of execution and said to the executioners, “The World-Honored One has already saved them; they must not yet be killed.”
"Kill him! he cried. He went again to the king's presence, and the World-Honored One said to the king, "I can cause this man not to commit robbery again.

The king immediately granted him his life; for the time being, he did not untie his bonds and send him to the World-Honored One’s place. At that time, wishing to deliver that man, the World-Honored One sat in the open air.

The bandit saw the Buddha from afar and, though bound, his fetters fell away of their own accord. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. The Buddha, observing the conditions of his past causes and connections, spoke to him accordingly.
The Dharma: the fruits of the practice of generosity and ethical discipline; the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that very moment, they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. He asked them, "Do you wish to go forth [into the homeless life]?
They replied, "World-Honored One, had we gone forth earlier, we would not have encountered this suffering today. We only pray that, out of great compassion, You will ordain us. The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus! At that moment, the bodies and garments of the five hundred thieves were transformed into the three robes;
bowls appeared spontaneously, and their deportment became dignified and orderly, as they all became śramaṇas.

The *Duchu Fenren Jing* (Sūtra on Delivering the Dung-Remover) in the *Lüyìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Vinaya) states: In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a son of a caṇḍāla who made his living by removing dung.
When the World-Honored One saw him from afar, he immediately called out to him. The man replied, "I am carrying impure dung; I dare not draw near."
The Buddha said, "I wish to deliver you. He took the man by the hand to the banks of the Ganges River and bathed his body.
Then, returning to the Jetavana Monastery, he commanded the bhikṣus to ordain him as a śramaṇa. The man exhorted himself with diligence and practiced with such earnest effort that he improved daily.

Before ten days had passed, he attained the fruit of arhatship; his six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, and he possessed mastery over emerging from and submerging into the earth. He then proceeded to the Great Hall.
Sitting upon a stone in the center, wearing robes mended from old rags, the King heard that the Buddha had ordained the son of a *caṇḍāla*.
Recalling that the Buddha was born into a noble clan of the Śākya lineage, and that his attendant disciples were all drawn from the four *varṇas*, he thought:
"How can he enter my palace to receive offerings and alms? I shall now go to reprimand the Tathāgata. Yet, as he looked before him, he saw the bhikṣu being saluted by various devas.
When King Bimbisāra went to pay his respects, he saw that as soon as the bhikṣu saw him, the monk sank into the stone and then emerged from it again.
The king went to the Buddha’s dwelling and asked, "What was the name of that bhikṣu just now? He possesses such supernormal power. The Buddha said, "This was a man who cleared away filth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, spoke a parable: "It is just like a fragrant and pure lotus flower growing amidst foul mud."
“Great King, would a man with sight take this flower? The King replied, “World-Honored One, the flower is exceedingly fragrant and pure;
I would take it to adorn myself. As for the filth, I would contemplate the mother’s womb. Within that womb, the flower of merit is produced.
Then the King said to the Buddha, “That person has gained a marvelous and inconceivable benefit. From this day forward, I request that this bhikṣu [be accepted].”
They provided the four requisites for their support without any deficiency.

Regarding the causal origin of the gift of food that saved the face-burning hungry ghosts, the *Ji-mièrán-èguǐ-jīng* (Sūtra on Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts) states: Ānanda quickly went to the Buddha’s presence and said, "World-Honored One, yesterday..."
At night, I saw a hungry ghost with one face; its body was emaciated, withered, and extremely hideous.
Fire blazed upon its face, its throat was like a needle, its hair was disheveled, and its fur and claws were long and sharp. Its body was as if burdened by a heavy load.
It spoke to me, saying, "In three days, your life will surely end and you shall be born among the hungry ghosts. I immediately asked it, "By what method or means can I avoid this?"

“May I be spared from this suffering. The hungry ghost replied, “If you were to give food and drink to as many hungry ghosts, brahmins, and sages as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, you would gain an increase in lifespan. World-Honored One, how may I now escape this suffering?
The Buddha said, “Do not fear. There is a *dhāraṇī* named ‘Light of All Virtues with Immeasurable Power.’”
Then he spoke the mantra: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatavajriye oṃ savara savara hūṃ*. First, take food and drink and place it on a clean plate.

Recite the mantra seven times. Standing inside the door with arms extended toward the outside, place the plate on the clean ground and snap your fingers seven times, scattering [the contents] in the four directions. As for those [beings as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges...
Before each of the hungry ghosts stood four *magadha-droṇas* and nine *āḍhakas* of food and drink.
Thus, all these ghosts were completely satiated. Having eaten this food, all those hungry ghosts cast off their ghostly bodies and were entirely reborn in the heavens.
If the four classes of disciples can constantly recite this mantra and offer food and drink [to these beings], such persons will immediately attain the full measure of immeasurable merit;
their complexion will be fresh and pure, their lifespan will be extended, and these hungry ghosts will constantly come to protect them,
ensuring they possess auspiciousness and peace and happiness.

The *Ullambana Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Saving His Mother* states: When Mahāmaudgalyāyana had first attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he desired to deliver his parents to repay the kindness of their nursing him.
He then used his eye of the Way (*mārgacakṣus*) to survey the world and saw that his deceased mother had been reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). He could not see her...
Reduced to skin and bone, she stood there. Maudgalyāyana was overcome with grief; he immediately filled his alms bowl with food and went to offer it to his mother.

When his mother received the bowl of food, she took the bowl with her left hand and began to eat by pinching the food with her right hand. Before the food had even entered her mouth, it transformed into glowing embers, so that she could not eat.
Maudgalyāyana cried out loudly, wailing and weeping as he hurried back to report everything to the Buddha exactly as it had happened.
The Buddha said: "Your mother’s roots of sin are deeply entrenched; this is not something you alone can overcome.
Though your filial piety moves heaven and earth, even the celestial deities and terrestrial spirits cannot help her.

It requires the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha of the ten directions for her to attain liberation. I shall now explain the method of salvation so that all who are in distress may be delivered."

May all be freed from sorrow and suffering. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one should prepare meals of a hundred flavors and the five fruits for the parents of seven generations past as well as for one's present parents.
One should fill basins with all the sweet and delicious things of the world and offer them to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions.
By making offerings to these monks who are observing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if [the merit reaches] one's present parents...
They shall have a lifespan of a hundred years, free from illness and all afflictions of suffering.

Furthermore, their parents for seven generations shall escape the three miserable realms and the sufferings of the hungry ghosts, being reborn among humans and devas with boundless merit and happiness.

Disciples of the Buddha who practice filial piety should constantly remember their parents in every thought-moment, and on the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should perform [this rite] for them.

The *Ullambana* Offering to the Buddha and the Sangha. 2. The *Buddha-jue-ying-er-guan-fo-san-mei-jing* says: In the kingdom
When the child was five years old, his father would constantly teach him to recite "Namo Buddha. Once, when the spirit-general Saṃjñeya was tormented by the fires of hunger, he seized the infant;
however, as the child recited "Namo Buddha," the king of ghosts was silenced and unable to eat, and fire issued only from his eyes.
The infant, struck with terror, cried out, "Namo Buddhāya. The World-Honored One heard this from afar with his divine ear.

By means of his supernormal powers, the Buddha arrived at the wilderness marsh and emitted light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows to illuminate the frightened child. The king of ghosts raised a massive boulder, intending to hurl it at the World-Honored One.

The Buddha entered the Fire-Light Samādhi, causing the great earth and the marshy wilderness to blaze intensely. Amidst the light, emanated Buddhas praised the mind of compassion. Yet the ghost still did not submit.
At that time, the Vajra Deity brandished a golden mallet in his hand and flourished a sharp, great sword, aiming it at the forehead of the king of ghosts.
The king of ghosts was struck with terror; he clasped the young child to his chest, knelt upright before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray—"
"Compassion has saved my life. The World-Honored One, like a compassionate father consoling a king of ghosts, drew near to the Vajra-commanding King of Ghosts and said to him:
"You must now quickly submit and take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and receive the five precepts. If you do not submit, you shall be crushed into fine dust.
The King of Ghosts joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have constantly devoured people; from now on, I shall not kill."
"What shall we eat? The Buddha commanded the King of Ghosts: "You need only refrain from killing; I shall command my disciples to constantly provide you with food.

Until the Dharma perishes, by my power, I will ensure that you remain satiated. Having heard this, the King of Ghosts rejoiced and prostrated himself. He received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
The King of Ghosts of the Vast Wilderness then addressed the Vajra Deity: "It is because of the Great Virtuous One that I have attained [this merit]."
Partaking of the flavor of the unsurpassed Dharma-nectar.
The *Vajrapāṇi-guhya-paripṛcchā-ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Great Sage, please deign to..."
"I am the King of Ghosts, Vīraśa, who dwells in the wilderness. Please deign to partake of a small meal and transform the assembly of ghosts and spirits.

When these wondrous and malevolent beings behold the Honored Tathāgata and hear the Dharma of the sutras, they shall immediately cast away their anger, malice, and harm. At that time, the Buddha silently accepted the invitation.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, went to his residence. After having received the food and drink, Guhyapāda addressed the Buddha, saying: "I only pray..."
With vast compassion, he expounds the Dharma according to the needs of the time. The Buddha said: "One should uphold sincere faith and follow the path of the Dharma with diligence.

Beholding the principle of purity and clarity, one knows that the fruit of action is never lost. One would rather lose body and life than commit an unrighteous act. Be benevolent and refrain from killing; do not take what is not given."

One does not engage in sexual misconduct. One does not commit false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech; nor does one harbor envy, malice, or delusion. One does not violate the ten unwholesome actions.
One practices the ten wholesome actions with the body and also encourages others to do so. One constantly upholds impartial faith.

Upon seeing various śramaṇas who uphold the precepts, possess the Dharma, and diligently practice cultivation with their resolve fixed on the Way, or upon seeing various virtuous friends and disciples of the Buddha, one always acts [with reverence].
With reverence and diligence, one should constantly follow and attend upon such virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra). They rescue others from peril and distress and exhort and transform people.

Through giving, one attains great wealth; through upholding the precepts, one is reborn in heaven; through extensive learning, one gains great wisdom; and through cultivation, one accords with the Way.

By practicing generosity, one becomes a being of great riches; by stinginess and greed, one becomes a hungry ghost (preta). By upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, one is born among humans; by violating the precepts, one falls into lower realms.

"In hell, those who harbor anger and malice fall into ugliness; those who are indolent abandon the Way; those with distracted minds fall into transgression; and the foolish cast themselves into darkness.

The retribution for good and evil arises from body, speech, and mind. When the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and his five hundred sons heard this Dharma, they attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *Sūtra of the Miscellaneous Jewels* (*Za bao zang jing*) states that the Mother of Ghosts sought her children: At that time, there was a great ghost king named Pañcika.
His wife gave birth to five hundred ghost sons, all of whom possessed the strength of great wrestlers. The youngest son was named Piṅgala. [In Chinese: 嬪伽羅. Flower... [text fragment].
He said, "This is my beloved son; his countenance is upright and handsome. This Hārītī was a fierce, malevolent, and tyrannical spirit who killed the children of men and women to eat them herself.
The people were distressed by her and appealed to the World-Honored One.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the World-Honored One took her son, Piṅgala, and covered him beneath his alms-bowl. For seven days, Hārītī flew throughout the world searching for him.

Unable to find him, he became sorrowful, anxious, and distressed. Having heard it said that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses all-encompassing knowledge, he went to the Buddha’s presence and asked where his son was. The Buddha replied, "You have five hundred sons; you have lost only one."
"Why do you cause such suffering, distress, and grief by searching for them? "The people of the world have perhaps one son, or three, five, or more;

yet you kill and devour them. The Mother of Ghosts addressed the Buddha, saying, "If I may now obtain Piṅgala, I shall never again kill the sons of worldly people. The Buddha then caused the Mother of Ghosts to see Piṅgala.
The child was beneath the alms bowl; although the five hundred sons exerted all their supernatural powers, they were unable to retrieve it. They returned to seek the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If you can now receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and refrain from taking life for as long as you live, I shall return your child to you.
The Mother of Ghost Children immediately followed the Buddha’s command and received the Refuges and the Five Precepts. Once this was completed, he returned her child.
"Son," the Buddha said, "you must uphold the precepts well. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were the daughter of King Kalmāṣapāda;
because you did not uphold the precepts, you have received this retribution as a hungry ghost."
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Child Who Gave Earth to the Wise and the Foolish* states: The World-Honored One and Ānanda entered a city to beg for food.
They saw a group of children playing in the road; they had gathered together earth and dust to construct houses and storehouses, using the soil as rice. There was...
A young boy, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, conceived the thought of making an offering. He immediately took some of what was called "rice" from the granary and offered it to the Buddha.
The Buddha then lowered his head and accepted the earth. He said to Ānanda, "Take this earth and smear it upon my floor in the vihāra.
Ānanda took it back to the monastery and smeared it upon the floor. The Buddha told Ānanda, "That young boy just now gave with great joy."
"By the merit of smearing the ground with earth and cow dung, after one hundred years have passed since my parinirvāṇa, you shall become a king named Aśoka.

Your younger son shall become his minister, and together they shall govern all the lands of Jambudvīpa, causing the Three Jewels to flourish and making extensive offerings. They shall distribute the relics throughout Jambudvīpa. Thus he spoke.
"I have established eighty-four thousand stūpas. Ānanda said to the Buddha, "If offering a single handful of earth yields such a reward as these many stūpas, [how much more so for other acts]?
The Buddha said, "In the past, there was a king named Prasenajit. A Buddha appeared in the world named Puṣya.
The king, together with his ministers, made offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha. At that time, the king thought to himself: 'Now this great...'"
The people of this kingdom have always been able to see the Buddha, pay him homage, and make offerings.
However, in other small kingdoms located in remote and secluded places, the people have no means to cultivate merit.

Therefore, it is appropriate to commission the production of images of the Buddha and distribute them throughout all the nations so that all the people may make offerings to them. He immediately summoned many master artists to produce Buddha images, obtaining eighty thousand.
Four thousand [people] were moved by the retribution of the many stupas.

Regarding the *Sūtra on Requesting Avalokiteśvara for Willow Branches and Pure Water*, it says: "At that time, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Candracchattra who went to visit the Buddha."

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "The people of this country have encountered a great and evil disease. Even the skilled physician Jīvaka, though he has exhausted all his arts and techniques, is unable to save them.
We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will rescue us from the suffering of illness and cause us to be free from affliction."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying: "Not far from here, standing directly to the west, is a Buddha named Amitāyus.
There dwell two bodhisattvas named Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who constantly deliver beings from suffering and distress through their great compassion.
You should now pay homage to them; for the sake of all sentient beings, you should entreat that Buddha and these two."
When the Bodhisattva spoke these words, within the Buddha’s radiance they beheld the Buddha of Infinite Life in the western quarter, together with two bodhisattvas.
Through the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, the Buddha and the two bodhisattvas emitted a great light that illuminated Vaiśālī, turning it entirely golden.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī immediately took willow twigs and pure water and offered them to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, out of pity, protects and rescues. He universally instructs all sentient beings that they should with a single mind recite:
