"Namo Buddha, Namo Dharma, Namo Saṃgha; Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the one of great compassion and great renown who rescues those in suffering and distress. At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "I..."
I shall now proclaim the divine mantra for protecting and saving sentient beings by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Those who recite and uphold this mantra shall be freed from fear, the harm of weapons and staves, poisons, and diseases, and shall attain freedom from all affliction. As these words were spoken, the people of Vaiśālī were restored to their original state.

The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish* regarding the Gathering of Flowers and Offering Them to the Buddha states: When the World-Honored One was traveling through the city of Rājagṛha, the king dispatched several hundred thousand palace ladies to gather flowers.
On that day, men and women, both young and old, all went out together to gather flowers. Having gathered them, they carried them back and entered [the palace].
From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One, whose physical marks and majestic radiance were towering and magnificent, like the moon among the stars or the newly risen sun illuminating the world.
Surrounded by a multitude of men and women before and behind him, he proceeded to the Buddha’s location, prostrated himself in salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Human life is difficult to preserve; the appearance of a Buddha in this world is difficult to encounter; and the meeting with the sutras and the Dharma is difficult to find. Now that [this moment] has arrived—"

To encounter [the Buddha] is like a sick person finding a physician. Since I am poor and lowly, moreover, I am subject to the constraints of official arrest and imprisonment, never possessing any freedom.
The King has issued a strict decree ordering me to gather flowers for tribute; if I ever fail to meet the appointed time due to some other circumstance, I shall be executed.

The appearance of a Buddha, a Sage, in this world is a rarity occurring only once in billions of kalpas. Would it not be better to sacrifice my own life to offer these flowers to the Buddha and scatter them before him?

O Noble Assembly, because you have received these compassionate instructions and listened to this profound Dharma of infinite wisdom, I—who for incalculable kalpas have been harmed by desire and gain beyond measure—have never failed to cherish my life for the sake of the Dharma.

Now, as I offer these flowers to the World-Honored One and the Triple Gem, even if I am harmed, I shall not fall into suffering but will surely be reborn in a good realm. I now take refuge in the One.

The King’s heart was deeply reverent. The Buddha, knowing his thoughts and perceiving that he had given rise to such wholesome intentions, felt great compassion for him. He fully expounded and taught the Dharma of the Mahāyāna:
the six pāramitās, the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, the three gates of liberation, and bodhi. All those who had come from China conceived the aspiration for the Way;
their minds understood the Buddha’s wisdom, reaching the stage of non-retrogression and the non-arising of phenomena. Subsequently, the Buddha bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
She shall become a Buddha named Miaohua (Wonderful Flower).
The *Xianyu Yinyuan Jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish) states: In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a poor woman named Nanda who was destitute and alone.
Seeing alone that the kings, ministers, and subjects were all making offerings to the Buddha, he thought to himself: "Due to my past transgressions, I have been born into poverty and low status.
Although I have encountered this field of merit, I lack the seeds [of virtue]. Deeply moved by this bitter realization, he reproached himself with profound remorse.

He then went out to beg for alms to await the opportunity for a meager offering; he did not rest until the end of the day, yet obtained only a single coin. He immediately took it to buy oil and went forth.
Arriving at the monastery, he presented it to the World-Honored One. Placing it within a lamp, he made this vow:
"I am now poor and offer this small lamp as an offering to the Buddha. By this merit, may I obtain the lamp of wisdom in future lives to extinguish the defiled darkness of all sentient beings.
Having made this vow, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed. Thus, throughout the entire night...

The lamps were all extinguished; only this one remained burning. At that time, Maudgalyāyana was on duty for the day. Having observed that it was already dawn, he gathered up the lamps and tidied away the implements.
Seeing this single lamp burning alone, its flame bright and its oil and wick undiminished as if new, he thought:
"To burn a lamp during the daytime is of no benefit; I shall extinguish it, intending to relight it at dusk. He immediately raised his hand to fan out the lamp. The lamp—
The flame remained as before, without any diminution. He then fanned it with his robe, yet the light of the lamp was not diminished.

Seeing that Maudgalyāyana intended to extinguish this lamp, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "This lamp cannot be extinguished by you. This is an object offered by one who has developed the great resolve for universal salvation.
The poor woman returned once more to pay homage to the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately bestowed upon her a prophecy. Ānanda...
Within a hundred *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Dīpapradyota, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Seeking the Buddha’s permission to leave the household life, the Buddha immediately granted it to him.

The *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish* concerning the offering of banners to the Buddha states: In the city of Kapilavastu, there was an elder whose wealth was immeasurable and beyond calculation.
He selected a woman of noble lineage and high reputation to be his wife. He provided various musical performances and made a resolve to prepare [offerings].
He fashioned long banners to offer to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as a source of joy.
His wife became pregnant, and when ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who was handsome and exquisite, surpassing all others.
On the day of his birth, great banners and canopies appeared in the void, covering the entire city. At that time, the multitude of people gave him the name Potalaka. When he reached the age of...

As he grew up, he went out of the city to play. There he saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns.
His heart was filled with great wonder and joy; he gazed upon him until his heart’s content. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He returned home to take leave of his parents, seeking to enter the Path. Out of their deep affection and concern for him, his parents could not oppose his wish.

Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he immediately became a śramaṇa. Through diligent cultivation, he perfected the three knowledges (*traividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
He was revered and honored by all devas and worldlings. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, there was a king named Bandhumat.
He collected the relics and constructed a stūpa made of the seven precious substances to make offerings to them. At that time, there was a man who built a long..."
He hung a banner atop the stupa, made a vow, and departed. By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Throughout his time among gods and humans, he was always sheltered above by banners and canopies, enjoying celestial bliss.
Even until today, he has encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way. If you wish to know who that person was who offered the banner to the Buddha at that time—
This person is the present Pataṅga.

Regarding the karmic conditions for obtaining a prediction [of enlightenment] through the gift of robes, the *Xiányú yīnyuán jīng* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish) states: "At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for food. A brahmin saw the Buddha..."
His robes were slightly torn. He immediately went to his home, took a piece of white woolen cloth, and offered it to the Buddha to be used for mending the robes.
The Buddha accepted it and immediately bestowed upon him a prediction: "In one hundred kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood. The elder and the householder both thought to themselves:
"How is it that with such a small gift, he bestows such a great reward? The World-Honored One said: "Long ago, there was..."

The great minister invited the Buddha to accept his offerings for three months, and the Buddha granted his consent. There was a king named Bandhumat who wished to invite the Buddha first to accept his offerings for three months.
The Buddha said to the king, "I have already accepted the invitation of the great minister. The king then said to his minister:
“The Buddha resides in my kingdom, and I wish to make offerings to him. Although you requested him first, you should now yield to me; once I have finished my offerings, you may then invite him.

The minister replied to the king: “If Your Majesty will guarantee my life and limb, and further guarantee that the Tathāgata remains permanently here, and furthermore ensure that the kingdom is forever peaceful and free from calamity—if you can guarantee these matters, [I shall do as you say].”
"I shall now cease my deliberations and listen to the King's prior invitation. The King then said, "You invite for one day, and I shall invite for another.
The minister agreed, saying, "So be it. Thus, they took turns providing food, each fulfilling their respective wishes. At that time, the great minister prepared the three robes.
Furthermore, he prepared seven-strip robes for the assembly of bhikṣus, giving one to each person until all were fully provided for.
Ānanda, you should know that the great minister who at that time prepared these garments to offer as a gift to the Buddha and the Saṅgha was none other than this very brāhmaṇa.
Having planted merit life after life, he has now encountered me and again offered white woolen cloth; therefore, he has attained such [a state].
This is the fruit of the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

The *Sutra of the Sea Dragon King Saving the Dragon from the Peril of the Robe* states: "There are four dragon kings: the first is named Āśvāsa (Inhaling), the second is named Mahāśvāsa (Great Inhaling), the third is named..."
Xiongpi (bears and cubs). There are four names for the immeasurable colors. Bowing at the Buddha’s feet, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Within the great ocean there are countless kinds of dragons; their various activities all arise from karmic retribution. There are large species and small species.
There are four kinds of garuḍas who constantly devour these dragons, as well as the wives and children of the dragons and other dragon species. We pray that the Buddha will protect them."
The nāgas of the ocean shall always attain peace and security. Thereupon, the World-Honored One removed his own saṃghāṭī robe and addressed the Nāga King of the Ocean:
"You should take this Tathāgata’s robe and distribute it among all the nāgas so that it reaches everyone. Even those who receive but a single thread [shall be blessed]."
The King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda) cannot violate it; those who uphold the prohibitive precepts will surely obtain their aspirations.
At that time, the various Dragon Kings each thought to themselves, "This Buddha’s *kāṣāya* robe is very small; how can it suffice for all the dragons throughout the great ocean?

The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the dragons, addressed the Dragon Kings, saying, "Suppose all the Dragon Kings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were each to divide [it]..."

The Tathāgata’s *kāṣāya* could never be exhausted. At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara took the Buddha’s *kāṣāya* and divided it himself into countless hundreds of thousands of pieces, giving them to the various dragon kings; yet the robe remained as it was before, never being exhausted.
Then the dragon kings, along with their wives and children, were filled with great joy and threw themselves before the Buddha, speaking with one voice: "Tathāgata..."
What you have spoken is ultimately without duality. You grant us the prediction of our attainment of the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Today we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of noble ones. We accept the prohibitive precepts and respectfully obey the Tathāgata.
From this day forward, all of us nāgas shall protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The *Dharani for Eliminating Calamities* states: At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was dwelling among the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.

He addressed the assembly of celestial beings who roam the void—the various lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the nine great planets (*graha*), the twenty-eight lunar lodgings (*rāśi*), the deities of the twelve zodiac signs, and all the holy ones.
O Assembly, I shall now proclaim the method for removing calamities through the *Candraprabha-mahātejas-tejo-dhāraṇī*, as taught by the Tathāgata Śālarāja in the past.

Should there be a place where a king or his ministers reside that is oppressed by the five planets, or visited by the eclipsing shadow (*Rāhu*), comets, portents, or malevolent stars; or [where] the natal mansion and lunar mansions belonging to them...

If the positions of the stars shift or enter into conflict, thereby creating various obstacles and difficulties, one should recite this dhāraṇī with a sincere mind and uphold it through reading and chanting;
all calamities and hardships will then be entirely extinguished. The dhāraṇī is spoken as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānām apratihataśāsanānām. Tadyathā. Oṃ kha kha.*
KHĀHE KHĀHE HŪṂ HŪṂ JVALA JVALA PRABHŪTA-JVALA TIṢṬHA TIṢṬHA STHIRI STHIRI ŚVATA ŚVATA ŚĀNTIKA ŚRĪYE SVĀHĀ.
This dhāraṇī can accomplish eighty thousand kinds of auspiciousness.

Regarding auspicious matters: it can eliminate eighty thousand kinds of inauspicious events. If all sentient beings receive and uphold it according to the Dharma, all calamities and disasters will be entirely extinguished;
misfortunes will be transformed into blessings, and all shall attain auspiciousness. The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly:

When calamities arise, one should install a Buddha image and perform the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) for protection, making offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and candles according to one's means,
so that all sentient beings may obtain immeasurable merit.
The *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states as proof:
"When Śākyamuni Buddha was seated upon a precious lion throne within the jewel-adorned assembly hall of Avalokiteśvara’s palace on Mount Potalaka,
at that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara secretly emitted his spiritual..."
A pervasive radiance illuminated the world, and the palaces of the devas and the palaces of the nāgas all shook violently.

At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "I possess a Great Compassion Heart Dhāraṇī which I now wish to proclaim, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, for the sake of eliminating all illnesses and attaining longevity, for the sake of obtaining abundance, and for the sake of extinguishing all evils."
It removes heavy karma and grave offenses, brings one far from fear, and can swiftly fulfill all aspirations.
Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will look upon me with compassion and grant his permission. The Buddha said, "Now is the very time; you should speak it quickly.

He further addressed the Buddha, saying, "If there are members of the fourfold assembly who wish to recite and uphold this, they should give rise to a heart of great compassion and first, with a sincere mind, invoke and remember my name. Then..."
Thereafter, one should immediately recite this divine mantra. This mantra can eliminate all grave offenses within the body.

If any sentient beings who recite and uphold this Great Compassionate Divine Mantra do not have all their requests fulfilled in their present life, it cannot truly be called the *Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī*. Thus spoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the assembly.
Before the assembly, he stood with palms joined in reverence and gave rise to great compassion for all sentient beings. He then recited this wondrous mantra-gāthā dhāraṇī.
Having spoken this incantation, precious flowers rained down in profusion from the heavens. All the Buddhas of the ten directions were filled with joy;
the heavenly Māras and non-Buddhists were struck with terror, their hair standing on end. The entire assembly attained the realization of the fruits of the path. No...
He gauged the minds of the assembly and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
The *Mahāmegha-vṛṣṭi-saṃcodana-sūtra* states: "The Buddha was dwelling within the palace of the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda."
Within the precious pavilion of the Great Cloud Wheel Palace, which is a treasury of mani-jewels of great majesty, he was together with an immeasurable assembly of nāga kings.
They immediately made offerings of incense, flowers, banners, flags, silk canopies, pearls, and necklaces, paying homage and prostrating themselves before the Tathāgata.
There, they listened to and received the True Dharma, and then addressed the Buddha, saying: "How may one cause all the nāga kings..."

They shall extinguish all suffering and attain peace and happiness. You shall cause sweet rain to fall in due season within this Jambudvīpa, so that trees, groves, medicinal herbs, and crops may all grow with rich flavor, and all people may experience complete joy.
The Buddha said to the Great Dragon King: "You now bring great benefit to those sentient beings. You are able to...
I ask about this matter. I have a single dharma; if you are able to practice it, it will cause all nāgas to eliminate all suffering and become fully endowed with peace and happiness.
That is to say: the practice of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

If there are devas or humans who practice great loving-kindness, fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, poison cannot harm them, blades cannot wound them, and internal or external enemies and thieves cannot invade them.

Whether asleep or awake, one shall always find peace and security. By the power of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one possesses great majesty and virtue; neither gods nor worldly people can disturb or confuse them.
Their physical appearance is upright and dignified, and they are loved and respected by all. All sufferings are extinguished, and the mind attains joy.

For this reason, O Dragon King, you should always practice that conduct of great loving-kindness through your actions of body, speech, and mind. Thus did the Buddha [teach] for the sake of the dragons.
The King preached various Dharmas; having heard them, the Dragon King’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
He then requested to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and practiced the conduct of great compassion.
The *Devanāga-abhyudgata-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: When the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment, the ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas all gathered in a great assembly.
Within the host of the Unconditioned Elephant King, the Buddha desired to proclaim the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas, so that they might know the profound realm of all Buddhas. At that time...
Between the two realms of the Desire and Form Heavens, he manifested a monastery made of the seven treasures as vast as a great trichiliocosm.
All the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts, together with the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the buddha-fields of the ten directions, gathered there simultaneously like clouds.
The Buddha then expounded upon various forms of adornment, various radiances, the causal conditions for the manifestations of great compassion, and the thirty-two karmas of the Tathāgata. The ten...

The powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the karmic causes for the thirty-two marks, the thirty-two obstacles to the Mahāyāna, and the thirty-two methods for swift accomplishment—such immeasurable jewels of Dharma as these, including supernormal knowledges, wisdom, eloquence, skillful means, practices, and vows;
the four immeasurable minds seeking the path to liberation; and the teaching of the *dhāraṇīs*.

The various benefits of the *dhāraṇī*, the equality of all sentient beings in the Dharma, and the karmic causes and conditions for the birth, suffering, and pleasure experienced by the various nāgas were explained.
It was taught that by taking the three refuges, one immediately attains the pure eye and achieves peace and security.

Next, it was taught concerning all the bodhisattvas without exception in all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, and all the nāgas, devas, and various classes throughout the billion triple-world systems.
All the great spirits and deities assembled without exception. To proclaim the profound Buddha-dharma and for the sake of protecting the world,
he entrusted the various lands of Jambudvīpa to Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, all the devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, spirits, and deities,
assigning them each to distribute and establish themselves so as to protect, sustain, and nourish all sentient beings.
To eliminate obstacles, protect the wholesome, and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time, the *Buddhabhāṣita Kṣitigarbha-daśacakraka-sūtra* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "You should know that there exists..."

There is a bodhisattva named Kṣitigarbha who assumes the form of a śrāvaka. Having already, throughout immeasurable and incalculable great kalpas, brought sentient beings to maturity in worlds devoid of Buddhas during the five turbidities of evil ages, he is endowed with inconceivable and supreme merits.
He benefits, brings peace and happiness to, and cures all diseases of all sentient beings throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
It relieves the oppression of affliction, sorrow, and suffering, and can fulfill all sought-after aspirations.

If there is anyone who takes refuge in and makes offerings for even the duration of a single meal, all their sought-after aspirations will be swiftly fulfilled. This is superior to taking refuge in and making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for a hundred kalpas.
As stated in the sutras regarding the degenerate age of the Final Dharma, the faculties of people at that time are ruined, like empty earthenware vessels.
[The world] is seen as being like one born blind; the five desires are like a stony field that does not produce crops; the ten non-virtues are like a foul-smelling body, filthy and impure.
This sutra can extinguish the afflictions of sentient beings and cause the Three Jewels to endure for a long time. The Buddha said:

"My disciples who follow my bequeathed Dharma—even those who are unworthy vessels or practitioners lacking precepts—though they should be punished and disciplined, must not be allowed to return to lay life. Entrust this to you to protect and uphold my Dharma."
The king, his ministers, and his officials shall enjoy longevity and peace and happiness, attaining ten kinds of meritorious benefits. As for these "Ten Wheels":
when a human king governs a state, he selects and appoints his ministers; he pacifies and protects the people and trains the military to resist enemies;

he undertakes and maintains public works and provides sustenance for those with skills and arts; he rewards the good and punishes the evil, establishes the Triple Gem, and transforms sentient beings by severing their ten non-virtuous actions.
It causes them to cultivate the ten wholesome actions; it enables the lineage of the Three Jewels and the Dharma-eye to remain unextinguished throughout the long night;
and it subdues Māra and his enmity, enabling practitioners to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
The *Prasenajit-praśna-sūtra* records that King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kośala addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray only that the Great Master will kindly instruct me in the dharma for a king.
The Buddha told the Great King: "Just as a father cherishes his children and constantly wishes for their well-being..."
He restrains evil conduct and exhorts the cultivation of wholesome deeds. The people of the country regard him as their own child, all harboring loyalty and filial piety;

the Son of Heaven, in turn, maintains a heart of grace and forgiveness, lightening taxes and levies while reducing corvée labor. He establishes offices and assigns duties without seeking excessive proliferation.
Dismiss and punish the wicked; reward and promote the virtuous and good. Those who are disloyal and unrighteous should be swiftly distanced.

Follow the ancient sage-kings and do not carry out executions. Those born into the human realm are moved by superior conditions; if one were to sever their life, they would certainly incur retribution.
You should always be single-mindedly respectful toward the Triple Gem and never give rise to wrong views. After my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall be entrusted to kings, ministers, and high officials;
you must protect it so that it does not decline or suffer loss. Thus, the torch of the True Dharma shall be maintained and the Wheel of the True Dharma shall be turned.

May it continue without interruption throughout the limits of the future. If one can practice in accordance with the teachings in this way, then the dragon kings within the realm will rejoice, the winds will be harmonious, and the rains will be timely.
All the devas will be filled with joy, and there will be abundance, peace, and security. All calamities and misfortunes will be eliminated, and the entire land will enjoy great tranquility.
The king’s person will be happy, his sovereign position forever secure, his blessings and prosperity extended, and he shall no longer suffer from anxiety or distress.
His lifespan shall be increased, and his fame shall now pervade the ten directions. The kings of foreign lands will all come to offer tribute;
the Son of Heaven of that land will be benevolent, yielding, loyal, and filial, teaching and transforming by means of the Dharma to relieve and succor the common people.
Among all nations, he shall be foremost, and we shall now all submit to him. After this Great Dharma King has relinquished his body—
One will attain rebirth in the heavens and experience supreme, wondrous bliss.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti, who possessed eloquence..."
He had entered unhindered into the profound Dharma-gate; he was skilled in the *prajñāpāramitā* and thoroughly proficient in skillful means (*upāya*).

By means of these skillful means, he manifested himself as being ill. Because of this illness, everyone went to inquire after his health. Vimalakīrti, on account of his physical ailment, extensively expounded the Dharma for them, saying:
"O worthy ones, this body is impermanent; it is without strength, without power, and without solidity. It is a thing that quickly decays and cannot [be relied upon]."
It is true. This body is afflicted by suffering and the convergence of manifold diseases. This body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped;
this body is like a bubble, unable to endure for long; this body is like a flame, born from craving and thirst;
this body is like a plantain tree, having no solidity within; this body is like a magical illusion, arising from perversion; this body is like a dream, a false perception.
This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma; this body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes and conditions;
this body is like a floating cloud, changing and vanishing in an instant; this body is like lightning, not remaining for even a single thought-moment; this body has no master and is like the earth.
This body is without self, like fire; this body is without life-force, like wind; this body is without a person, like water;
this body is unreal, with the four great elements as its abode; this body is empty, devoid of "I" and "mine";
this body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles; this body is inactive, driven by the power of the winds; this body is impure and foul.
It is filled [with impurities]. This body is false and deceptive; though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, it must inevitably return to decay and extinction.
This body is a calamity, afflicted by over a hundred ailments. This body is like a dilapidated well, pressed down by old age. This body is without permanence, for death is its certain end.
It is only fit to be regarded with weariness and revulsion.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Mañjuśrī, having received the Buddha’s holy command, went to him to inquire after his illness. Vimalakīrti had prepared only a single bed and was lying upon it because of his sickness. Mañju...
The World-Honored One spoke these special words: "Householder, can this illness be endured? Is there any improvement from your treatment, and has it not worsened?
The World-Honored One asks you with great earnestness: what is the cause from which this illness arises? How long has it been since its birth? And how shall it be extinguished?"
Vimalakīrti said: "From ignorance and craving, my illness arises. Because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill.
If all sentient beings were to become free from illness, then my illness would cease. For the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas enter the cycle of birth and death;
as long as there is birth and death, there is illness. If sentient beings were to attain liberation from illness, then the Bodhisattva..."
"I am no longer ill. From what cause does this sickness arise? The sickness of a bodhisattva arises from the mind of great compassion.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "How should one console a sick bodhisattva? Vimalakīrti replied, "One should speak of the impermanence of the body, but not speak of revulsion toward the body;
speak of suffering in the body, but not speak of delighting in nirvāṇa; speak of non-self in the body, yet..."
One teaches and guides sentient beings; one speaks of the emptiness and quiescence of the body, but does not speak of ultimate extinction.

One speaks of repenting for past transgressions, but does not speak of entering the past. Out of compassion for the illnesses of others based on one’s own illness, one should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in previous lives;
one should resolve to benefit all sentient beings, recollect the merits one has cultivated, and mindfully attend to pure livelihood without giving rise to [defilements].
Free from distress, one should constantly arouse diligence to act as a King of Physicians to treat all illnesses.
In this way, one should console and encourage a sick bodhisattva so as to bring them joy.
Regarding the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* on the Repentance of the Golden Drum, it says: At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa dreamed of a golden drum and verses of repentance during the night.

He related this to the Tathāgata, saying: "In my dream, I saw a golden drum from which issued a wondrous sound capable of completely extinguishing all sufferings of the three periods of time. The earth...

The sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; the hardships of poverty and destitution, as well as all other forms of existence—may the sound produced by this golden drum completely extinguish all such sufferings. For those who are without support, without refuge, and without protection, I act as their place of refuge.
May the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who possess great compassion, bear witness to my humble sincerity and have pity upon me.
Please accept my confession. For whatever evil deeds I have committed throughout a hundred kalpas, I shall give rise to great sorrow and suffering because of these causes and conditions.
World-Honored Ones of Great Compassion currently dwelling in the ten directions, who are able to remove all fears of sentient beings:
I pray that you will accept this sincere confession of mine, so that my terrors may be entirely eliminated. All the defilements and karmic stains that I possess—only...
I pray that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the present, shall wash away [these transgressions] with the water of great compassion and purify them.
All past evils I now fully repent; the sins committed in the present I reveal with a sincere heart. Those not yet committed, I dare not commit again;
those already committed, I dare not conceal. Regarding the three types of physical karma, the four types of verbal karma, and the three types of mental karma—now...
I fully repent. I repent for all ten kinds of evil karma committed through body, speech, and mind.
Whatever evil karma I have created that ought to result in an evil retribution, I now sincerely repent before the Buddha.
Whatever wholesome dharmas exist in this land and in other worlds, I dedicate them all; may the merit of the good deeds I have cultivated through body, speech, and mind—may they...
In a future age, they shall realize the Unsurpassed Way.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various kinds of precious flowers."
[The assembly was] solemn. A multitude of bodhisattvas had come from various and diverse buddha-fields, possessing mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sporting with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Mahāmati Bodhisattva was their leader; all the Buddhas had poured water upon his crown.
He was well-versed in the meaning of the objective realms manifested by his own mind, [perceiving] the various kinds of sentient beings, their various minds and forms, and the immeasurable...

The gates of liberation appear universally according to the various types [of beings]. He has attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati praised the Buddha with a verse: "The world is free from arising and ceasing; it is like flowers in the sky."
All phenomena are like illusions; they are far removed from mind and consciousness, and far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. The world is ever like a dream.
Knowing that there is no self in persons or phenomena, and that afflictions and the objects of cognition are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
There is no nirvāṇa for all things; there is no Buddha who has entered nirvāṇa, nor is there a nirvāṇa belonging to a Buddha. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
Whether existence or non-existence, it is entirely free from these two. The Sage observes with tranquil stillness; this is the transcendence of birth.

This is called non-grasping; it brings tranquility in this life and future lives. Having praised him with these verses, [the Bodhisattva] inquired about the meaning of one hundred and eight points, as well as the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
At that time, the World-Honored One explained each of them in detail and earnestly exhorted him: "My disciples who practice cultivation should cultivate loving-kindness."
The mind shall not consume any kind of meat, nor onions, leeks, garlic, and the like, nor various intoxicants that lead to heedlessness.
One who eats meat lacks a heart of compassion and is forever turned away from true liberation.

The Preface to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* regarding the Three Contemplations of Perfect Enlightenment states: When the Tathāgata entered the land of quiescent light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), ordinary beings and sages shared a single source.

He manifested his enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), and the principal and the retinue assembled together. Mañjuśrī first inquired about the cause of the original arising, and the Bhagavat, the Most Honored One, first raised the theme for investigation.
The fruit of ultimate completion illuminates this true essence and extinguishes those dream-forms. Knowing there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes the cycle of rebirth?
Various illusory transformations arise within the awakened mind; when illusion is exhausted, awakening becomes perfect. The mind penetrates and the Dharma is pervasive.

The mind is originally the Buddha, yet due to the arising of thought, it drifts and sinks. The shore truly does not move, yet it appears to rush by because of the movement of the boat. Suddenly eliminate the false ruler; [emptiness]...
The flower does not arise anew; the source of craving is gradually exhausted. Gold has no further ore to refine; in principle, there is nothing to be cultivated or realized.

Wisdom appears to have gradations, yet each subsequent stage recognizes the errors of the preceding ones. How much more so for one who has forgotten delusion and the arising and ceasing of phenomena, whose virtues are equal to perfect luminosity!

Nevertheless, even a fine horse in the stable stirs at the shadow of the whip, and a great jewel buried in dust requires a method of treatment. Therefore, the three contemplations are clarified and made pure.

Entering both the true and the false, the various wheels alternate and intermingle, cultivated singly and in combination, and perfected in their totality. The four signs (lakṣaṇa) subtly influence the spirit, while the flower-like awakening resists and rejects them.

As the four maladies emerge from the body, the mind-flower shines forth with clarity. Furthermore, one establishes long, medium, and short-term goals, applying the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of mindful vigilance and mental collection.

By training alternately in specific and universal methods, the obstacles of karma and the obstacles of afflictions are dissolved and extinguished. One achieves the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*), and as stillness reaches its ultimate limit, partiality is awakened.
The Buddha-fields of hundreds of thousands of worlds appear before one. Thus, hearing these five names surpasses the merit of giving away the jewels of a world-system;

explaining the meaning of even half a verse excels that of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This is truly because there is no dharma that it does not sustain and no capacity for awakening that it does not reach.
Those who uphold this sutra shall be protected by Vajrapāṇi morning and evening, ensuring they do not regress. Their households shall forever be free from calamities and obstacles;
epidemics shall be eradicated, and their wealth and treasures shall abound.
Regarding the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: Ānanda was captured by the spells of the great sorceress Matangi, and his precept-body was on the verge of being destroyed.

The World-Honored One emitted a hundred rays of light from the crown of his head; within these lights were thousand-petaled precious lotuses, upon which transformation Buddhas sat and proclaimed the Dharma.
Divine Incantation. Ānanda returned to the Buddha’s presence. The Buddha preached this sutra, titled *The Great Buddha-Crown King of Śūraṅgama*, which fully encompasses the myriad practices.
It is the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.

Through the seven locations where the mind was sought and the eight ways in which seeing was analyzed, as well as the flying light, the striking and touching, and the opening and closing of the precious hand, he revealed that the true nature is immovable and that the wondrousness of one's own mind is inherent.
Illumination. The constant light manifests before one, its nature pervading the Dharma-realm. Cessation is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others.

Mañjuśrī selected among the various sages twenty-five perfect methods of penetration (*avavāda*), yet he took Avalokiteśvara’s entry into the Way through hearing as the true essence of the teaching for this land.
It is the source of the origin for the twelve classes of beings within the five turbidities. Only by practicing the three gradual stages can it be eliminated. From...
The advancement of practice through the Stage of Dry Wisdom; the four preparatory stages of the Ten Faiths, Ten Abidings, Ten Practices, and Ten Transferences;

the fifty-five stages including Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment; the causal conditions for birth within the three realms across the seven destinies and ten classes based on the ten causes;
the various demonic activities within the domains of the five aggregates during the ten types of *dhyāna*; and next, the cultivation of *samādhi* to sever [the roots of] killing and stealing.
Regarding lustful delusions, the merit of practicing and realizing the mantras at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*):

The Buddha said, "If a person were to offer the seven precious treasures to all Buddhas, it would not equal the merit of a single thought-moment in revealing this Dharma-door to those of later learning.

If a person has committed the four grave offenses or the ten *pārājika* transgressions and should have entered hell, their karmic obstacles shall be extinguished in a single thought-moment. By practicing according to the teaching, they will directly achieve [enlightenment]."
Bodhi. There are no further demonic activities.
The title of the Dharma-treasure of the Prajñā Emptiness states: "The Buddha [taught this] at Vulture Peak Mountain, the Jetavana Grove, the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, and the Bamboo [Grove]."
The sixteen assemblies were preached in various locations within the forest gardens. The original text from the Western Regions consisted of two hundred thousand verses.

This work encompasses all eight sections—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Prasphutapada*, *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Suvikrāntavikrāmī*, *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā*, and *Vajracchedikā*—which were previously circulated separately in this land.
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty obtained the complete version in the Western Regions and translated it at Yuhua Monastery.

The Prajñāpāramitā in six hundred fascicles exhausts the entirety of the Śūnyatā school. Initially, the Dharma Master intended to follow the public's wishes by following Kumārajīva’s translation, eliminating redundancies and repetitions;
however, during the night, he experienced a most terrifying event in a dream, whereupon he returned to the extensive translation.
He immediately beheld a most sublime vision and thus did not dare to edit it, but translated it according to the Sanskrit original.

On the day the translation was completed, Prajñāpāramitā emitted light, the devas rained down flowers, celestial music resounded in the air, and extraordinary fragrances wafted intensely. The Dharma Master said:

"This is a scripture for the protection of the state and a great treasure for humans and devas. The sutra itself records that in this land there shall be those who delight in the Mahayana; the King..."
Your servant’s fourfold assembly of followers shall transcribe, uphold, recite, and disseminate [this teaching], whereby they shall all attain rebirth in the heavens and ultimate liberation.
Prajñā is called the Mother of all Buddhas; it is one among the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). The other five perfections have not yet received this great name.
Only this Prajñā, the Perfect Teaching, alone is called supreme and great;

it is the deep reservoir of all wonders, the profound source of all wisdom, the fundamental origin of the myriad dharmas, and the ultimate perfection of all sages. Therefore, the preceding five [teachings] serve merely as auxiliaries.
It serves as an auxiliary to Prajñā; it alone bears this great name. "Prajñā" is translated here as "wisdom.
"True emptiness" refers to the twenty-one kinds of emptiness.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra on the Entrustment of the Prajñāpāramitā* states: The Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

Having finished teaching the Dharma of the fourteen right practices and other teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the sixteen great kings, including King Prasenajit, [he spoke as follows].

He further instructed the king, saying: "When various calamities and disasters arise within your realm, you should invite one hundred Dharma masters to arrange one hundred high seats and recite this sutra twice each day.
If immeasurable spirits and deities hear this sutra, they will protect your kingdom;
the karmic rewards of humans and devas shall all be fulfilled, and all disasters and difficulties will be completely extinguished. Thus spoke the Buddha.
"King Prasenajit, after my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, because all sentient beings will commit evil karma, various calamities will arise in all lands.
At that time, the kings and others, in order to protect themselves, their crown princes, their sons, their queens, their retinues, their ministers,
their common people, and their entire kingdoms, should immediately receive and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā."
Pāramitās. All shall attain peace and happiness. I entrust this Dharma to the king, and not to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
Why is this? Without the sovereign power of a king, it is impossible to establish the True Dharma and protect the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, he addressed King Prasenajit: "I now admonish you all: after my parinirvāṇa..."
When the True Dharma is about to perish, this sutra and the Three Jewels shall be entrusted to various kings to establish and protect them.

Great King, in the future age of the five turbidities, all kings, princes, and ministers will, relying on their own high status, destroy my teaching and prohibit my disciples from leaving the household life to build stupas and images. From this day forward, you must extensively ordain bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding nuns constructing Buddhist stupas, temples, scriptures, and images:
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
the Wondrous Scripture of the Lotus Flower, states that the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak with bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, bodhisattvas, and Śakra-devendra...

Śakra, the Great Brahmā King, the Four Great Kings, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, together with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were all present.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly flowers rained down, the earth shook in six ways, and light from the white tuft between his eyebrows was emitted, universally illuminating the world.
Rising from samādhi, he addressed Śāriputra: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter:
to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

For this reason, they preach this wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle and bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas. Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only once in a long time."
...it appears but once in an age, like the udumbara flower. First, it reveals the provisional teaching of the illusory city; finally, it bestows the secret of the crest-jewel.
Although the three chariots differ in their vehicles, the single rain nourishes all universally. It causes all to know for themselves that they will certainly become Buddhas.
While this sutra was being preached, the Stūpa of Many Treasures emerged from the earth, and the Buddhas of the ten directions assembled to bear witness. Six...
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten thousand Ganges Rivers, along with their retinues, shall protect and propagate it.

Those who uphold this sutra and rejoice in it will possess immeasurable merits, such as the purification of the six sense faculties. As for those who enter the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* and various *samādhis*:
Beholding the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as solemn and majestic, one realizes that the Buddha is eternally present and never perishes;

those who have attained realization know this to be a realm beyond the reach of thought or speculation. The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai realized the Samādhi of the Revolving Dhāraṇī and expounded the wondrous Dharma for ninety days.
There is no practice of upholding [the Dharma] more flourishing than this sutra.
Regarding King Śuddhodana falling ill, the *Śuddhodana-nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "At that time, King Śuddodhana was suddenly stricken by a grave illness; the four great elements within his body..."
At that same time, his body was being ravaged; his limbs were about to give way, his breath was unsteady, and death would soon come.
He addressed the kings, saying: "Though my life is coming to an end, I do not consider it a suffering.

My only regret is that I shall not see my son Siddhārtha, nor my second son Nanda. Furthermore, I regret that I shall not see my grandson Ānanda, the son of King Droṇodana, nor my great-grandson Rāhula. My...
"If I were able to see these sons of mine, though my illness be grave and I have not yet escaped birth and death, I would not consider it a hardship.
King Śuklodana said to King Śuddhodana: "I have heard that the World-Honored One is at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha."

It is more than two thousand li distant from here. Your Majesty is now increasingly frail; were you to dispatch a messenger, the road is so remote that we fear the delay would render it of no benefit.
We only pray that Your Majesty will not grieve so deeply or harbor anxious thoughts for your sons.
King Śuddhodana replied to King Śuklodana: "Although my sons and their like are far away, my hope for them remains undiminished.

Once my son has attained Buddhahood, through his great compassion he will constantly employ supernormal powers—seeing all with the divine eye and hearing all with the divine ear—to rescue and receive sentient beings.
Those who are ready to be saved, he shall deliver and liberate with a heart of loving-kindness and pity. It is, for example, as if there were a person..."
Surrounded by bandits, or encountering enemies, one becomes terrified and loses all sense of strategy; no longer hoping for self-rescue, one seeks only protection and refuge.
Relying on those with power, one desires rescue and protection to attain liberation.
It is like a person who, having fallen gravely ill, seeks a skilled physician to treat the disease; my situation today, as I gaze upon the World-Honored One, is just like this.
The Record of the Manifestations and Transformations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Part Two (1) and Part Two (2).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Baocheng of Baoen Temple.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (or *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*) states: At that time, the World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain.

With his divine ear, he heard from afar that the King, his father Śuddhodana, lay ill in the city of Kapilavastu and his life was about to end; he longed with thirsty devotion to see his sons, and the Buddha [responded].
Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, and the others, by means of their supernormal power, leaped into the air and arrived at Kapilavastu in an instant.
They emitted a great radiance that shone upon the King’s body, bringing relief from his suffering. The Buddha, together with Nanda and the others, traveled through the air and arrived;
the Buddha then entered the palace. When the King saw that the Buddha had arrived, he raised both hands and said: "I pray only that..."
"The Tathāgata stroked my body with his hand, causing me to find peace. I was oppressed by illness, and the pain was unbearable; my life was about to depart.
Now that I have seen you, my son, my suffering has been immediately dispelled. He further said, "Your vow has already been fulfilled, and you have also satisfied the wishes of sentient beings.
I am now afflicted by a grave illness; I pray that you will deliver me from this calamity. The Buddha said, "I only pray, O Father King, do not [further...]"
Filled with grief and anxiety, he placed his hand upon the forehead of the King, his father, and said, "Though my life is about to end, you may set your mind at ease.
The King then took the Buddha’s hand, placed it upon his own heart, and declared, "Now that I behold you, my wish is fulfilled."
His heart leaped with joy, and he rose from his bed. "The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has brought great benefit;
those who have been able to see him or hear his teachings are all individuals of great merit possessing auspicious marks. Today the World-Honored One is my son;
he has treated me with such exceeding kindness that I must not abandon him. At that time, the Father King remained at the place where he lay.
With palms joined, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One. At that moment, the Buddha’s palm rested upon the king’s heart;
as impermanence confronted him, his life ended, his breath ceased, and he suddenly passed into the next world.
The *Biqiuni jing* (Sūtra on the Nirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana) states: At that time, King Śuddhodana’s life came to an end and his breath ceased.
Then the Śākya clansmen bathed the king’s body with various fragrant waters, wrapped it in fine white cotton cloth, and enshrouded it in a coffin. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Reflecting upon future generations, [the Tathāgata considered] that people would become violent and fail to repay the kindness of their parents' upbringing, becoming unfilial children.
For the sake of establishing ritual laws for such sentient beings of the future, the Tathāgata personally desired to carry the coffin of his father, the King.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all came to attend the funeral; they knelt long and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We pray that you will grant us [this honor]."

They requested to carry the coffin of their father, the King, and the Buddha granted their request. The Four Heavenly Kings each transformed themselves into human form and lifted the coffin onto their shoulders with their hands.
All the people of the kingdom wept without exception. The Tathāgata personally took a censer in his hand and walked before the coffin.
They proceeded to the burial site, where the Buddha and the great assembly together piled up fragrant wood and placed the coffin upon it.
He set fire to it from above. The entire assembly wept even more bitterly. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The world is entirely impermanent; it is suffering, empty, and without self. It possesses no solidity; it is like an illusion, like a magical transformation, like a mirage, and like a flame.
It is like the moon reflected in water; life does not endure for long. You all, people, should diligently apply yourselves with vigor and exhort yourselves."
Exert yourselves to forever leave birth and death behind; only then shall you attain great peace.
Having lifted the fire to cremate the Great King’s body, the various kings each took five hundred jars of scented water to extinguish the flames.

Once the fire was extinguished, they vied with one another to collect the bones and place them within a golden casket. They immediately erected a stupa upon it, hanging silk banners, canopies, and various [ornaments].

Regarding the offering of bells to stupas and temples, the *Ekottarika Āgama* (The Numerical Discourses), in the section on "The Buddha Saving the Śākyas," states: King Prasenajit begot a crown prince named Virūḍhaka. When he was one year old...
At the age of eight, he went to the house of his maternal uncle Mahānāma of the Śākya clan outside the city of Kapilavastu.
A new hall had been constructed there, furnished with various seats, and the Buddha and the Saṅgha were invited to be seated therein for offerings.
When Prince Vidūḍabha ascended the seat and sat down, all the Śākyas saw him and together reviled and insulted him. The prince sighed and immediately spoke to the brahmin Bhāradvāja: "After me..."
"When I ascend the throne, I shall take my revenge. Later, King Prasenajit passed away, and Prince Viḍūḍabha was established as king.
At that time, the brahmin Bhārgava said to him, "Your Majesty, you must remember the insults and humiliations inflicted upon the Śākyas. The king replied, "Very well.
He immediately assembled the fourfold army and marched toward the kingdom of Kapilavastu to wage war against the Śākyas. When the World-Honored One heard this...

Having done so, he immediately used his supernormal power to go to the side of the road and sit beneath a withered tree. At that time, King Virūḍhaka saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath the tree;
he immediately alighted from his chariot, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One:
"There are other fine trees; why do you not sit under them? For what reason does the World-Honored One remain here today?"
He sat beneath this withered tree. The World-Honored One said, "The shade of one's own kinsmen is superior to that of outsiders.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "The shade of kinsmen is cool; From the Śākya clan the Buddha has emerged. All are my branches and leaves."
Therefore, he sat beneath this tree. At that time, King Virūḍhaka thought to himself: "The World-Honored One has today emerged from the Śākya clan;
I should not go to wage war against him, but ought rather to turn back here and return to my own land. Thus he thought three times.
The Buddha, by means of his supernatural power, stopped him on three occasions.

Regarding the preaching of the Dharma for his mother, the *Mahāmāyā Sūtra* states: While the Buddha was observing the three-month summer retreat beneath a Pāriñjataka tree in the Nandana Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Tathāgata sat cross-legged and emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light. Within these lights...
Upon each of the thousand lotuses sat a thousand transformation Buddhas. The majestic radiance of the sun, moon, and stars was eclipsed and did not appear.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "Go to my mother’s place and tell her that I am here. Upon hearing this, milk flowed forth from the Buddha-mother’s breasts like white lotuses;
she then entered directly into the Tathāgata’s mouth. Seeing his mother’s heart filled with joy within, the Tathāgata [accepted it].

She paid her respects and said to her mother: "Wherever the body travels, it is accompanied by both suffering and pleasure. One should cultivate *nirvāṇa* to forever leave behind both suffering and pleasure.
Having heard this, the Buddha’s mother applied herself with focused mindfulness; all her fetters were subdued, and she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All sentient beings within the five realms of existence do so because of the faults and afflictions of *kleśa*. Thus, bound by these fetters, they cannot attain liberation for themselves."
[He] said: "I vow that in a future life I shall attain perfect enlightenment and shall sever this root of suffering for all beings. The Buddha said:
"The reason sentient beings do not attain liberation is entirely due to greed, hatred, and delusion, which cause them to remain perpetually in birth and death.
Even the desire to seek rebirth in heaven is difficult to achieve; how much more so the hope of escaping birth and death? [If one] loses [this opportunity] while in the world...
Having a good reputation, they are abandoned by wise friends and kinsmen alike. At the moment of death, they experience extreme terror and fear;
their consciousness becomes dazed and confused, only then realizing their remorse. All of this is due to the afflictions of the three poisons.
If one wishes to seek the sublime fruit of liberation, one should sever the root of suffering. These foolish worldlings are entangled by the fetters. [Thus spoke] the great assembly gathered there.
Having heard these words, he wailed with grief and was overcome with distress.

Regarding the initial creation of the image, the *Zaoxiang jing* (Sūtra on the Creation of Images) states: While the Buddha was observing the three-month summer retreat in the celestial palace, preaching the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana...
Longing for the Buddha with thirsting devotion, he made a vow to create an image.
Viśvakarman, whose craftsmanship was peerless, manifested as a craftsman and began work on the day of the Buddha’s initial birth; it was completed in no time.
The Buddha manifested three jeweled stairways descending from heaven, accompanied by the various devas, their majestic power blazing and their radiance resplendent, like the full moon in the sky.
Surrounded by the multitude of stars, he was like the rising sun with its variegated clouds of dawn reflecting in all directions. Brahmā, holding a white parasol, stood to his right;
Śakra, holding a white fly-whisk, attended him on the left. The various devas descended through the air, while celestial music resounded and exquisite incense rained down flowers from the void.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings presented subtle and wondrous offerings. The Buddha told King Udayana, "Among my disciples, you shall be the first to establish the standard;
no one else can equal you in causing all sentient beings to attain the great benefit of faith, thereby securing vast merit and roots of goodness.
The Lord of Devas addressed the King, praising his merit in creating the image while the Buddha was in the heavens.
"You should rejoice in this virtue. The Buddha said, "If a person fashions images of the Buddha out of gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, or tin, using various colored silks for decoration;

or carves them from fragrant wood, jade, or stone; or weaves or embroiders them—even if they are as small as a single finger—they will obtain immeasurable merit and various rewards of fortune, and shall not be born in peripheral or inferior lands with lowly status."
Born into families of impure lineage, wrong views, or poverty, one will instead be reborn among humans and devas, endowed with perfection and surpassing all others.

One shall be free from the suffering of illness and not be harmed by poisons, weapons, or various calamities. One shall not fall into the three miserable realms nor undergo the retribution of suffering.
All manner of sins will be extinguished, and all manner of blessings will be attained.

The *Sūtra on Bathing the Buddha Image* states: The Buddha addressed the devas and people of Mahāsthāna, saying, "A human body is difficult to obtain; an encounter with a Buddha’s world is difficult to meet.
In the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, I was a layperson (*avadātavasana*). Throughout successive kalpas, I accumulated merit. Every time...
He felt self-reproach. Transmigrating through the five realms of existence, he did not crave wealth or treasures and had nothing for which he felt attachment.
He eventually became the crown prince of a king. He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month; upon descending to the earth, he took seven steps, raised his right hand, and declared:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored. I shall be the unsurpassed teacher for gods and men. When the prince was born, the earth shook greatly.
Movement. The Brahma Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Four Heavenly Kings each held twelve kinds of fragrant bathing water to bathe the Prince’s body.
The Prince attained the Way of the Buddha and manifested the Dharma to deliver the deluded masses. The Buddha said:

"The reason for using the eighth day of the fourth month is that at the juncture between spring and summer, calamities and transgressions are all exhausted, and while all things are universally born, the toxic vapors have not yet [arisen]."
It is now the season when it is neither cold nor hot, and the climate is harmonious and temperate; this is precisely the day on which the Buddha was born.
All good sons and good daughters, after the passing of the Buddha, should with a sincere mind recollect the Buddha and the power of his immeasurable merits.
By bathing the images of the Buddha as if he were still present, one shall obtain immeasurable merit beyond calculation. The devas, nāgas, and spirits will constantly follow and protect such persons.
[The Buddha] protected him. The Buddha said: "A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha's sutras are difficult to encounter.

If one can personally diminish one's own share for wife and children, and offer five households' worth of wealth to bathe the image of the Buddha, then whatever vows were made when the Buddha was in the world shall all be fulfilled.

Those who seek to transcend the world and attain the path of non-action (asaṃskṛta), and who desire forever not to meet with the cycle of birth and death, should seek to practice with diligent effort."
Regarding the aforementioned path,
the *Banniehuan jing* (Sutra on the Parinirvana of the Buddha’s Mother and Her Aunts) states: At that time, the Buddha’s aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with [the nun] Cūḍā...

Five hundred impoverished women arrived together at the place where the Buddha was; standing with palms joined, they addressed the Buddha, saying, "We cannot bear to witness the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha and the Arhats.

We wish to enter nirvāṇa first. The Buddha silently granted his consent. The Buddha’s maternal aunt rubbed his feet with her hands and said, "I am spared from witnessing the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Master of the Dharma, and the Lord of Heaven pass into extinction."
"The Teacher of Men, the Illuminator of the Three Realms—henceforth we shall no longer behold him. Thus spoke the five hundred *bhikṣuṇīs* (divine maidens), as described above;
the Buddha also approved of their words. The Buddha then expounded for them the hardships of the body: birth, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and vexation.
Furthermore, he praised the peace of Nirvana—desirelessness, purity, emptiness, wishlessness, and non-conceptuality. [Thus it was] for many [who attained] purity.
The bhikṣuṇīs, including Bhadrā Kāpileyī, were all filled with joy; they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves, and departed.

Returning to the vihāra, they arranged five hundred seats and each took her place. Mahāprajāpatī manifested her supernatural power of *ṛddhi*, causing herself to vanish from her seat and sink into the earth.
Coming from the east, he manifested transformations in mid-air at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.

He walked back and forth through the sky, sometimes sitting and sometimes lying down. From his upper body water issued forth while fire issued from his lower body; from his lower body water issued forth while fire issued from his upper body.
Then, sinking into the earth, he flew from the west, manifesting transformations as before, appearing throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
His supernormal powers were beyond measure; he emitted great radiance that illuminated all darkness and shone upon the heavens.
The five hundred *pudgalas* likewise manifested such transformations. They entered *nirvāṇa* simultaneously. The Buddha exhorted the venerable ones to prepare five hundred funerary monuments.
They offered banners and streamers and conducted the cremation according to the Dharma.
As the *Mahāmāyā Sūtra* states regarding the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa: "At that time, Māra Pāpīyas came to where the Buddha was and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the past, I entreated the World-Honored One to enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the World-Honored One replied to me, saying:

'Because my disciples—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—are not yet fully perfected, it is therefore not yet appropriate for me to enter parinirvāṇa. Now, World-Honored One, the fourfold assembly..."
"All is complete; that which was to be delivered has been finished. I only pray, O Sugata, that you will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Māra: "Excellent, Pāpīyan! You should know that after three months, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
When Māra Pāpīyan saw that the Buddha had granted his request, he leaped for joy, unable to contain himself, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet before returning.
He returned to the celestial palace. At that time, having granted the Māra’s request that he enter parinirvāṇa three months hence, the Tathāgata immediately relinquished his immeasurable lifespan;
yet, through his supernormal powers, he sustained his life for those three months. Thereupon, the great earth shook in six ways, the sun lost its brilliance, and wind and rain became unnatural;
among the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, there was none who was not struck with terror.
They came to where the Buddha was, filling the air. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, you have often said that one who possesses the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) can remain for the duration of a kalpa, or even for less than a kalpa, dwelling in the world according to their own will.

Why then does the Tathāgata not remain long in the world, being subject to the same nature as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)? The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You should know that all conditioned phenomena..."
"All phenomena are thus; they cannot endure forever. Having heard this, Ānanda was overwhelmed by confusion and distress, unable to restrain himself.
He wailed and wept bitterly, deeply repenting and reproaching himself.

Regarding the Buddha’s finger moving the stone, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the city of Kuśinagara, there were three hundred thousand strongmen who heard that the World-Honored One had entered nirvāṇa and was traveling along this road toward the Śāla grove. Consequently, these strongmen leveled and prepared this path. Thus it is said.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested as a śramaṇa and went to where the Mallas were, speaking these words:
"What are you young boys doing? When the Mallas heard this, they all became resentful and said to the śramaṇa:
"Why do you now call us 'young boys'? The śramaṇa replied: "Your great assembly consists of three hundred thousand people; [if you consider] the entirety of their lives..."
"The strength of my power cannot move this stone blocking the path; why then am I not called a 'child'?
The strongman said, "If you consider me a child, you should know that you yourself are a powerful great man.
Then the śramaṇa lifted the stone with two toes of his feet and spoke again, "Strongman, you are now able to move this stone out [of the way]."
[The Mallas asked,] "Is it possible on the Path? The śramaṇa took a stone in his hand and cast it into the midst of space.
All the strongmen were struck with terror and immediately sought to flee. The śramaṇa said, "You should not give way to fear.
The strongmen spoke again, saying, "Śramaṇa, is this stone permanent or is it impermanent? The śramaṇa blew upon it with his mouth, and the stone immediately shattered and crumbled away as if—
[The stone] was reduced to fine dust. Upon seeing this, the Malla cried out, "O Śramaṇa, this stone is impermanent!
He immediately felt remorse and reproached himself, thinking, "Why have we relied upon our sovereign physical strength, life, and wealth to give rise to such arrogance?
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, abandoned his manifested form and returned to his original shape to preach the Dharma for him. When the Malla saw this, [he attained realization]. All...
All of them gave rise to the bodhicitta.
The *Śarīrāṃśa-padmaprabha-sūtra* states: At the Bahudā River, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying, "I am now utterly exhausted; I may enter [parinirvāṇa]."
The Buddha bathed in the river. Having removed his saṃghāṭī robe and placed it on the riverbank, he entered the water to bathe.
Once he had finished bathing, the Buddha said to Ānanda, "Ānanda, you should contemplate my body adorned with the thirty-two marks. In three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the World-Honored One will proclaim for me what will happen to all sentient beings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
Regarding matters such as making offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, the Buddha told Ānanda:

"When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, he will enter the Vajra-samādhi and shatter this physical body into pieces like mustard seeds. Thus, one portion of these relics shall go to the realm of the devas;
one portion of the relics shall go to the world of the nāga kings; and one portion of the relics shall go to the world of the yakṣas."

At that time, the devas, nāga kings, and Vaiśravaṇa, King of Devas, all made offerings of incense and flowers to the relics, reverently prostrating as if they were beholding the Buddha’s own body. They all gave rise to the supreme vow for unexcelled bodhi.
As for the remaining relics in Jambudvīpa, there will be a king named Aśoka in the future who, for the sake of making offerings to the relics, shall construct eighty-four thousand [stūpas].

Furthermore, sixty thousand kings each built stupas to enshrine and honor the relics, offering them with various flower garlands, blended incenses, lamps, music, and prostrations, thereby planting the roots of merit for unsurpassed bodhi.
Some left the household life with pure faith, donned the dharma robes, and applied themselves diligently to the path of cultivation; they all exhausted their outflows and attained parinirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata possesses great majesty and virtue; because that Dharma-body relies upon the birth-body, the immeasurable merit obtained from making offerings to the relics of the birth-body is entrusted to the various devas.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Padmavaktra-sūtra*) states: At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished instructing Ānanda on the distribution of the relics, he further thought to himself:

"In order to cause the Buddha-dharma accomplished through my diligent and arduous cultivation of the path for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas to abide long in the world, I shall go to the abodes of the various devas to entrust the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, the Tathāgata...

He immediately ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, having seen the World-Honored One, prepared a high seat and said to the Buddha, "I pray that you will accept this seat.
The World-Honored One sat upon it, and the assembly of hundreds of thousands prostrated at the Buddha's feet.
The Buddha addressed Śakra: "You should now know that I, too, shall before long enter parinirvāṇa. I hereby entrust these teachings of the Buddha to you."
"I entrust this to you; you must protect and uphold it. Śakra, King of the Devas, wept until his face was drenched with tears, and said:
"How swift is the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One! The Dharma-eye of the World-Honored One is forever extinguished here.
As for what the Buddha has taught, it shall be within my power to protect, revere, and make offerings to it. The Tathāgata formerly descended from the Tuṣita Heaven...
O Mother of the Gods, I and the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods constantly provide protection. When the Buddha was born, I likewise came with the various devas to protect him.
When he sat beneath the Bodhi tree, defeated the hosts of Māra, and attained Perfect Enlightenment, I and the devas also came to protect him.
When he turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park, I and the assembly of devas also constantly [provided protection].
"Protect! I now lack the power to prevent the Tathāgata from entering parinirvāṇa, nor do I have the power to protect him.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached various dharmas, exhorting, comforting, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening Śakra and the devas, commanding them to protect the Buddha-dharma so that it might long abide in the world.
The *Sūtra on Entrusting the Dragon King Padmavaktra* states: At that time, the Tathāgata entrusted Śakra and the various devas to protect the Buddha-dharma.
Having vanished from the heavens, he immediately appeared in the palace of the Naga King Sāgara. At that moment, the Naga King beheld the Tathāgata.
Upon his arrival, he immediately prepared a seat for the Tathāgata. The Buddha sat upon that seat, and hundreds of thousands of nāgas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha addressed the Nāga King, saying: "You should now know that the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa.
I entrust the Buddha-dharma to you; you must protect it and ensure that it is not severed. Nāga King, you should know this world of nāgas—"
"There are various evil nāgas who frequently give rise to anger and ignorance regarding sin and merit; being wicked and violent, they destroy my Dharma.
For this reason, I now entrust this Buddha-Dharma to you. At that time, the Nāga King wept, his tears falling like rain upon his face, and said:
"World-Honored One, we nāgas are blind and lack the eye of wisdom; for this reason, we are now born as animals."
"Among those born [in this world], if the Dragon World becomes empty after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall lose our lives and not know where we shall be reborn in the future.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the teachers of sentient beings; why do you now wish to enter parinirvāṇa? The Eye of the World is about to perish.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached various Dharmas for the Dragon King, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, and entrusted [the teaching] to Śākyamuni.
The Nāga King Kāla, the Nāga King Takṣaka, the Nāga King Nanda, the Nāga King Upananda,
the Nāga King Vāsuki, the Nāga King Anavatapta, the Nāga King Mānasvin, the Nāga King Śubhara,
the Nāga King Mucilinda, and the Nāga King Kṛṣṇa— each with several hundreds of thousands of retinues— were commanded to protect the Buddha-dharma.
He shall dwell long in the world without interruption.
As stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "The Buddha was at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara, at the Ārāḍa..."

Between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Ajitavatī River, surrounded by eight billion bhikṣus, at the time of his parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month, he uttered a great sound and proclaimed universally to all sentient beings:
"Today, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, out of compassion for sentient beings and protection of sentient beings, regards them all equally, as if they were his only son. Great!
