The World-Honored One perceived that he was about to enter parinirvāṇa and said, "If there is anything you doubt, you may now ask all your questions.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from the gate of his face—light of blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and agate colors—which shone throughout the trichiliocosm and even reached all Buddha-lands in the ten directions. Sentient beings of the six realms who encountered this light...
Their sinful defilements and afflictions were all completely extinguished; they were all filled with lamentation, sorrow, and distress.

Raising their voices, they wept bitterly, wailing and crying out in grief and agony, beating their breasts and shouting loudly as tears fell like rain. "Alas, our compassionate father! How painful! How bitter!
At that time, the fourfold assembly said to one another, "We must go quickly to the city of Kuśinagara, where the Mallas dwell."
They prostrated on the ground to pay homage and entreated the Tathāgata not to enter parinirvāṇa. They further spoke these words:
"The world has become empty and the merit of sentient beings is exhausted; unwholesome karmas increase and appear in the world.

From this day forth, we shall have no protector, no one to revere, and we shall be destitute, orphaned, and exposed. Having had these thoughts, they all went to where the Buddha was and touched their heads to his feet in veneration.
Wiping away his tears with his robe, he spoke, saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will not enter parinirvāṇa. The World-Honored One remained silent, and his wish was not granted;
at that moment, [the assembly] wailed and wept.

The *Sūtra on the Weeping of the Deva-Dragons and the Lotus-Faced One* states: At that time, when the World-Honored One departed from the Bodhi tree, Śakra-devānām-indra, together with the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
Suyāma, along with the assembly of the Yāma devas; Tuṣita, along with the assembly of the Tuṣita devas; and Nirmāṇarati, each with their respective assemblies of devas [all followed him].
At that time, they raised their voices in piteous weeping, shedding tears like rain; wiping away their tears with their hands, they spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata’s countenance is most subtle and wondrous, surpassing all beings without peer. Such a body, adorned with such extraordinary excellence, shall before long enter parinirvāṇa.
At that moment, Vemacitra, the Asura King, together with the host of asuras... Sa... [text continues]
The Naga King Kāla with his host of nāgas; the Deva King Virūḍhaka with his host of kumbhāṇḍas;
the Deva King Virūpākṣa and the Deva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra with their hosts of nāgas; the Deva King Vaiśravaṇa;
the Great Yakṣa General Sañjikā; and the Great Yakṣa General Maṇibhadra, together with the yakṣas.

The assembly—the earth deities, celestial deities, forest deities, Vajrapāṇi, the deity of the Lumbinī grove, the deity of Kapilavastu, the deity of the Bodhi tree, and the hosts of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings—raised a great cry, wailing and weeping, and spoke these words:
"The Buddha is the father of all sentient beings; he will soon pass away. The Buddha said: "You must not..."

Weeping, their hearts became bewildered and distressed. "How could there be anyone in this world who, having taken birth, could cause these conditioned phenomena born of the harmony of causes and conditions to endure for long?
It is impossible for these impermanent phenomena to be forced not to perish and disintegrate.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma in various ways, causing their minds to open and understand, so that they gave rise to great joy. The devas and nāga kings [bowed] with the crowns of their heads...
Having paid homage to the World-Honored One, each returned to their original place.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* records that the King of Māras then recited a spell: "At that time, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, together with an immeasurable multitude of sons and daughters of the gods..."

Having prepared various foods and drinks, he approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated himself, and requested of the Buddha: "I pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept my offering.
Once you have accepted my offering, if there are any sons or daughters of good family who invoke the name of the Mahāyāna..."
Whether they be true or false, we shall all provide protection for such persons by means of this fearless mantra.
And he spoke this mantra: *Tāṭa-cchaṭa-ṭālā tāṭi-lūlūle mahālūlūle aramāramadara-svāhā*.
The Māra King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this mantra is able to cause all..."
It enables those with distracted minds to attain profound and wondrous meditative concentration; it can cause all who are terrified to be free from their fears;
it can cause those who act as Dharma-preachers to possess uninterrupted eloquence; and it is capable of subduing all non-Buddhists.

All who are able to protect the True Dharma shall be protected by this mantra, as if wearing a divine sword. What I have spoken of regarding this mantra-ritual is true and authentic. If there should be anyone...

"Whoever can rely upon this mantra, whether they are staying in the wilderness amidst predatory beasts, poisonous creatures, or the perils of water and fire, all such calamities shall be entirely eliminated if they uphold or recite it.
Today we have all been freed from these various hardships and deceptions;

we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our offering and grant his seal of approval for the divine mantra we have spoken. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Māra:
The King said, "I do not accept your offerings of food and drink, for the sake of bringing peace and security to all sentient beings;

however, I shall now accept your gift of the Dharma, which is this divine mantra. At that time, the Great Lord Śakra, seeing the Buddha emit a great radiance that illuminated the entire world, prostrated himself and offered praise.

Regarding Cunda’s later offering, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: In the kingdom of Kuśinagara, there was an elder named Cunda who, together with five hundred sons of elders, felt deep sorrow and grief.
He prostrated before the Buddha, his tears falling like rain, and with palms joined, he addressed him.
“Buddha, we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our final offering, so that I and all sentient beings may together receive liberation.
The World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying: “I shall accept your request for this final offering.
You, Cunda, should not give rise to sorrow or distress; you should instead feel great joy. You must not now entreat the Tathāgata to remain here permanently.”
O World, you should contemplate that the world is entirely impermanent; the nature of all sentient beings is likewise so.
Even if one remains long in the world, in the end one must inevitably perish. Though one may be born in the heavens of long life, one’s lifespan must also surely come to an end.
All accomplishments will eventually fail; all that exists is subject to total extinction. The vigorous are destroyed by old age; the strong are oppressed by illness. Thus it is for all human life.
There is death; impermanence cannot endure for long. Wives, children, elephants, horses, and wealth—all are likewise so.
All the various kinsmen and relatives in this world shall be separated; there remains only the suffering of birth and old age, and the great affliction of sickness and death.
Cunda, wailing with tears, again entreated him, saying, "I pray that you will compassionately remain for a long time. The World-Honored One replied, "Cunda, do not weep."
Weeping only disturbs the mind. You should practice right mindfulness and understand that all conditioned things lack any solid substance.
Cunda addressed the Buddha: "If the Tathāgata does not take pity on remaining in the world, then the world will become a void; how could we help but weep? The Buddha said:
"Cunda, it is because I have compassion for you and all sentient beings that I enter parinirvāṇa. Such is the nature of all Buddhas."
This principle applies to all dharmas in this way.
The *Sūtra on the Final Chapter of the Mahāparinirvāṇa of Subhadra* states: At that time, Subhadra heard from the Buddha the discourse on the Great Parinirvāṇa... [text continues] ...extremely...
Having realized the profound and wondrous Dharma, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having cherished and protected the True Dharma, he abandoned all wrong views;
his deep faith in the Buddha’s teachings became firm and unshakable. Desiring to leave the household life, the Buddha said to him, “Welcome! and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

The water of the wisdom of the Dharma-nature poured into the source of his mind; he was no longer bound by attachments. With outflows exhausted and his mind liberated, he attained the fruit of arhatship. Then, before the Buddha, he [prostrated] for a long time...
Kneeling with palms joined, his grief and joy mingled as he deeply reproached himself and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I regret that this poisonous body of mine has, throughout long kalpas, constantly deceived and deluded me, causing me to remain submerged for a long time in ignorance and false views.

I have been drowning in the dharmas of the three realms and of external paths, doing immense harm. Now is a great occasion of celebration; having received the grace of the Tathāgata, I am able to enter the True Dharma. Worldly...
"O Honored One, ocean of wisdom, your compassion is immeasurable. I humbly reflect that even if I were to sacrifice my body over successive kalpas, I could not repay this brief moment of grace.
Weeping with tears that I cannot restrain, I address the Buddha again: 'I am advanced in years and my remaining life is short;
I have not yet escaped the manifold sufferings, and the transition of suffering presses upon me. I only pray, World-Honored One, do not enter parinirvāṇa.'"
"Wait," [said the Buddha]. The World-Honored One did not grant his permission. Subhadra raised his voice and wept bitterly;

casting his whole body upon the ground, he fell into a swoon and remained unconscious for a long time before regaining consciousness. With tears streaming down and his throat choked with sobs, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I cannot bear to see the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa. It would be better for me to pass away first; I only pray that the World-Honored One will enter nirvāṇa later."
Having spoken these words, he was choked with grief and longing; at that very moment, he entered *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha then commanded the great assembly to cremate his remains with various kinds of fragrant wood.
The *Sūtra on the Manifestation of Vajra-Dūṣī Vajra* states: At that time, when the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, the multitudes of devas and humans all came to make offerings.
Only the Brahma King Śaṅkhacakraka did not come to pay his respects. Thereupon, the great assembly detested his arrogance.
He dispatched various mantra-adepts to go there and seize it; however, they saw that the city was surrounded by moats of all kinds of impurities, and they died upon violating the mantras.
He then urged forth immeasurable Vajra-holders to go, yet no one could capture it. The great assembly was filled with sorrow.
At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his power of great universal knowledge, emanated from his left heart an indestructible vajra.
He then manifested great supernatural powers before the assembly and, leaping up into the air, went to where the Brahmā King was.
Pointing at those impure substances, he transformed them into the great earth. The Vajra declared: "You are greatly deluded! I, the Tathāgata, am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you..."
"Why do you not go? Thus, the Brahma King Śikhin resolved to go to the place where the Tathāgata was. At that time, Vajra again addressed the assembly, saying:
"If there are sentient beings in the world who are afflicted and disturbed by various devas, evil māras, or non-Buddhists, they need only recite my mantra.
This shall cause all sentient beings to be forever freed from poverty and always abide in peace and happiness. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you should uphold it."
This mantra vows to deliver sentient beings so that the Buddha-dharma shall not perish but endure long in the world.
He then spoke the Great Perfect Dhāraṇī Divine Mantra, the Vimalacāraṇa (Ugly Trace) Spell:
Oṃ bhrūṃ bhruṃ ma-hā-prahaṇa ḍi khaṃ śi khaṃ vi-ki-vi-ma-na-si oṃ muḥ bhruṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ.

Svāhā. If there are sentient beings who recite and uphold this mantra, they shall forever be free from suffering and hardship; whatever they seek shall be as they wish, their every desire fulfilled, and they shall attain great auspiciousness.
The *Tathāgata-avyākṛta-dharmasthiti-sūtra* states: When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda, saying:

"After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Final Dharma, my disciples will abandon the Buddha’s true teaching; they will become excessively greedy for gain and offerings, and will practice various frivolous disputations regarding me."

Within the Dharma, they fail to properly cultivate bodily discipline, mental concentration, and wisdom. They engage in mutual strife, plotting to seize one another's property and slandering one another.
They become addicted to various fine garments, dwellings, and furnishings. These evil factions gather together;
even if some among them maintain the precepts, they insult and disparage one another, such that in a mere instant, they all violate their vows. For these reasons, devas and nāgas...
The assembly’s sorrow and distress were entirely dispelled. Ministers and elders failed to give rise to pure faith toward the Triple Gem and instead insulted and disparaged them;
by these causes and conditions, the True Dharma was brought to extinction.

From that time forward, the evil deeds of the bhikṣus grew ever deeper, and the ministers and elders became increasingly disrespectful. Yet the remaining influence of the Triple Gem had not yet vanished.

They were all utterly extinguished. Therefore, at that time, there were again bhikṣus who had few desires and were content, who guarded the prohibitive precepts, practiced meditative concentration, delighted in extensive learning, and upheld the teachings of the Tathāgata’s Tripiṭaka.

They analyzed and expounded them in detail for the fourfold assembly, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings. There were also kings, ministers, elders, and householders.
Good men and women of faith who cherish the True Dharma, making offerings and paying respect to the Triple Gem,
honoring, praising, protecting, and upholding it without regard for anything else—
know that they are all inconceivable Bodhisattvas born at this time through the power of their original vows to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata, together with all...
He brings great benefit to sentient beings.
Regarding his final instructions, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should all know that by this..."

I have realized the Dharma for myself and attained perfect enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.

Within this Dharma, you should live in harmony and accord, without giving rise to disputes. Having received the same teacher and being of one essence like water and milk, you should diligently train yourselves within my Dharma.
The twelvefold division of the teaching that I have spoken— namely, the sūtra, the geya, the vyākaraṇa,
the gāthā, the udāna, the nidāna, the itivṛttaka, the jātaka, the vaipulya, the adbhutadharma, the avadāna, and the upadeśa—
you should properly receive, uphold, weigh, analyze, and practice according to the specific matters, just as...
"In no long time, after three months, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus threw themselves to the ground.
The Buddha said, "Cease, all of you; do not harbor grief or distress. Among heaven, earth, humans, and things, there is none that is born and does not end.
It is impossible for anything conditioned to remain unchanging. I have also previously taught that what is joined through affection is impermanent."
[He] departed. "The body is not one's own; life does not endure long. I am old, and my remaining lifespan is but little.
What was to be done has been accomplished; now I shall relinquish my life-force. You, bhikṣus, must restrain yourselves, fix your minds, and guard your hearts.

If you are not negligent regarding my Dharma, you will be able to extinguish the root of suffering and bring an end to birth, aging, and death. He further addressed the bhikṣus: "As for what I have now..."
What is it that I am admonishing you with? The Māra Pāpīyān has just now requested that I enter parinirvāṇa quickly.
The World-Honored One did not respond, but silently granted his consent. This is the final instruction left at the time of his passing.
The *Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* states: At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvāṇa, it was the middle of the night, silent and still.
For the sake of his disciples, he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma: "After my parinirvāṇa, you bhikṣus, you must revere, treasure, and honor the *prātimokṣa*.
It is like encountering light in the darkness, or a poor man finding a treasure. You should know that this is [the foundation]."
"O Great Master, even if I were to remain in the world, it would be no different from this.
Those who uphold the pure precepts must not engage in buying and selling, nor trade, nor establish fields and houses. They must not keep people as subjects, slaves, or livestock.

All cultivation of plants and all possession of wealth and treasures should be avoided at a distance, as one would avoid a pit of fire. One must not cut down grass or trees, nor plow the soil or dig the earth."

Compounding medicinal decoctions, divining good or bad fortune, observing the stars above, calculating the waxing and waning of the calendar, and performing astrological computations—none of these should be practiced.
One should restrain the body and moderate one's food, living in purity and self-sufficiency. One must not involve oneself in worldly affairs or serve as a messenger for official missions.

One should not practice incantations or elixirs of immortality, nor cultivate intimacy with or show familiarity toward persons of high rank; all such things are improper. One should instead maintain personal integrity.

With a mind of right mindfulness, one seeks deliverance. One must not conceal faults or manifest wonders to delude the masses. Regarding the four types of offerings, one should know moderation and contentment;
whatever offerings one receives should not be accumulated. This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts.
The precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation; therefore, they are called *prātimokṣa*. By relying on these precepts, one attains birth [in the higher realms].
Regarding the various meditative concentrations and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering, you should maintain pure precepts without allowing them to be impaired or deficient.
If one can maintain pure precepts, then wholesome dharmas will arise; if there are no pure precepts, none of the various virtuous merits can be produced. I wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
This is my final instruction. Regarding the ritual for cremation, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, upon your nirvāṇa, by what ritual procedure shall the cremation be performed?"
Vīra Tathāgata, the Buddha said: "When I enter nirvana, it shall be like the passing away of a Cakravartin King; after seven days have elapsed, I shall be placed in a golden coffin.
Then, the finest fragrant oils shall be poured into the coffin until it is full, and the lid of the coffin shall be sealed securely."
The four sides of the coffin should be adorned with an intermingling of the seven precious jewels. All manner of banners, streamers, incense, and flowers should be used for offerings.
After seven days have passed, the golden coffin should be opened again. One should wash and bathe the body of the Tathāgata with various exquisite perfumed waters.
Then, the entire body should be wrapped in the finest *tūla* cotton. Next, it should be further wrapped in fine, soft white woolen cloth.

Cotton wool was wrapped around the Tathāgata’s body, and he was then placed into the golden coffin. Furthermore, fragrant oil was poured into the coffin until it was full, and the lid was closed tightly.
Then, a seven-jeweled chariot was constructed from ox-head sandalwood, aloeswood, and all manner of fragrant woods, adorned with every kind of precious gem.
The jeweled coffin was carried upon this chariot to the site of the cremation, accompanied by countless jeweled banners and pennants.
Innumerable jeweled canopies, jeweled robes, all manner of incense and flowers, and all kinds of music surrounded [the Tathāgata] on every side as they made offerings with profound grief.
All the great assemblies of devas and humans should each perform the cremation using sandalwood.

Once the Tathāgata’s cremation is complete, the fourfold assembly of devas and humans shall collect the relics and place them in vases of the seven precious gems, [and establish them] within that city in four...
A stūpa made of the seven treasures arose in the middle of the thoroughfare. The stūpa opened with four gates and enshrined the śarīra relics.

It was venerated by all devas and humans; it could serve as a field of merit for humans and devas, enabling sentient beings to attain great merit, escape the suffering of the three realms, and enter into true liberation.

Regarding the ritual for constructing a stūpa, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at what location should the Tathāgata be cremated?
The Buddha said, "It may be done outside the city of Kuśinagara. Ānanda further addressed the Buddha, saying, "Once the cremation has been completed..."

"Where shall the stūpa be erected? The Buddha told Ānanda, "It shall be erected at the crossroads within the city of Kuśinagara as a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels, thirteen stories high, topped with a *cakra* (wheel) finial, adorned with an intermingling of all manner of exquisite gems, and decorated with all the wonderful flowers and banners of the world;
its four sides shall have railings adorned with the seven precious jewels."

It was adorned; every kind of ornamentation was applied without exception. On each of the four sides of the stupa, a gate was opened. Between each successive tier, the windows were aligned one with another.
Within it were enshrined the precious caskets containing the Tathāgata’s śarīra, which the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly gazed upon and made offerings to.
At that time, Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying: "How should the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly distribute the Tathāgata’s śarīra?"

[They] offered a beneficial供养 (pūjā). The Buddha said: "All devas and humans shall take the relics of the Buddha and, with a mind of equanimity, distribute them throughout the three realms and all six paths of the world for offerings. Why is this? The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as if they were his only child;
he bestows equal benefit and protection upon the sentient beings of the world, which can cause your merit and virtue to become immeasurable. At that time...
The great assembly of devas and humans wept with sorrow, unable to restrain themselves. The World-Honored One addressed the assembly at large:
"You, devas and humans, do not grieve so greatly. Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his śarīra remains for you to constantly offer worship.
Furthermore, the Dharma Jewel shall remain forever in the world, enabling sentient beings to take refuge with deep sincerity. To make offerings to the śarīra is precisely..."
He beheld the Buddha, who was no different from when he was in the world.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: 'The time for me has now arrived; my entire body..."

"Painful. Having spoken these words, he immediately entered the first dhyāna. From the first dhyāna he emerged and entered the second dhyāna; from the second dhyāna he emerged and entered the third dhyāna;
from the third dhyāna he emerged and entered the fourth dhyāna. From the fourth dhyāna he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite space;
from the sphere of infinite space he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite consciousness; from the sphere of infinite consciousness he emerged and entered the sphere of nothingness.
From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the sphere of nothingness; from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of cessation.

Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he re-enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the sphere of nothingness;

from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. From the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of infinite space. From the sphere of infinite space, he emerges.
From the sphere of emptiness, he entered and emerged from the fourth dhyāna; from the fourth dhyāna, he entered and emerged from the third dhyāna;
from the third dhyāna, he entered and emerged from the second dhyāna; from the second dhyāna, he entered and emerged from the first dhyāna.

At that time, having thus entered and emerged from the various dhyānas in both direct and reverse order, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly: "With my Buddha-eye, I have surveyed all beings throughout the three realms and the six destinies."
The great earth, containing sentient and insentient beings—such as these three realms—are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature and ultimately quiescent, identical in character to empty space.
All dharmas are fundamentally liberated from the original limit of ignorance; though one seeks them throughout the ten directions, they cannot be found, for their root does not exist.
Since the root is absent, all causal branches and leaves are entirely liberated, and thus ignorance is liberated.
Therefore, one attains liberation from everything up to old age and death. For this reason, I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence, which is named Great Nirvana;
thus I enter extinction beneath the twin śāla trees.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states: "At that time, the Buddha was at Kuśinagara in the grove of twin śāla trees, surrounded before and behind by the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas. On the fifteenth day of the second month, he approached his parinirvāṇa."

Having entered various meditative absorptions to instruct the assembly, he lay down on his right side upon a couch made of the seven precious gems, with his head toward the north, his feet pointing south, his face toward the west, and his back toward the east. There were four pairs, or eight trees, of śāla trees surrounding him.
A pair [of trees] stood to the west before the Tathāgata; a pair stood to the east behind the Tathāgata;
a pair stood to the north above the Tathāgata’s head; and a pair stood to the south at the Buddha’s feet.
When midnight arrived and he entered the fourth *dhyāna*, all was silent and without sound. At that very moment, he passed into *parinirvāṇa*. Having entered *nirvāṇa*, that *śāla* grove—
The two pairs in the east and west merged into a single tree; the two pairs in the south and north merged into a single tree.
They hung down and covered the precious couch, sheltering the Tathāgata. At that moment, the trees suddenly turned a dismal white, like white cranes.
Their branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, and trunks all burst asunder and fell away, gradually withering and decaying. At that time, throughout the entire Buddha-world...
The great earth shook violently; all the oceans became turbid, boiling, and surging with waves;
all rivers, streams, brooks, torrents, springs, and sources were completely dried up; and the great earth stood in a state of empty stillness, shrouded in profound darkness.
The brilliant radiance of the sun and moon no longer shone at all. Suddenly, a black wind rose up in fury and shook the earth, fanning up dust and sand that darkened the world.
All the herbs, roots, and medicinal plants were utterly crushed and broken. All the devas filled the void of space.
Lamentation and weeping shook the world. *The Recorded Manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*, Part II (2);
*The Recorded Manifestations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*, Part II (3).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Bǎochéng of Bào'ēn Temple.
The *Vajrapāṇi-vajrānurāga-sūtra* states:

At that time, when the World-Honored One was first entering nirvana, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada saw the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and, overcome with grief and distress, spoke these words: "The Tathāgata abandons me and enters..."
Regarding this state of cessation: from this day forth, I am without refuge, without reliance, without protection, and without guardianship.
Misfortune, affliction, and calamities have suddenly gathered all at once; the poisoned arrow of sorrow has deeply pierced my heart. To whom shall I entrust this vajra-pestle for its protection?
Who will immediately cast it aside? From now on, whom shall I serve? Who will show me compassion and instruct me? Furthermore...
"At what time shall we behold the Honored One’s countenance and hear his various words, longing for the Tathāgata? Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Malla:
"Why do you not now recall the few words spoken by the World-Honored One? The Buddha said: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
nothing remains. They cannot be relied upon as they are subject to change; all that is gathered must eventually disperse and perish. High...
That which meets must inevitably part; that which is born must inevitably die.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like trees on a steep riverbank, or like drawings upon water that vanish as soon as they are made.
They are like bubbles on the water or dew upon a blade of grass, unable to remain for long. Human life is as swift as an arrow shot from a bow.
Traversing the world with speed as swift as the sun and moon, the life of a human being passes even more rapidly than that.
One should understand and realize that impermanence brings about ruin and decay. If there is anything remaining to be accomplished in the Buddha’s work, he will not enter *nirvāṇa*.

Only when the Buddha’s work is fully completed will he enter *nirvāṇa*. He entrusts this Buddha-dharma to devas and humans; all those whose suffering has been exhausted shall no longer undergo rebirth.
"You all should not give rise to great sorrow and distress.
The *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, concerning the dream of the Buddha’s mother, states: At that time, the Buddha’s mother Mahāmāyā beheld five [omens] in the heavens."
The signs of decline appeared: first, the flowers upon his head withered; second, sweat broke out from beneath his armpits; third, the light from the crown of his head vanished;
fourth, his two eyes blinked repeatedly; fifth, he took no pleasure in his own seat. Furthermore, during that night, he experienced five kinds of evil dreams:
first, he dreamed that Mount Sumeru collapsed and the waters of the four oceans dried up; second, he dreamed of various rākṣasas holding... in their hands.
Sharp swords vied with one another to gouge out the eyes of all sentient beings. At that time, a black wind blew, causing all the rākṣasas to flee in haste toward the Snowy Mountains.
In the third dream, the various devas of the desire and form realms suddenly lost their jeweled crowns and snapped their necklaces;
they could not remain on their seats, and their bodies lacked radiance, appearing like a mass of ink. In the fourth dream, the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels was...

From atop a high banner, precious jewels rained down constantly, providing for all beings. Four venomous dragons spat fire from their mouths, blowing the banner down and sucking up the wish-fulfilling jewel;
a fierce and violent evil wind then blew it away, submerging it in a deep abyss.
In the fifth dream, five lions descended from the sky, biting Māyā’s breast and entering her left side; her body and mind were in pain as if she had been struck by a blade.
A sword. At that time, having seen this dream, Mahāmāyā was immediately startled awake and spoke these words:
"During my sleep just now, I suddenly beheld these inauspicious omens, which cause my body and mind to suffer extreme distress.
These five kinds of evil dreams are most terrifying; they must concern my son, the Śākya Tathāgata."
This was an evil omen of his entry into parinirvāṇa. He then related in detail to the other devaputras the events he had witnessed in his dream.
[He then] ascended to heaven to inform his mother.
The *Mahāmāyā-sūtra* states: The Venerable Aniruddha ascended to the heavens and, dwelling in the presence of Mahāmāyā, spoke these verses:

"The Great Master, the most supreme among gods, the one who skillfully guides all the world, has now been swallowed by the great makara fish of impermanence within the ocean. He is in the kingdom of Kuśinagara."
"Between the twin trees in the Śāla grove, he shall soon depart through the eastern gate of the city; there, with various offerings, he shall be cremated.
The eight classes of devas and humans will fill the air, their wailing shaking the three thousandfold world system to its core.
Having heard this verse, Mahāmāyā fainted and fell to the ground; after a long while she regained consciousness and spoke these words: "Last night, I obtained..."
Fifth, as for the evil dream: one should know with certainty that the Buddha is entering *nirvāṇa*. Now, indeed, Aniruddha has come and said he has already passed into extinction.
How bitter it is that the Eye of the World is extinguished! How swift it is that the merit of gods and humans is exhausted!
How can he enter *nirvāṇa* all at once? The evil thief of impermanence is exceedingly ferocious; how can he bear to harm my very life?
The son of the Awakened One then spoke these verses in the midst of the assembly: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas, we have always been mother and son;
now that you have attained perfect enlightenment, this bond is finally severed. Yet, even so, you shall enter parinirvāṇa this very day.
It is like a great and lofty tree upon which many birds dwell together; at dawn they each depart, but at evening they return."
"I have gathered with you as mother and child, together beneath the tree of birth and death. Now that we have attained the fruit of the Way, this root source shall be forever severed.
Furthermore, having entered parinirvāṇa, there will be no time when we meet again. Having spoken these verses, Mahāmāyā wept and lamented, unable to restrain her grief.
The *Buddhamātṛ-māyā-puṣpa-vyūha-sūtra* states: At that time, Mahāmāyā, surrounded by a retinue of celestial maidens, descended from the sky and approached the site of the coffin.
Shedding tears in profound grief, she spoke these words: "Together with [him] in the past, for immeasurable..."
"Throughout kalpas we have long been mother and child, never having parted for even a moment. Yet today, all at once, there is no hope of seeing one another again.
Alas, how tragic! The merit of sentient beings is exhausted; as they are now about to fall into confusion, who shall provide guidance?
I shall immediately scatter celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers upon the coffin."
And he spoke these verses: "Now, within these twin trees, the assembly of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings hear only the sound of weeping;

they do not know what is being said, for none can understand their words. Filling the ground, those who were mother and child to you have, through kalpas of accumulated affection, now been scattered by the wind of impermanence to various places. May all sentient beings dwelling in suffering..."
"I longed for the nectar of the Dharma. Why then have you now so swiftly entered nirvana? Lying hidden within your heavy coffin, do you know that I have come here?
Having spoken this verse, he looked toward the Tathāgata’s saṃghāṭī robe, alms bowl, and mendicant’s staff;
grasping them with his right hand, he struck his head with his left and threw his entire body to the ground like a collapsing great mountain, wailing in grief.
Falling into a state of profound grief, he spoke these words: "My son formerly clung to these things, which brought vast merit and benefited the world, bringing welfare to gods and humans.
Now these objects are empty and without a master. Alas! How bitter! The pain is beyond description.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, the fourfold assembly, and the Buddha’s mother, Mahāmāyā, were likewise filled with such sorrow and distress. Their grief increased even further.
Overcome with grief, tears fell from her like rain.
Then, as the *Māyā-sūtra* states,
at that time the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural power, caused the lid of the coffin to open of its own accord.
He then rose from within the coffin with palms joined, displaying the majestic and vigorous bearing of a lion king first emerging from its den.

From the pores of his body, he emitted a thousand rays of light; from each ray of light emerged a thousand transformation Buddhas, all of whom joined their palms toward Mahāmāyā and addressed her in a soft, Brahma-like voice, inquiring after her well-being: "You have traveled a great distance to descend here to this Jambudvīpa."
"Ti! It is the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that such is their course; pray do not weep. He then spoke a verse to his mother:
"Among all fields of merit, the field of the Buddha is supreme. Among all women, the precious jade-woman (*strī-ratna*) is supreme.
May the son born of me surpass all others without peer, Able to give rise to the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha throughout the three times. Therefore, I [follow] from..."
The coffin was raised. With palms joined in reverence, they joyfully offered praise to repay the kindness of her birth and to manifest their feelings of filial devotion.
"Though all Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, the Treasures of Dharma and Saṅgha abide forever. May our mother not grieve; observe closely the nature of impermanence.
When Mahāmāyā heard these verses, she was somewhat comforted; her countenance briefly brightened like a blooming lotus. At that time...
The World-Honored One took leave of his mother and spoke these verses: "Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life is firmly established;
what was to be done has all been accomplished; there is no further existence to be undergone. May you, Mother, comfort yourself; there is no need for bitter grief or distress."
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss.
After the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he immediately closed the coffin. The entire trichiliocosm shook throughout.
Māyā circumambulated the coffin and returned to the heavens.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its latter section, states: "At that time, all the people within the city of Kuśinagara wept and shed tears."

They entered the city together and immediately fashioned a golden coffin adorned with the seven precious gems. They prepared exquisite white woolen cloth, sandalwood, aloeswood, and all manner of miscellaneous incenses, along with immeasurable fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies.
With tears streaming from their eyes in sorrow, they brought these offerings to the Buddha’s location to present them in worship.
At that time, the great assembly wailed and choked with grief; their tears filled their eyes, and their lamentation shook the great trichiliocosm.

With deep and profound reverence, each person wrapped their hands in white woolen cloth and assisted the Tathāgata into the golden coffin. Once fragrant oil was poured to full capacity, they immediately closed the coffin doors.
At that time, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, out of a desire for merit and with virtuous minds, collectively sought to encompass the Tathāgata’s virtues;
they did not allow the great assembly of devas and humans to lift the Buddha together.

The coffin. They then deliberated together and dispatched four strong men, peerless in their physical might, to remove the garments they were wearing and, with focused resolve, request that they lift the holy coffin of the Tathāgata.
Desiring to enter the city to personally extend their offerings, they exerted all their supernatural power, yet were unable to move it.
At that time, eight more powerful strong men from within the city were sent to the location of the Buddha’s coffin. They removed the garments they were wearing...
They removed their robes and together lifted the golden coffin; yet, even by exhausting all their supernatural powers, they could not move it.

The city of Kuśinagara again dispatched sixteen great strongmen to the site of the coffin. They stripped off the garments they were wearing and together lifted the Buddha’s coffin, but still it could not be moved.
At that time, Pukkusa said to the strongmen: "Even if all the men and women within this city were to exert themselves to the utmost..."
"Small ones! Even when they attempted to lift the Tathāgata’s coffin to enter the city, they were unable to do so; how much less could you all possibly move the Tathāgata’s coffin?
The golden coffin raised itself up."

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states: "At that time, the World-Honored One, with great compassion universally covering all, caused all beings in the world to attain a mind of equanimity and receive blessings without distinction.
Within the Śāla grove, he personally raised his coffin and ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
He slowly traveled through the sky, entering the western gate of Kuśinagara and exiting through the eastern gate."
He circled to the right in the air and entered through the southern gate of the city. Gradually traveling through the air, he exited through the northern gate.

Mounting into the air, he circled to the left and re-entered through the western gate. Moving slowly through the air, he exited through the eastern gate. Traveling through the air, he circled to the left and entered through the northern gate of the city.
Gradually traveling through the air, he exited through the southern gate. Mounting into the air, he circled to the right and returned to enter through the western gate, just as before.
Thus they circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara to the left and right for seven rounds.
At that time, as the Tathāgata’s golden coffin made of the seven precious gems was entering the city, the entire great assembly wailed and choked with sobs.

Each person held countless exquisite pieces of fragrant wood—sandalwood, aloeswood, and all manner of precious incenses—which perfumed the entire world. They also carried countless jeweled banners and streamers.
Taking incense, flowers, and necklaces, they proceeded to the site of the cremation and made offerings with deep sorrow.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and the various hosts of devas each held celestial precious incense and made offerings with grief.

Then the Tathāgata’s great and holy jeweled coffin gradually moved through the air to the site of the cremation; slowly descending from the sky, it was placed upon a bed of the seven treasures. Thereupon—

After another seven days had passed, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, along with a vast multitude of countless people, again brought incense and flowers to the front of the Buddha’s coffin, prostrating themselves in worship and making offerings. The entire assembly wailed and wept in profound grief.
The world shook, and people fell to the ground in confusion and distress.

The *Buddha-xian-shuang-zu-chu-tai-jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha Manifesting His Two Feet at Birth) states: "At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his majestic spiritual power; within the golden coffin, he was silent and still."
The devas offered worship by burning incense and scattering flowers. Mahākāśyapa, leading five hundred disciples from the kingdom of Magadha, arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa that day, he wept and wailed, unable to restrain himself.
The World-Honored One, hearing Kāśyapa’s arrival with his divine ear, immediately extended both feet from within the coffin. When Kāśyapa saw them, he...
With her hands she grasped and stroked [the Buddha's body], weeping so uncontrollably that she could not restrain herself. Kāśyapa spoke in verse, saying: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
Those who are born must inevitably die. Without birth, there is no death; This cessation is the supreme bliss.

The Buddha’s teaching has been entered, And those to be delivered have been fully encompassed. I travel this path in utter solitude; In deep regret, I do not see the Buddha. The entire Dharma-realm..."
"All are empty; the physical body shall likewise be so. It is without old age, sickness, or death; it is unconditioned and unborn.

Though one may dwell for a lifespan as vast as a hundred Ganges-sands, one must ultimately return to extinction. How much more so for me, the Celestial Honored Teacher, who dwelt in this world and was subject to defilement?
At that time, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples circumambulated the golden coffin seven times and stood to one side. Ānanda held the coffin toward the west.
At the northern corner, Nanda held the coffin at the northeast corner. The various devas followed behind, together lifting the golden coffin.
They proceeded forty-nine paces from the twin trees and set the golden coffin down for enshrinement. The devas and people piled ox-head sandalwood incense upon the golden coffin.
The Brahma Kings and Śakra-devānām-indra, leading the hosts of devas, stood in the void and scattered flowers.
As they made their offerings, at that time Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples’ bodies trembled so violently that they could not support themselves;
their minds became turbid and bewildered, and they broke into loud, bitter weeping.
Regarding the fact that ordinary fire does not ignite [the coffin], the *Latter Part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"At that time, the entire assembly of devas and humans together lifted the Great Sage’s precious coffin of the Tathāgata and placed it upon the incense pavilion. Simultaneously, they wailed and wept. At that time, within the city of Kuśinagara, there were four..."
A strongman, his body adorned with jeweled ornaments, held a seven-jeweled torch as large as a chariot wheel, its blazing light illuminating everywhere.
He attempted to cremate the Tathāgata by casting the torch into the incense tower, but the flame was naturally extinguished upon reaching it. Kāśyapa said:
"The precious coffin of the Great Sage cannot be burned even by the torches of the three realms; how much less could it be consumed by your strength? Within the city...

Furthermore, there were eight great *mahābalavegavanta* (powerful giants) who each took torches of the seven precious gems, their flames blazing in all directions, and threw them toward the location of the coffin;

yet they too were all extinguished. Within the city, there were again sixteen extremely powerful giants, each holding a great torch of the seven precious gems, who came and threw them at the incense tower;
these too were entirely extinguished. Within the city, there were again thirty-six extremely powerful giants, each...
They brought great torches of the seven precious gems and cast them into the fragrant tower, yet they were all extinguished.

At that time, all the sea deities took up countless flaming torches of the seven precious gems from the fire within the ocean and cast them into the fragrant tower, yet they too were all extinguished.
Then Kāśyapa addressed the Mallas and the entire assembly: "You should know that even if all the devas..."
"The torches possessed by all people cannot cremate the precious coffin of the Tathāgata; you need not trouble yourselves with such strenuous efforts.
At that time, the men, women, devas, humans, and the great assembly within the city again mourned deeply.

Each offered the incense and flowers they held while wailing and weeping in worship. Simultaneously, they prostrated and circumambulated it seven times to the right, their cries of lamentation resounding loudly.
The great trichiliocosm shook; those who were deluded and unconscious fell to the ground.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states: "At that time, by the power of his great compassion, the Tathāgata caused fire to surge forth from within his chest."
Outside the coffin, the cremation proceeded gradually over the course of seven days; it was only after the Incense Pavilion had been burned that the fire was finally extinguished.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings each thought to themselves: "I shall douse the fire with scented water to extinguish it, and quickly collect the relics to offer them in the heavens.
Having formed this thought, they simultaneously descended, each holding a vase made of the seven precious gems filled to the brim with scented water.
Upon arriving at the site of the cremation, the Four Heavenly Kings poured the fragrant water from their golden jars onto the fire all at once.

Once poured, the intensity of the flames increased even further, and they were not extinguished at all. At that time, the ocean deity Sāgara, the Dragon King, along with the deities of the rivers and streams, seeing that the fire would not be extinguished, each thought to themselves:
"I shall take fragrant water and pour it onto the fire to extinguish it. They hurriedly gathered their belongings.
Having made this reflection, they each took precious vases filled with scented water and went to the site of the cremation, pouring the water onto the fire all at once.
Yet, although the water was poured, the intensity of the fire remained as before and did not extinguish at all. Then Loutou addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"Your greed is great. You dwell in the heavens; if you were to take the relics alone and ascend to heaven..."
“Palaces! How can those dwelling on earth go there to make offerings? He spoke again to the sea deity:
“You are in the great ocean and rivers; if you were to take the Tathāgata’s relics alone, how could those dwelling on earth go there to make offerings?
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all repented and each returned to their celestial palaces. At that time...
The Sāgara Dragon King of the great ocean, as well as the deities of the rivers and streams, all likewise repented. Truly, it was as the Holy One had said.
Having repented, they each returned to their own palaces.
Regarding the distribution of the *śarīra*, the *Caturmahārājakāyika-garbha-sūtra* states: "At that time, there were eight great kings:

King Udayana, King Mūrdhaja, King Duṣyanta, King Ajātaśatru, the four lords of military forces, the most preeminent lord of military forces, the lord of military forces of handsome countenance, and the lord of military forces of blazing splendor."
The General of the Army and the Vajra General of the Army—these eight great kings contended for the śarīra.
Each led his own host and stood apart on one side, each saying, "I alone should obtain the Buddha’s śarīra. The minister Upagika admonished them, saying:
"O Kings, do not dispute. The śarīra should be divided so that all may offer worship. Śakra Devānām Indra manifested in human speech and said, "We gods, too, should have a portion.
The Naga King Anavatapta, the Naga King Mucilinda, and the Naga King Elāpattra said, "We, too, should have a portion. Upāgi said, "Gentlemen, wait! The śarīra should..."
They divided it together, making three portions: one portion for the devas, one portion for the nāga kings, and one portion for the eight kings.
A golden jar with a capacity of over ten *shi* was used; this minister coated the interior of the jar with honey and used the jar as a measure to divide the śarīra.
The devas obtained their share of the śarīra and returned to the heavens to erect a stūpa; the nāgas obtained their share of the śarīra and returned to the dragon realm.
The palace erected a stūpa. The eight kings obtained the śarīra relics and each returned to their own country to erect stūpas.
Upagika erected a stūpa for three pecks of śarīra relics in a golden urn, including the urn itself. For the forty-nine bushels of ash and soil, he erected forty-nine stūpas.
At the site where the cremation took place, he also erected a precious stūpa forty-nine *zhang* high, making offerings of incense, lamps, and suspended silk banners.

Banners and canopies were displayed, and music continued without interruption throughout the day and night. By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, light was emitted at night no different from that of the day.
Divine kings constantly provided protection.

The *Dachaitian jing* (Sūtra on Entering the Womb) concerning the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka states: Seven days and seven nights after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa addressed the five hundred arhats, saying:
"You five hundred persons must all go to the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions. Then the arhats...

Gather here all together! The Buddha has now entered parinirvāṇa and his cremation is complete. Desiring to expound the Dharma-body of the Buddha’s true nature, you must assemble quickly to hear these subtle and wondrous words.
By means of their supernormal powers, they reached the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions;
having gathered the Arhats, a multitude of eighty-four million came to assemble here. Ānanda!

With single-minded concentration, he contemplated until all defilements were extinguished; he attained great enlightenment with radiant clarity. The assembly of noble ones praised him, and the devas sang songs of praise.

Ānanda then ascended the high seat. Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying: "Regarding the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, you must be careful not to allow even a single word or a single syllable to be omitted.
Compile the Bodhisattva Piṭaka into one collection, and likewise compile the Śrāvaka Piṭaka."
[The teachings] were compiled in one place; the Vinaya Piṭaka was likewise compiled and recorded in one place. At that time, Ānanda raised his voice and proclaimed: "Thus have I heard:
at one time, the Buddha and [the assembly] were dwelling in such-and-such a place. Kāśyapa and all the noble assembly wept and lamented, unable to restrain themselves, exclaiming:
"Alas! Old age and death are like an illusion, like a magical transformation. Yesterday we saw the Buddha, and today..."

Having already stated "Thus have I heard," the first collection of sutras emerging from the womb is the *Tsa-pao-tsang* (Miscellaneous Treasury). Second is the *Chung-yin-tsang* (Intermediate State Treasury).
Third is the *Mo-ho-yen Fang-ting-tsang* (Mahāyāna Vaipulya Treasury). Fourth is the *Chieh-lü-tsang* (Vinaya Treasury). Fifth is the *Shih-chu P'u-sa-tsang* (Ten Stages Bodhisattva Treasury).
Sixth is the *Tsa-tsang* (Miscellaneous Treasury). Seventh is the *Chin-kang-tsang* (Vajra Treasury). Eighth is the *Fo-tsang* (Buddha Treasury). These constitute the teachings of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha’s sutras and Dharma are complete.
Regarding the construction of the stupa by King Aśoka, the *Aśokarāja-avadāna* states: At that time, King Aśoka went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery and approached the Elder Ya...
He stepped forward, joined his palms, and said, "I shall now construct eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas within Jambudvīpa.
The Elder replied, "Excellent, excellent! If Your Majesty wishes for the stupas to be completed all at once, I shall shield the sun with my hand while the Great King constructs them;
let it be proclaimed throughout the realm that when the sun is shielded by my hand, they must all be finished."

The stūpas were erected. Having heard these words, the king returned to his palace and immediately fashioned eighty-four thousand precious caskets, adorning them with gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Within each precious casket, he placed one relic.
He further fashioned eighty-four thousand precious urns, eighty-four thousand precious parasols, and eighty-four thousand bolts of brocade for decoration. Each relic...
The yakṣa Li-fu dispatched messengers throughout Jambudvīpa to construct a precious stūpa at every location where there were one hundred million people.
Thereupon, the spirits each took a portion of the śarīra and went forth in the four directions to erect stūpas.
One yakṣa, carrying a single śarīra, arrived at the kingdom of Takṣaśilā intending to build a precious stūpa. The people of that country said, "In our kingdom, the common people..."
"Thirty-six *koṭis*. Now you must give me thirty-six caskets. At that time, the yakṣa returned and reported all the aforementioned matters to the king.
The king thought to himself, "The multitude of people is vast. If it were done in this way, the relics would not suffice to fill Jambudvīpa.
I must employ a skillful means to withhold them. He then dispatched the yakṣa again and spoke to him, saying:
"Place one relic in each of one hundred million locations and erect a jeweled stupa for each. The King further declared: 'In one hundred million places, provide one relic;
in fewer than one hundred million places, do not provide any at all.'"

Regarding King Aśoka’s acquisition of the jewels, the *Aśokarājāvadāna* states: After King Aśoka had completed the construction of the eighty-four thousand precious stupas, the King of Siṃhala presented him with five wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*).
Having received the jewels, the king bestowed one upon the stupa of the Buddha Jāti and another upon the stupa of the Buddha [Śākyamuni].
The Stūpa of Attaining Enlightenment; third, the Stūpa of the Buddha Turning the Wheel of Dharma; fourth, the Stūpa of the Buddha Entering Nirvana.
Having one remaining pearl which he wished to give to the ladies of the court, yet fearing that if he gave it to one they would resent it, he sent a messenger into the palace and said:
Whosoever possesses the most excellent garments and ornaments should be given this jewel. All the ladies-in-waiting were dressed in fine clothes and adorned with ornaments;
however, there was one junior lady named Sujātā who, mindful of the Buddha’s words regarding the precepts, refrained from wearing clothes and ornaments.
Having observed the eight precepts, she wore pure white garments, her deportment being perfectly composed and dignified. The King’s heart [was moved] of its own accord.
Nevertheless, he felt great reverence. King Aśoka observed the attire and ornaments of the queens and concubines in succession;
when he came to Queen Sujaṭā, he asked: "All the other ladies are dressed in fine garments; why are you wearing plain clothes and remaining so silent? Queen Sujaṭā replied:
"The Buddha has said that modesty and shame are the finest garments, and the observance of the precepts is [the true ornament]."
"Necklaces [are made of] the sound of the Dharma; I now observe the eight precepts as my necklaces and wear the pure garments of shame and remorse.
Reciting the scriptures serves as my music. When the King heard these words, he was filled with joy and delight.
He spoke again to his consort, saying: "I have previously declared that to whoever wears the foremost, supreme garments and necklaces, I shall grant [a reward]."

"Precious jewel! You are now the foremost; I give this precious jewel to you. When the other ladies-in-waiting saw that she had received the precious jewel, they subsequently all emulated her and undertook the observance of the eight precepts.
The *Dharmaguptaka-dharmakośa-sūtra* (付法藏經) states: When Mahākāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the most supreme Dharma to Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable One, you should know that formerly the World-Honored One entrusted the Dharma to me; I am now aged and decrepit, and am about to enter parinirvāṇa."
“Ānanda, I now wish to entrust to you the supreme eye of the world. You should diligently guard and protect this Dharma.
Ānanda replied, “So be it; I shall receive your instruction. Thereupon, Ānanda expounded the sublime Dharma to transform all sentient beings.

Indeed, due to his great merit from past lives, his wisdom was profound and vast, and he was widely learned and profoundly insightful. He was praised by the Buddha as foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
First: He was able to receive and uphold the entire Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, just as the great vast ocean receives the waters of a hundred rivers.
His fame was lofty and far-reaching, known by all; such merits were inexhaustible. I shall now explain the causes and conditions accordingly.
In a past age, during the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, he was a śramaṇa who kept a śrāmaṇera and instructed him to recite.
He recited [the scriptures], exhorting and instructing day and night without ceasing or slackening. If there was even the slightest omission in the recitation, he would immediately reprimand him.
At that time, this śrāmaṇera focused his mind on reading and reciting; from then on, he mastered the meaning of the sutras.
His wisdom became profound and subtle, his dhāraṇī-retention and memory powerful, and his vast learning immeasurable. The śrāmaṇera of that time was none other than myself, Mahākāśyapa.
The Venerable [Kāśyapa] said to Ānanda: "I now entrust this Jewel of the Dharma to you.
Elder, should you later enter nirvana, there is in the great city of Rājagṛha a householder named Śāṇakavāsin. He is of lofty talent, courageous, and possesses great wisdom;
he has already planted deep roots of merit in the past. He shall build a monastery for the Buddha, and you should ordain him as a monk. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
He entrusted the entire Dharma-treasury to him.

Regarding Kāśyapa entering meditative absorption, the *A-yü-wáng-zhuàn* (Aśokarājāvadāna) states: "After the Venerable Kāśyapa had completed the compilation of the Dharma-treasury, he entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda."

"I now wish to enter *nirvāṇa*. I entrust the Dharma to you; guard it well. Kāśyapa then went to King Ajātaśatru to bid him farewell and said to the gatekeeper, "Mahākāśyapa wishes to enter *nirvāṇa*; he has come to inform you.
At that time, Kāśyapa arrived at Mount Kukkuṭapāda among the Three Peaks, sat down upon the grass, and thought to himself: "I..."

Now, wearing the *pāṃśukūla* robes given by the Buddha and carrying his own bowl and robes, [Kāśyapa] remains until the appearance of Maitreya so that his body shall not decay, allowing all the disciples of Maitreya to behold him. At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways.
Just as Kāśyapa was about to enter meditative absorption, he thought: "When Ānanda and King Ajātaśatru come, this mountain shall..."
He opened it for him so that he might enter; when he was about to depart, the mountain closed once more. Śakra Devānām Indra scattered celestial incense and flowers as an offering to Kāśyapa.
Having paid homage and made offerings, the mountain immediately closed of its own accord, covering the Venerable One’s body.
The deity of this mountain cave is named Piṇḍola. Seeing that Kāśyapa had entered parinirvāṇa, he spoke these words: "Today, the Mountain of Dharma..."
All is in ruins. The Dharma-ship has sunk; the Dharma-tree has been toppled; the Dharma-ocean has run dry.
Today all the māras rejoice greatly, while all devas and humans weep with sorrowful longing. At that time, King Ajātaśatru dreamed that the celestial beam had broken and collapsed.
Having awakened, his heart was filled with alarm and fear. The gatekeepers came and informed the king, saying, "Just now, Kāśyapa arrived and announced that he wished to enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, the king went with Ānanda to Mount Kukkuṭapāda; the mountain opened of its own accord.
Having made offerings and prostrations, they returned with tears in their eyes.

Regarding Śāṇakavāsin receiving the Dharma, the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (or *Fu fazang jing*) states: At that time, as Ānanda was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Śāṇakavāsin, saying: "The Buddha..."
The Dharma-eye was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa; Kāśyapa entrusted the Dharma to me; and I now entrust this treasury of the Dharma to you.
You must diligently guard and protect this Dharma, so that all sentient beings may partake of the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Śāṇakavāsin replied, "I accept your instruction. I shall protect such a sublime Dharma and act as a great bright lamp for the sake of all beings."
Thereupon, he extensively bestowed the unsurpassed medicine of the Dharma to treat the disease of afflictions and deliver all sentient beings. His virtue was lofty and far-reaching;
having long cultivated vows and practices, he possessed vast learning, dhāraṇī-retention, and inexhaustible eloquence. Now, I shall expound upon that mass of his merits.

In the distant past, during a previous kalpa, I was a merchant leader. Seeing a Pratyekabuddha afflicted by a grave illness, his vital energy and life-force exhausted and feeble, I halted there with my fellow merchants.
We sought out physicians and medicines to treat him, serving him with all our hearts so that he lacked for nothing.
His illness was subsequently cured and his strength fully restored. This Pratyekabuddha was wearing a saṃghāṭī robe.
The merchant leader offered him exquisite garments and addressed him, saying, "Great Sage, these Śāṇa robes are extremely coarse and worn;
I pray that you will accept the clothing I have offered. The Pratyekabuddha said, "Donor, you should know:
it was with these very robes that I left the household life and attained the Way, and it is with these again that I shall enter Nirvāṇa. Ānanda then entrusted the Dharma to him.
He said, "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Mathurā, he looked at me and commanded:

'In this country there is a son of a householder named Upagupta. After my parinirvāṇa, he will bring about great benefit; you should later deliver him, cause him to leave the household life, and entrust him with the treasury of the Dharma.'"
The *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (or *Dharmagupta-cūḍā-saṃkhyāna*) and the *Dharmaguptaka-dharmagaṇḍī-sūtra* state: The Venerable Ānanda entrusted the Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin and addressed him, saying:
"In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Mathurā, he charged me with these words: 'In this country there is an elder named Gupta.'"
His son was named Upagupta. After my parinirvāṇa, he will bring about great benefit and convert immeasurable sentient beings;

you should cause him to renounce the world. When the time for your own nirvāṇa arrives, entrust the Dharma-treasury to him. Śāṇakavāsin, wishing to transmit the Dharma to him, observed whether Gupta had fathered a son.
Entering meditative concentration and reflecting, he knew that one had not yet appeared in the world. He then went to...
Guptaśaya. Gupta asked, "Why are you alone without a companion? He replied, "Householder, I have no stipend;
I shall only be accompanied by one who has left the household life out of faith. Gupta spoke again, "I delight in worldly affairs and cannot leave the household life.
However, if a son is later born to me, I shall offer him to you. Later, a son was born named Upagupta, who at the age of twelve—
Śreṇika was skilled in market transactions. Upāli approached him and preached the Dharma to him.
Gradually, through skillful means, he instructed him to practice mindfulness, using black and white pebbles as counters: whenever an evil thought arose, he was to drop a black pebble;
whenever a wholesome thought arose, he was to drop a white pebble. Upagupta respectfully received and upheld this instruction.

He maintained mindfulness without distraction. Whenever a thought of good or evil arose, he would immediately cast a stone into the bowl. At first, the black stones predominated while the white ones were few. As he gradually practiced, the white and black became equal.
By not ceasing to fix his mindfulness, his mind became increasingly pure; there were no more black stones, only white ones.
His wholesome thoughts having flourished, he attained the first fruit of the path. Śāṇakavāsin then entrusted him [with the teaching], saying: "You..."
One should guard it.
The *Buddhamitra-dhvaja-parigraha-dharmakośa-sūtra* states: The Venerable Buddhamitra thought to himself, "My teacher Nandi has entrusted the Dharma to me."
"I, how shall I proclaim the True Dharma so that all sentient beings may universally obtain benefit?
He further thought, "This king now possesses great wrong views; I should go there first to subdue him. He personally carried a red banner and walked before the king.
The king asked, "Who is this person walking before me? He replied, "Great King, I am a wise man skilled in..."
He was capable of debate and desired to seek a trial before the king. At that time, the king issued a proclamation:
"Let all the brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders within the realm who are intelligent, erudite, and skilled in speech assemble in my palace to engage in discussion with a śramaṇa.
Thereupon, all the heterodox followers of false views vied with one another to come and gather like clouds.

At that time, the great king had spread carpets and cushions upon the main throne hall. Maitreya immediately ascended the Dharma seat and engaged in debate with the various non-Buddhists using boundless arguments.
Those of shallow intelligence were defeated by a single word; those who possessed much cleverness and eloquence had their arguments exhausted after a second exchange.
Seeing that all these men were reduced to logical bankruptcy, the king personally entered into discussion with Maitreya, beginning the debate himself.
When the speaker’s arguments were exhausted, Guṇamati thought to himself, "In debating with the king, I should not manifest my own superiority.
He then said to him, "The depth and shallowness of this meaning, Your Majesty, you yourself understand. At that moment, the king realized he had been defeated;

he turned away from his heterodox mind, took refuge in the True Dharma with reverence and faith, accepted the Three Refuges as a disciple of the Buddha, and propagated [the teaching] throughout his own kingdom.
Through the transformation of the Way, at that time five hundred followers of the heretical Nirgrantha teachers in this country came to the place of Maitreya and all went forth together as monks.
Aśvaghoṣa was thus defeated in debate.
The *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (Fu fǎzàng jīng) states: There was a Mahāsattva named Aśvaghoṣa, whose wisdom was profound and discerning, and whose superior insight transcended all others.
There was no difficult question he could not refute or subdue. He maintained that a real self exists and was exceedingly arrogant.

However, he heard that there was a Venerable One named Pūrṇaśa, whose wisdom was deep and far-reaching, who was widely learned and profoundly erudite, and who taught that all dharmas are empty, devoid of self, and devoid of person.
With a mind of contempt, he went to him and spoke these words: "I can destroy all the discourses of the entire world, like hailstones crushing grass.
If these words of mine are false and not truthful, I shall surely cut out my own tongue to atone for my offense.
Puṇṇaśa said: "Within the Buddha-dharma there are generally two truths. If one proceeds according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)..."
"I" is merely a provisional designation; in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all things are entirely empty and quiescent. When sought in this manner, how could a "self" ever be found?
At that time, Aśvaghoṣa’s mind was not yet subdued; relying on his own intellectual acumen, he still considered himself superior. Puṇṇa said to him:
"Reflect carefully; do not speak falsely. Let us now determine for certain who is superior. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa thought to himself:
"Conventional truth is a mere designation and is certainly not real; the nature of ultimate truth is further empty and quiescent."
"Since these two truths are both unattainable, and as they do not exist at all, how can they be destroyed? I am now certainly inferior to him;
I wish to cut out my tongue to apologize for my defeat. Pūrṇa said, "My Dharma is compassionate; there is no need to cut out your tongue.
You should rather shave your head and become my disciple. Thereupon, the Venerable One ordained him and caused him to leave the household life.

And he addressed him, saying: "I entrust this treasury of the Dharma to you for your keeping. You should, in the future, receive and uphold it with a sincere heart, so that all beings in future ages may universally benefit."
Regarding Nāgārjuna’s composition of the treatises, the *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (Fu fazang jing) states: The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa transmitted the Dharma to the Elder Vīra.
As Vīra was about to pass away, he entrusted the Dharma-treasury to a great being named Nāgārjuna and thereafter relinquished his life. Subsequently, Nāgārjuna extensively [propagated it].

He circulated the Eye of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and adorned himself with sublime merit. Possessing celestial acumen and extraordinary insight, he required no second inquiry into matters;
he erected the banner of the Dharma and subdued those of heterodox paths. At that time, the king of South India held deeply erroneous views.
They served non-Buddhist teachers and slandered the True Dharma. To convert them, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna went to the king’s presence.
The king asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am an omniscient one.
The king commanded that all the Brahmins be assembled to engage in extensive debate with the śramaṇa and the various non-Buddhists. When the non-Buddhists heard of this matter, they were alarmed.
They had all come together in great numbers, harboring anger and jealousy as they vied with one another in debate. Thereupon, Nāgārjuna ascended the seat;
those who were ignorant and shallow were defeated by a single word, while those possessing slight intelligence were exhausted in both rhetoric and reasoning after being questioned a second time.
Thus, immeasurable non-Buddhist heretics of false views were all subdued, and they shaved their hair and beards to go forth together into the homeless life. In this manner, it continued...

He turned toward the vast salvation of sentient beings, even unto their being infinite in number. He extensively expounded and analyzed the meaning of the Mahāyāna, composing the *Upadeśa-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses.

Furthermore, he composed treatises such as those on the adornment of the Buddha-way and the skillful means of great compassion, each consisting of five thousand verses, thereby causing the Mahāyāna to shine forth in the world. He also composed the *Abhaya-śāstra*, totaling one hundred thousand verses. Within [this work]...
This treatise, consisting of five hundred verses, originated from the Abhayagiri school. Its exposition of the profound flavor of the meaning subdues all external paths like a victorious banner.
According to the *Biography of Deva* (*Tīpó chuán*), the Bodhisattva Deva was profoundly learned and possessed extraordinary eloquence.
In that country, there was a Mahādeva (Great Lord) whose blessings could fulfill any wish one sought in this present life. Deva went before the deity and said: "The deity..."
Devadatta reflected, "My heart holds that my life is subject to fate. The deity said, "That which I lack is my left eye; if you can give it to me, you may take it out.
Devadatta replied, "I shall respectfully follow the divine mandate," and immediately took the eye from his left hand and gave it to him.
By the power of the deity, as soon as it was removed, it grew back. He continued to demand it without ceasing, taking out dozens of eyes from morning until evening. The deity said:
This is the supreme gift. Whatever wish you seek shall surely be fulfilled according to your aspiration. Having spoken thus, he withdrew.
He donned the shaven-headed robes and, at a crossroads, prepared a high seat and proclaimed these three propositions: "Among all holy ones, the Buddha is the most supreme;
among all dharmas, the Buddha-dharma is the most correct and supreme; among all those who save the world, the Sangha is [the foremost]."
"First: if there is any scholar from the eight directions who is able to refute these words of mine, I shall cut off his head to atone for my defeat.
To establish principles without clarity is the mark of folly; I do not begrudge cutting off my head to atone for my defeat.
When the masters of debate from the eight directions heard these words, they also gathered together and each made a vow, saying: "We are not his equal," as Deva spoke.
"The Dharma I practice sustains all things through benevolence. You should shave your hair and beard to become my disciples;
each of you should compose treatises on names and principles to establish boundless discourses. Those whose words and reasoning are both deficient shall all have their hair shaved and become monks.

Deva was a disciple of Nāgārjuna. Before people had yet placed their faith in him, he sought to propagate the True Dharma; thus, he prayed to the deities and made vows, by which means he established a great [monastery].
In the arena of debate, he subdued all non-Buddhists.

This is a commentary on the *Record of Attaining the Way* composed by Vasubandhu. Regarding the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu: he was the secular younger brother of the Bodhisattva Asaṅga; in the Dharma, [he was his] younger...
The Master had originally belonged to the Sarvāstivāda school; he composed five hundred treatises to clarify the Hīnayāna and refute the Mahāyāna, such that no one in India dared to oppose him.
Asaṅga was a Bodhisattva of the First Ground who, observing that his younger brother’s karmic conditions for the Mahāyāna were nearing maturity, feigned illness to summon him back.

When they had traveled for only one station, he sent a disciple to receive them; that night, they stayed together in the same lodging. During the night, the disciple recited a verse from the Mahāyāna:
"If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm."
